chapters.title: The Golden Bird
paragraphs: A certain king had a beautiful garden, and in the garden grew a tree that bore golden apples. The apples were counted regularly, and just as they were starting to ripen, the king found that one went missing every night. This made him very angry, and he ordered the gardener to watch under the tree all night long. The gardener sent his eldest son to keep watch, but around midnight the young man fell asleep, and by morning another apple was gone. Next the second son was told to watch, and at midnight he fell asleep too, and in the morning another apple had vanished. Then the third son offered to take a turn. At first the gardener refused, afraid some harm might come to him, but in the end he gave in, and the young man lay down under the tree to watch. As the clock struck twelve, he heard a rustling in the air, and a bird of pure gold came flying in. While it was snapping at one of the apples with its beak, the gardener’s son jumped up and shot an arrow at it. The arrow did the bird no harm, though it shook loose a golden feather from its tail before it flew away. In the morning the golden feather was brought to the king, and the whole council was summoned. They all agreed it was worth more than everything the kingdom owned. But the king said, “One feather is no use to me. I must have the whole bird.”

So the gardener’s eldest son set off, sure he would find the golden bird easily. After he had gone a short way, he came to a wood, and at the edge of it he saw a fox sitting. He took up his bow and got ready to shoot. But the fox said, “Don’t shoot me, and I’ll give you good advice. I know what you’re after: you want to find the golden bird. This evening you will reach a village, and there you will see two inns facing each other. One of them is bright and lovely to look at. Don’t go in there. Spend the night in the other, however poor and shabby it seems.” But the son thought, “What could an animal like this know about it?” So he shot his arrow at the fox and missed, and the fox lifted its tail over its back and ran into the wood. The young man went on his way and in the evening reached the village with the two inns. In one of them people were singing, dancing and feasting. The other looked dirty and poor. “I’d be a fool,” he said, “to go into that rundown place and pass up this charming one.” So he went into the grand inn, ate and drank as much as he pleased, and forgot the bird and his own country too.

Time went by, and since the eldest son did not come home and no word of him arrived, the second son set out, and the same thing happened to him. He met the fox, who gave him the same good advice. But when he came to the two inns, his eldest brother was standing at the window of the one where the merrymaking was, and he called to him to come in. The second son could not resist the temptation. He went in, and just like his brother he forgot the golden bird and his country.

More time went by, and now the youngest son wanted to go out into the wide world to look for the golden bird. For a long while his father would not hear of it. He was very fond of this son, and feared that some misfortune would befall him too and keep him from coming back. But the young man would not settle at home, and in the end it was agreed that he could go. When he reached the wood, he met the fox and heard the same good advice. This son was grateful to the fox and did not try to kill it, as his brothers had done. So the fox said, “Sit on my tail, and you’ll travel faster.” He sat down, the fox began to run, and off they went over stock and stone so fast that their hair whistled in the wind.

When they reached the village, the son followed the fox’s advice. Without even looking around, he went to the shabby inn and rested there all night in comfort. In the morning the fox came again and met him as he was setting out. “Go straight ahead,” it said, “until you come to a castle. In front of it a whole troop of soldiers lie fast asleep, snoring. Pay no attention to them. Go into the castle and keep walking until you come to a room where the golden bird sits in a wooden cage. Beside it stands a beautiful golden cage, but don’t try to take the bird out of the plain cage and put it in the fine one, or you’ll be sorry.” Then the fox stretched out its tail again, the young man sat down, and off they went over stock and stone until their hair whistled in the wind.

In front of the castle gate everything was just as the fox had said. The son went in and found the chamber where the golden bird hung in a wooden cage, with the golden cage standing below it, and the three golden apples that had been lost lying close by. Then he thought, “It would be absurd to carry off such a fine bird in this shabby cage.” So he opened the door, took hold of the bird and put it into the golden cage. But the bird let out such a loud scream that all the soldiers woke up. They seized him and carried him before the king. The next morning the court met to judge him, and when everything had been heard, it sentenced him to death, unless he brought the king the golden horse that could run as swiftly as the wind. If he did that, he would be given the golden bird as his own.

So he set out on his journey once more, sighing, in deep despair, when suddenly his friend the fox met him and said, “You see now what has happened because you didn’t listen to my advice. Still, I will tell you how to find the golden horse, if you’ll do as I say. Go straight on until you come to the castle where the horse stands in his stall. The groom will be lying beside him, fast asleep and snoring. Lead the horse away quietly, but be sure to put the old leather saddle on him, and not the golden one that hangs close by.” Then the son sat down on the fox’s tail, and off they went over stock and stone until their hair whistled in the wind.

Everything went well, and the groom lay snoring with his hand on the golden saddle. But when the son looked at the horse, he thought it a great pity to put the leather saddle on it. “I’ll give him the good one,” he said. “I’m sure he deserves it.” As he picked up the golden saddle, the groom woke and shouted so loudly that all the guards ran in and took him prisoner. In the morning he was brought before the court again and sentenced to die. But it was agreed that if he could bring the beautiful princess to them, he would live and be given the bird and the horse as his own.

He went on his way, very sorrowful. But the old fox came to him and said, “Why didn’t you listen to me? If you had, you would have carried off both the bird and the horse. Still, I will give you advice once more. Go straight on, and in the evening you will arrive at a castle. At twelve o’clock at night the princess goes to the bathing-house. Walk up to her and give her a kiss, and she will let you lead her away. But make sure you don’t let her go and say goodbye to her father and mother.” Then the fox stretched out its tail, and off they went over stock and stone until their hair whistled again.

When they reached the castle, everything was as the fox had said. At twelve o’clock the young man met the princess on her way to the bath and kissed her, and she agreed to run away with him. But she begged him, with many tears, to let her say goodbye to her father. At first he refused, but she wept harder and harder and fell at his feet, until at last he gave in. The moment she entered her father’s house, however, the guards woke up, and he was taken prisoner again.

He was brought before the king, who said, “You will never have my daughter unless you dig away, within eight days, the hill that blocks the view from my window.” This hill was so huge that the whole world could not have carried it off. After he had worked for seven days and done very little, the fox came and said, “Lie down and go to sleep. I’ll do the work for you.” In the morning he woke and the hill was gone. He went cheerfully to the king and told him that, now the hill was removed, he must give him the princess.

The king had to keep his word, so the young man and the princess went off together. Then the fox came and said to him, “We’ll have all three: the princess, the horse and the bird.” “Ah,” said the young man, “that would be wonderful, but how can you manage it?”

“If you will only listen,” said the fox, “it can be done. When you come to the king and he asks for the beautiful princess, you must say, ‘Here she is!’ He will be overjoyed. Then you will mount the golden horse they are to give you and reach out your hand to say farewell, but shake hands with the princess last. Then swiftly lift her onto the horse behind you, dig your spurs into his sides, and gallop away as fast as you can.”

All went well. Then the fox said, “When you come to the castle where the bird is, I’ll stay at the door with the princess, and you will ride in and speak to the king. When he sees that it is the right horse, he will bring out the bird. But you must sit still and say you want to look at it, to see whether it is the true golden bird. And when you have it in your hand, ride away.”

This too happened as the fox had said. They carried off the bird, the princess mounted again, and they rode on to a great wood. Then the fox came and said, “Please kill me, and cut off my head and my feet.” But the young man refused to do it. So the fox said, “Then I will at least give you some good advice. Beware of two things: don’t ransom anyone from the gallows, and don’t sit down beside any river.” Then it went away. “Well,” thought the young man, “it’s no hard matter to follow that advice.”

He rode on with the princess until at last he came to the village where he had left his two brothers. There he heard a great noise and uproar, and when he asked what the matter was, the people said, “Two men are about to be hanged.” As he came nearer, he saw that the two men were his brothers, who had turned robbers. So he said, “Is there no way to save them?” But the people said no, unless he were willing to hand over all his money to the scoundrels and buy their freedom. He did not stop to think it over. He paid what was asked, his brothers were released, and they went on with him toward home.

When they came to the wood where the fox had first met them, it was so cool and pleasant that the two brothers said, “Let’s sit down by the river and rest a while, and eat and drink.” He said yes, forgot the fox’s warning, and sat down by the river. While he suspected nothing, they came up behind him, threw him down the bank, took the princess, the horse and the bird, and went home to the king their master. “We won all this by our own efforts,” they said. There was great rejoicing, but the horse would not eat, the bird would not sing, and the princess wept.

The youngest son fell to the bottom of the riverbed. Luckily it was nearly dry, but his bones were almost broken, and the bank was so steep that he could find no way out. Then the old fox came once more and scolded him for not following its advice, since otherwise no harm would have come to him. “Still,” it said, “I can’t leave you here. Grab hold of my tail and hang on tight.” Then it pulled him out of the river, and as he climbed onto the bank, it said to him, “Your brothers have set guards to kill you if they find you in the kingdom.” So he dressed himself as a poor man and came secretly to the king’s court. He had hardly stepped through the doors when the horse began to eat, the bird began to sing, and the princess stopped weeping. Then he went to the king and told him all about his brothers’ treachery. They were seized and punished, and he was given the princess again; and after the king’s death he inherited the kingdom.

A long while later, he went walking one day in the wood, and the old fox met him and begged him with tears in its eyes to kill it and cut off its head and feet. At last he did so, and in an instant the fox was changed into a man. He turned out to be the brother of the princess, who had been lost for many, many years.

chapters.title: Hans in Luck
paragraphs: Some men are born lucky. Everything they do or try to do turns out right—everything that comes their way is pure gain—all their geese are swans—all their cards are trumps—toss them any way you like, and like a cat they will always land on their feet and only move on all the faster. The world may well not think of them as they think of themselves, but what do they care about the world? What can it know about the matter?

Neighbor Hans was one of these fortunate souls. He had slaved away for his master for seven long years. Finally he said, “Master, my time is up. I want to go home and see my poor mother again, so please give me my wages and let me leave.” The master replied, “Hans, you have served me faithfully and well, and your pay will match that: it will be generous.” And he handed him a lump of silver as big as his head.

Hans took out his handkerchief, wrapped the piece of silver in it, slung it over his shoulder, and set off for home. He plodded along lazily, dragging one foot after the other, when a man came into view, trotting merrily along on a fine horse. “Ah,” said Hans out loud, “what a wonderful thing it is to ride! There he sits, as comfortable and cheerful as if he were at home in the chair by his own fire. He never trips over a stone, he saves on shoe leather, and he gets where he’s going without even noticing.” Hans hadn’t spoken quietly enough, and the rider heard every word. “Well, friend,” he said, “why are you on foot, then?” “Oh,” said Hans, “I have this load to carry. It’s silver, true enough, but it’s so heavy I can’t hold my head up, and I’ll have you know it hurts my shoulder terribly.” “How about a trade?” said the horseman. “I’ll give you my horse, and you give me the silver. That will spare you a lot of trouble, lugging such a weight around.” “Gladly,” said Hans. “But since you’re being so good to me, I should warn you of one thing: you’ll have a hard time dragging that silver about.” All the same, the horseman got down, took the silver, helped Hans into the saddle, put the reins in one of his hands and the whip in the other, and said, “When you want to go very fast, smack your lips loudly and cry ‘Jip!’”
Hans was delighted as he sat up on the horse. He straightened his back, stuck out his elbows, turned out his toes, cracked his whip, and rode off cheerfully, now whistling a lively tune, now singing,

“Without worry or woe,
Tomorrow can go!
We’ll laugh and be merry,
Sing neigh down derry!”

After a while he felt like going a little faster, so he smacked his lips and cried ‘Jip!’ The horse took off at a full gallop, and before Hans understood what was happening, he had been thrown and was lying on his back by the roadside. The horse would have run away altogether if a shepherd, who happened to be coming along driving a cow, hadn’t stopped it. Hans came to his senses and got back on his feet, thoroughly annoyed, and said to the shepherd, “Riding is no joke when you’re unlucky enough to get hold of a beast like this one, that stumbles and bucks you off as if it wanted to break your neck. Anyway, I’m done with it for good. Now your cow, I like a great deal better than this fancy animal that played me such a trick and ruined my best coat in this puddle, which, by the way, doesn’t smell much like a bouquet. You can stroll along behind that cow at your leisure, in good company, and have milk, butter and cheese every day as well. What I wouldn’t give to have such a prize!” “Well,” said the shepherd, “if you’re so fond of her, I’ll swap my cow for your horse. I like to do a good turn for my neighbors, even if it costs me.” “Done!” said Hans cheerfully. “What a generous heart that man has!” he thought. Then the shepherd jumped onto the horse, wished Hans and the cow good morning, and rode away.

Hans brushed off his coat, wiped his face and hands, rested a little, and then calmly drove his cow along, convinced he had made a very lucky bargain. “As long as I have a bit of bread (and I’ll always be able to find that), I can eat butter and cheese with it whenever I like. When I’m thirsty, I can milk my cow and drink the milk. What more could I want?” When he reached an inn he stopped, ate all of his bread, and spent his very last penny on a glass of beer. After resting, he set off again, driving his cow toward his mother’s village. But as noon came on, the heat grew worse, and by the time he found himself on a wide heath that would take more than an hour to cross, he was so hot and parched that his tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth. “I know what to do about this,” he thought. “I’ll milk my cow and quench my thirst.” So he tied her to a tree stump and held out his leather cap to milk into, but not a drop came. Who would have guessed that this cow, which was supposed to give him milk, butter and cheese, had been completely dry all along? Hans had never thought to check.

While he was trying his luck at milking, and going about it very clumsily, the restless animal decided he was a nuisance, and finally gave him such a kick on the head that it knocked him flat, and he lay there senseless for a long time. Luckily a butcher soon came by, pushing a pig in a wheelbarrow. “What’s the matter with you, my good man?” said the butcher, helping him up. Hans told him what had happened: that he was thirsty and had wanted to milk his cow, but the cow turned out to be dry as well. The butcher then handed him a flask of ale. “Here, drink and pull yourself together,” he said. “Your cow will never give you milk. Can’t you see she’s an old animal, good for nothing but the slaughterhouse?” “Oh dear, oh dear,” said Hans, “who would have thought it? What a shame, to take my horse and give me only a dry cow! If I kill her, what good will she be? I can’t stand cow meat; it isn’t tender enough for me. But a pig now, like that fat gentleman you’re wheeling along so comfortably, that would be something. At the very least it would make sausages.” “Well,” said the butcher, “I don’t like to refuse when someone asks for a kind, neighborly favor. To oblige you, I’ll trade, and give you my fine fat pig for your cow.” “Heaven reward you for your kindness and self-sacrifice!” said Hans, handing over the cow. He lifted the pig out of the wheelbarrow and led it away, holding the string that was tied to its leg.

So he walked on, and now everything seemed to be going his way. He had met with some misfortunes, it was true, but he was well repaid for them all now. How could it be otherwise, with the traveling companion he had at last found?

The next person he met was a countryman carrying a fine white goose. The man stopped to ask the time, which led to more conversation, and Hans told him all about his luck: how he had made so many good bargains, and how the whole world was smiling on him. The countryman then told his own story, saying he was taking the goose to a christening. “Feel how heavy it is,” he said, “and it’s only eight weeks old. Whoever roasts and eats it will find plenty of fat on it, it has lived so well!” “You’re right,” said Hans, weighing it in his hand. “But if it’s fat you’re talking about, my pig is nothing to sneeze at.” Meanwhile the countryman had begun to look serious and shake his head. “Listen,” he said, “my good friend, you seem a decent fellow, so I can’t help doing you a favor. Your pig could get you into trouble. In the village I just came from, the squire has had a pig stolen out of his sty. When I saw you, I was dreadfully afraid you had the squire’s pig. If you do, and they catch you, it will go badly for you. The least they’ll do is throw you in the horse pond. Can you swim?”

Poor Hans was badly frightened. “Good man,” he cried, “please get me out of this trouble. I don’t know where the pig was born or raised, but for all I can tell it may have been the squire’s. You know this country better than I do. Take my pig and give me the goose.” “I ought to get something extra for that,” said the countryman. “Giving a fat goose for a pig, indeed! Not everyone would do as much for you. But I won’t be hard on you, since you’re in trouble.” Then he took the string in his hand and led the pig off down a side path, while Hans went on toward home without a care. “After all,” he thought, “that fellow’s been well and truly fooled. I don’t care whose pig it is, but wherever it came from, it has been a very good friend to me. I’ve got much the best of the bargain. First there will be a splendid roast. Then the fat will keep me in goose grease for six months. And then there are all those beautiful white feathers. I’ll stuff them in my pillow, and I’m sure I’ll sleep soundly without anyone rocking me. How happy my mother will be! A pig, indeed! Give me a fine fat goose any day.”
When he reached the next village, he saw a scissor grinder at his wheel, working and singing,

“Over hill and over dale
So happy I roam,
Light work and good living,
The whole world’s my home;
So who is as cheerful as I?”

Hans stood watching for a while, and at last said, “You must be doing well, master grinder! You seem so happy at your work.” “Yes,” said the other, “mine is a golden trade. A good grinder never puts his hand in his pocket without finding money there. But where did you get that beautiful goose?” “I didn’t buy it. I gave a pig for it.” “And where did you get the pig?” “I gave a cow for it.” “And the cow?” “I gave a horse for it.” “And the horse?” “I gave a lump of silver as big as my head for it.” “And the silver?” “Oh, I worked hard for that, seven long years.” “You’ve done well for yourself so far,” said the grinder. “Now if you could find money in your pocket every time you reached into it, your fortune would be made.” “That’s true, but how could that be done?” “How? Why, you have to become a grinder like me,” said the other. “All you need is a grindstone; the rest comes by itself. Here’s one that’s hardly the worse for wear. I wouldn’t ask more than the price of your goose for it. Will you buy?” “How can you ask?” said Hans. “I’d be the happiest man in the world if I could have money whenever I put my hand in my pocket. What more could I want? Here’s the goose.” “Now,” said the grinder, handing him an ordinary rough stone that was lying beside him, “this is a first-rate stone. Work it well enough, and you can make an old nail cut with it.”

Hans took the stone and went on his way with a light heart. His eyes sparkled with joy, and he said to himself, “I must have been born at a lucky hour. Everything I could want or wish for just comes to me. People are so kind; they seem to think I’m doing them a favor by letting them make me rich and give me good bargains.”
Meanwhile he was growing tired, and hungry too, because in his joy at getting the cow he had given away his last penny.

At last he could go no farther, since the stone wore him out terribly, and he dragged himself to the bank of a river to have a drink of water and rest a while. He set the stone down carefully beside him on the bank, but as he bent over to drink, he forgot about it, nudged it slightly, and down it rolled, splash, into the stream.

For a while he watched it sink through the deep, clear water. Then he jumped up and danced for joy, and dropped to his knees again and thanked Heaven, with tears in his eyes, for its kindness in taking away his one burden, the ugly, heavy stone.

“How happy I am!” he cried. “Nobody was ever as lucky as I am.” Then he got up with a light heart, free of all his troubles, and walked on until he reached his mother’s house, where he told her how easy the road to good luck was.

chapters.title: Jorinda and Jorindel
paragraphs: Once there was an old castle that stood in the middle of a deep, gloomy forest, and in the castle lived an old fairy. This fairy could take any shape she liked. All day long she flew about as an owl, or prowled the countryside as a cat, but at night she always turned back into an old woman. If a young man came within a hundred paces of her castle, he became rooted to the spot and could not move a step until she came and freed him, which she would not do until he had given his word never to return. But if a pretty girl came within that distance, she was changed into a bird, and the fairy put her in a cage and hung her up in a room of the castle. Seven hundred of these cages hung in the castle, and every one held a beautiful bird.

Now there was once a girl named Jorinda. She was prettier than all the pretty girls anyone had ever seen, and a shepherd boy named Jorindel loved her dearly, and the two were soon to be married. One day they went for a walk in the forest to be alone together, and Jorindel said, “We must be careful not to go too near the fairy’s castle.” It was a beautiful evening. The last rays of the setting sun shone brightly through the tall tree trunks onto the green undergrowth below, and turtledoves sang from the tall birches.

Jorinda sat down to watch the sun, and Jorindel sat beside her. Both felt sad, they didn’t know why, as though they were going to be parted forever. They had wandered a long way, and when they looked around to see which way to go home, they found they had no idea which path to take.

The sun was sinking fast, and already half of it had gone down behind the hill. Suddenly Jorindel glanced behind him and saw through the bushes that without realizing it they had sat down right beneath the old castle walls. He shrank back in fear, turned pale, and trembled. Jorinda was just singing,

“The ring-dove sang from the willow bough,
Alas! Alas!
He mourned the fate of his darling mate,
Alas!”

when her song broke off suddenly. Jorindel turned to see why, and saw that his Jorinda had been changed into a nightingale, so that her song ended in a mournful _jug, jug_. An owl with fiery eyes flew three times around them, and three times it screeched:
“Tu whu! Tu whu! Tu whu!”

Jorindel could not move. He stood fixed like a stone, and could not weep, or speak, or lift a hand or foot. Now the sun sank completely, and the gloomy night came on. The owl flew into a bush, and a moment later the old fairy came out, pale and gaunt, with staring eyes and a nose and chin that almost met.

She mumbled a few words to herself, snatched up the nightingale, and carried it off in her hand. Poor Jorindel saw that the nightingale was gone, but what could he do? He had no voice, and he could not move from where he stood. Finally the fairy returned and sang in a rasping voice:

“Until the prisoner is fast,
And her doom is cast,
Stay there! Oh, stay!
When the charm is around her,
And the spell has bound her,
Be gone! Away!”

All at once Jorindel was free. He dropped to his knees in front of the fairy and begged her to give Jorinda back to him. But she only laughed at him and told him he would never see her again. Then she walked off.

He begged, he wept, he grieved, and none of it did any good. “What is going to become of me?” he cried. He couldn’t return to his own home, so he went to a village where nobody knew him and took work minding sheep. Again and again he circled as close to the hated castle as he dared, but it was no use. He never heard or saw anything of Jorinda.

Then one night he had a dream. In it he found a beautiful purple flower with a precious pearl lying at its heart. He dreamed that he picked the flower and carried it into the castle, that everything he touched with it was released from the spell, and that there he got his Jorinda back.

When he woke in the morning, he started searching the hills and valleys for this lovely flower. For eight long days he looked for it without success, but on the ninth day, early in the morning, he found the beautiful purple flower. In its heart was a big dewdrop, as large as a precious pearl. He picked the flower, set off, and traveled day and night until he reached the castle again.

He came within a hundred paces of it, and this time he was not frozen to the spot as before. He found that he could walk right up to the door. Jorindel was overjoyed to see it. He touched the door with the flower and it flew open, so he went in through the courtyard, following the sound of all the birds singing. At last he reached the chamber where the fairy sat, with seven hundred birds singing in seven hundred cages. When she saw Jorindel she was furious and shrieked with rage, but she could not get within two yards of him, because the flower in his hand protected him. He looked at the birds, but alas, there were so many nightingales! How could he ever tell which one was his Jorinda? While he was wondering what to do, he saw the fairy take down one of the cages and hurry out through the door with it. He ran, or flew, after her and touched the cage with the flower, and Jorinda was standing in front of him. She threw her arms around his neck, as beautiful as ever, as beautiful as on the day they had walked together in the wood.

Then he touched all the other birds with the flower, and they all turned back into their old shapes. He took Jorinda home, where they were married and lived happily together for many years. So did a good many other young men whose sweethearts had been made to sing alone in the old fairy’s cages for far longer than they liked.

chapters.title: The Travelling Musicians
paragraphs: An honest farmer had a donkey that had served him loyally for many years, but now the animal was getting old, and with every day he was less able to do his work. His master was sick of feeding him and began thinking of getting rid of him. The donkey saw that trouble was brewing, so he slipped quietly away and set out on the road to the great city. “There,” he thought, “I could become a musician.”

After he had gone a short way, he noticed a dog lying at the side of the road, panting as though he were tired out. “Why are you panting like that, my friend?” asked the donkey. “Oh dear,” said the dog, “my master was going to beat me to death because I’m old and weak and no longer any use to him for hunting. So I ran away. But how am I supposed to earn my living now?” “Listen,” said the donkey, “I’m on my way to the great city to be a musician. Why don’t you come along and try your luck at the same thing?” The dog said he would be glad to, and the two of them trotted on together.

Before long they came upon a cat sitting in the middle of the road with a miserable look on her face. “My dear lady,” said the donkey, “what is the matter? You seem quite downhearted.” “Oh, how can anyone be cheerful when her life is in danger?” said the cat. “I’m getting old, and I would rather doze by the fire than chase mice around the house. So my mistress seized me and meant to drown me. I was lucky enough to escape, but now I have no idea what I’m going to live on.” “Well,” said the donkey, “you must certainly come with us to the great city. You’re a fine night singer, and you could make your fortune as a musician.” The cat liked the idea and joined them.

A little later, as they walked past a farmyard, they saw a rooster perched on a gate, crowing at the top of his lungs. “Bravo!” said the donkey. “You certainly make a magnificent racket. What’s it all about?” “Well,” said the rooster, “I was just announcing that we would have good weather for washing day. But my mistress and the cook are not grateful for my trouble. They have threatened to cut off my head tomorrow and make soup of me for the guests coming on Sunday!” “Heaven forbid!” said the donkey. “Come with us, Master Chanticleer. Anything is better than staying here to lose your head. Besides, who knows? If we sing in tune, we might manage some sort of concert. So come along.” “Gladly,” said the rooster, and the four of them went merrily on together.

They could not reach the great city in a single day, so when night fell they went into a wood to sleep. The donkey and the dog lay down under a big tree, and the cat climbed into its branches. The rooster felt that the higher he roosted, the safer he would be, so he flew up to the very top of the tree. There, as was his habit before going to sleep, he looked in every direction to make sure all was well. Doing so, he caught sight of something bright and shining far away. He called down to his companions, “There must be a house not far off, because I can see a light.” “If that’s so,” said the donkey, “we should move on, since this is hardly the best place to spend the night.” “And a bone or two, or a bit of meat, would do me no harm,” added the dog. So they set off toward the place where Chanticleer had seen the light. As they came closer it grew larger and brighter, until they finally reached a house where a gang of robbers lived.

The donkey, as the tallest of them, walked up to the window and looked inside. “Well, Donkey,” said Chanticleer, “what do you see?” “What do I see?” replied the donkey. “I see a table laid out with all sorts of good things, and robbers sitting around it enjoying themselves.” “That would be a fine place for us to stay,” said the rooster. “It would,” said the donkey, “if only we could get in.” So they put their heads together to work out how to drive the robbers out, and at last they came up with a plan. The donkey stood on his hind legs with his front hooves against the window ledge. The dog climbed onto his back, the cat scrambled up onto the dog’s shoulders, and the rooster flew up and sat on the cat’s head. When everything was ready, a signal was given and they began their music. The donkey brayed, the dog barked, the cat mewed, and the rooster crowed. Then they all burst through the window at once and tumbled into the room among the broken glass with a horrible crash. The robbers, who had already been badly frightened by the opening of the concert, had no doubt that some terrible goblin had burst in on them, and they fled as fast as their legs would carry them.

With the way clear, our travelers sat down and finished off what the robbers had left, as hungrily as if they expected never to eat again for a month. When they had had enough, they put out the lights and each looked for a sleeping place to suit him. The donkey lay down on a pile of straw in the yard, the dog stretched out on a mat behind the door, the cat curled up on the hearth beside the warm ashes, and the rooster flew up to a beam at the top of the house. They were all tired from the journey, and soon they were asleep.

But around midnight the robbers saw from a distance that the lights were out and everything seemed quiet. They began to think they had run off too hastily, and one of them, who was braver than the others, went to see what was happening. He found everything still, so he walked into the kitchen and felt around until he found a match to light a candle. Then he noticed the cat’s glittering, fiery eyes, took them for live coals, and held the match up to them to get a light. But the cat did not see the joke. She leaped at his face, spitting and scratching. He was terrified and ran for the back door, but there the dog jumped up and bit him in the leg. As he crossed the yard, the donkey kicked him, and the rooster, woken by the commotion, crowed with all his might. The robber ran back to his comrades as fast as he could and told the captain that a horrible witch had got into the house and spat at him and scratched his face with her long bony fingers. He said that a man with a knife had hidden behind the door and stabbed him in the leg, that a black monster in the yard had hit him with a club, and that the devil himself had sat on the roof and shouted, “Throw the rascal up here!” After that the robbers never dared go back to the house. But the musicians liked their new quarters so much that they settled there, and there they are still, I dare say, to this very day.

chapters.title: Old Sultan
paragraphs: A shepherd had a faithful dog named Sultan, who had grown very old and lost all his teeth. One day the shepherd and his wife were standing together in front of the house, and the shepherd said, “I’m going to shoot old Sultan tomorrow morning. He’s no use to anyone now.” But his wife said, “Please let the poor loyal creature live. He has served us well for many years, and we ought to keep him fed for the rest of his days.” “But what can we do with him?” said the shepherd. “He hasn’t a tooth in his head, and the thieves aren’t afraid of him at all. He has served us, it’s true, but he did it to earn his keep. Tomorrow is his last day, you can count on it.”

Poor Sultan was lying close by and heard everything the shepherd and his wife said to each other. He was terrified to think that tomorrow would be his last day, so that evening he went to his good friend the wolf, who lived in the wood, and told him all his troubles and how his master meant to kill him in the morning. “Don’t worry,” said the wolf. “I’ll give you some good advice. Every morning, very early, your master goes out to the field with his wife, and they take their little child along and lay it down in the shade behind the hedge while they work. Now, you lie down close beside the child and act as if you’re watching over it. I’ll come out of the wood and carry it off, and you must run after me as fast as you can. I’ll drop it, and then you can carry it back. They’ll think you saved their child, and they’ll be so grateful that they’ll look after you as long as you live.” The dog thought this was an excellent plan, and it was carried out just so. The wolf ran off a little way with the child, and the shepherd and his wife screamed, but Sultan soon caught up and carried the poor little thing back to his master and mistress. Then the shepherd patted him on the head and said, “Old Sultan has saved our child from the wolf, so he shall live and be well looked after and have plenty to eat. Wife, go home and give him a good dinner, and let him have my old cushion to sleep on for as long as he lives.” From then on Sultan had everything he could wish for.

Soon afterward the wolf came to congratulate him. “Now, my good fellow,” he said, “you must keep quiet and look the other way when I want a taste of one of the old shepherd’s fine fat sheep.” “No,” said Sultan. “I will be true to my master.” The wolf thought he was joking, though, and came one night looking for a tasty bite. But Sultan had told his master what the wolf intended, so the shepherd lay in wait for him behind the barn door. While the wolf was busy picking out a fat sheep, the shepherd laid a heavy stick across his back and gave his coat a thorough combing.

The wolf was furious. He called Sultan “an old rogue” and swore he would get his revenge. Next morning he sent the boar to challenge Sultan to meet in the wood and settle the matter. Sultan had no one to ask to be his second except the shepherd’s old three-legged cat. So he took her along, and as the poor thing hobbled painfully on, she held her tail straight up in the air.

The wolf and the wild boar reached the spot first. When they saw their enemies approaching, with the cat’s long tail sticking straight up, they thought she was carrying a sword for Sultan to fight with. Every time she limped, they thought she was bending down to pick up a stone to throw at them. They decided they didn’t care for this kind of fighting, so the boar lay down behind a bush and the wolf jumped up into a tree. Sultan and the cat arrived, looked around, and wondered why nobody was there. The boar, however, had not hidden himself completely, because his ears were sticking out of the bush. When he twitched one of them a little, the cat saw something move and, thinking it was a mouse, pounced on it, biting and scratching, so that the boar leaped up, grunting, and ran off, bellowing, “Look up in the tree. The one to blame is sitting there!” So they looked up and spotted the wolf sitting among the branches. They called him a cowardly rascal and would not let him come down until he was thoroughly ashamed of himself and had promised to be good friends with old Sultan again.

chapters.title: The Straw, the Coal, and the Bean
paragraphs: A poor old woman lived in a village. She had gathered a dish of beans and meant to cook them, so she built a fire on her hearth. To make it burn faster, she lit it with a handful of straw. As she tipped the beans into the pot, one slipped away without her noticing and landed on the floor next to a piece of straw. Soon after, a glowing coal jumped out of the fire and dropped down beside them. The straw spoke first. “Dear friends, where have you come from?” The coal answered, “I was lucky to leap out of the fire. If I hadn’t escaped by sheer force, I would certainly have died—I would have been burned to ashes.” The bean said, “I got away with a whole skin too. But if the old woman had put me in the pot, I would have been boiled to broth without a shred of mercy, just like my comrades.” “And do you think my luck would have been any better?” said the straw. “The old woman has sent all my brothers to their deaths in fire and smoke. She grabbed sixty of them in one go and took their lives. I was lucky to slip through her fingers.”
“But what are we going to do now?” asked the coal.

“Well,” said the bean, “we’ve been lucky to escape death, so I think we should stay together like good companions. And in case some new misfortune catches us here, let’s leave together and make our way to a foreign country.”

The other two liked the idea, and the three of them set off together. Before long they came to a little brook. There was no bridge and no plank to walk on, and they had no idea how to get across. The straw had a good thought. “I’ll lie down straight across the water,” she said, “and you can walk over me like a bridge.” So the straw stretched herself from one bank to the other. The coal, who was hot-headed, stepped boldly onto the brand-new bridge. But when she reached the middle and heard the water rushing underneath her, she grew afraid after all. She stopped and dared not go any farther. Then the straw began to burn, snapped in two, and dropped into the stream. The coal slid in after her, hissed as she touched the water, and gave up her last breath. The bean had wisely stayed behind on the bank. She couldn’t help laughing at what had happened, and once she had started she couldn’t stop. She laughed so hard that she burst. That would have been the end of her too, if a tailor hadn’t happened to be sitting by the brook to rest, on his travels in search of work. He was kind-hearted, so he took out his needle and thread and sewed her back together. The bean thanked him very sweetly, but the tailor had used black thread, and that is why all beans have had a black seam ever since.

chapters.title: Briar Rose
paragraphs: Once upon a time, in a country far away, where in those days there were fairies, there reigned a king and queen. They had plenty of money, plenty of fine clothes, plenty of good food and drink, and a coach to ride in every day. Yet although they had been married for many years, they had no children, and it grieved them deeply. One day the queen was walking beside the river at the bottom of the garden when she saw a poor little fish that had flung itself out of the water. It lay on the bank, gasping and nearly dead. The queen felt sorry for the fish and threw it back into the river. Before it swam off, it raised its head out of the water and said, “I know what you wish for, and it will come true as thanks for your kindness to me—you will soon have a daughter.” What the little fish had foretold soon happened. The queen gave birth to a girl so beautiful that the king could not stop gazing at her for joy. He declared that he would hold a great feast, celebrate, and show the child to the whole land. So he invited his relatives, his nobles, his friends and his neighbors. But the queen said, “I want the fairies there too, so that they will be kind and good to our little daughter.” Now there were thirteen fairies in the kingdom, but the king and queen had only twelve golden dishes for them to eat from, so one of the fairies had to be left out. Twelve fairies came, each with a tall red cap on her head, red shoes with high heels on her feet, and a long white wand in her hand. When the feast was over, they gathered in a ring and gave the little princess their best gifts. One gave her goodness, another beauty, another riches, and so on, until she had everything good in the world.

Eleven of them had just finished giving their blessings when a great commotion broke out in the courtyard. Word came that the thirteenth fairy had arrived, wearing a black cap on her head and black shoes on her feet, and carrying a broomstick in her hand. A moment later she came up into the dining hall. Since she had not been invited to the feast, she was furious. She scolded the king and queen harshly and set about taking her revenge. “In her fifteenth year,” she cried, “the king’s daughter will be pricked by a spindle and fall down dead.” Then the twelfth of the friendly fairies, who had not yet given her gift, stepped forward. She said that the evil wish had to come true, but that she could soften its harm. So her gift was this: when the spindle pricked the king’s daughter, she would not really die, but would only fall asleep for a hundred years.

Still, the king hoped to spare his beloved child from the threatened evil altogether. He ordered every spindle in the kingdom to be bought up and burned. Meanwhile the gifts of the first eleven fairies all came true, for the princess grew so beautiful, well-mannered, good and wise that everyone who knew her loved her.

On the very day she turned fifteen, it happened that the king and queen were away from home and she was left alone in the palace. She wandered around by herself, looking into all the rooms and chambers, until at last she came to an old tower. A narrow staircase led up to a little door, and in the door was a golden key. When she turned it, the door sprang open, and there sat an old woman, spinning away busily. “Well, good mother,” said the princess, “what are you doing in here?” “Spinning,” said the old woman, nodding her head and humming a tune, while the wheel went buzz! “How prettily that little thing goes round!” said the princess. She took the spindle and tried to spin. But she had barely touched it when the fairy’s prophecy came true. The spindle pricked her, and she dropped lifeless to the floor.

But she was not dead. She had only fallen into a deep sleep. The king and queen, who had just come home, fell asleep too, and so did their whole court. The horses slept in the stables, the dogs in the yard, the pigeons on the roof, and even the flies slept on the walls. The fire on the hearth stopped blazing and went to sleep. The jack stopped turning, and the spit with the goose on it for the king’s dinner stood still. The cook had been about to box the kitchen boy’s ears for some mistake, and was pulling him by the hair. She let him go, and both fell asleep. The butler had been slyly tasting the ale, and he fell asleep with the jug at his lips. And so everything stood still and slept soundly.

Soon a great hedge of thorns grew up around the palace. Every year it became higher and thicker, until at last the whole palace was surrounded and hidden, and not even the roof or the chimneys could be seen. But a story spread through the land about the beautiful sleeping Briar Rose (for that was the king’s daughter’s name). From time to time, several kings’ sons came and tried to break through the thicket into the palace. None of them ever managed it, because the thorns and bushes seized them as if with hands. They stuck fast there and died miserably.

After many, many years, a king’s son came to that land. An old man told him about the thicket of thorns, and how a beautiful palace stood behind it, where a wonderful princess named Briar Rose lay asleep with all her court. He also said that his grandfather had told him how many, many princes had come and tried to break through the thicket, but had all stuck fast in it and died. Then the young prince said, “That doesn’t frighten me. I’m going to see this Briar Rose.” The old man tried to stop him, but the prince was determined to go.

That very day the hundred years came to an end. When the prince reached the thicket, he saw nothing but beautiful flowering shrubs. He passed through them easily, and they closed up behind him as thick as ever. At last he arrived at the palace. In the courtyard lay the dogs, asleep, and the horses stood in the stables. On the roof the pigeons sat sound asleep with their heads tucked under their wings. When he went inside, the flies were sleeping on the walls and the spit stood still. The butler had the jug of ale at his lips, about to take a drink. The maid sat with a fowl in her lap, ready to be plucked. In the kitchen the cook still had her hand raised, as if about to strike the boy.

He went on farther. Everything was so quiet that he could hear his own breathing. At last he came to the old tower and opened the door of the little room where Briar Rose was, and there she lay, fast asleep on a couch by the window. She looked so beautiful that he could not take his eyes off her. He bent down and kissed her. The moment he kissed her, she opened her eyes, woke up, and smiled at him. They went out together, and soon the king and queen woke too, and all the court, and they stared at one another in amazement. The horses shook themselves, and the dogs jumped up and barked. The pigeons pulled their heads from under their wings, looked around, and flew off into the fields. The flies on the walls started buzzing again. The fire in the kitchen blazed up. Round went the jack and round went the spit, with the goose on it for the king’s dinner. The butler finished his drink of ale, the maid went on plucking the fowl, and the cook gave the boy the box on the ear.
And then the prince and Briar Rose were married, the wedding feast was held, and they lived happily together for the rest of their lives.

chapters.title: The Dog and the Sparrow
paragraphs: A shepherd’s dog had a master who paid him no attention and often left him to go terribly hungry. Finally he could stand it no longer. He ran away, feeling miserable and downhearted. On the road he met a sparrow, who asked him, “Why so gloomy, my friend?” “Because,” said the dog, “I’m starving, and I have nothing to eat.” “If that’s all it is,” said the sparrow, “come with me to the next town, and I’ll get you plenty of food in no time.” So the two of them set off together for the town. When they came to a butcher’s shop, the sparrow said to the dog, “Wait here a moment while I peck a piece of meat down for you.” She settled on the shelf, glanced carefully around to be sure nobody was watching, and then pecked and scratched at a steak lying near the edge, until at last it dropped to the ground. The dog snatched it up, hurried off into a corner with it, and gobbled it down. “Well,” said the sparrow, “you can have more if you like. Come along to the next shop, and I’ll peck down another steak for you.” When the dog had finished that one too, the sparrow said, “Well, my good friend, have you had enough now?” “I’ve had plenty of meat,” he answered, “but I’d like a bit of bread to follow it.” “Then come with me,” said the sparrow, “and you’ll have that too.” She led him to a baker’s shop and pecked at two rolls lying in the window until they tumbled out. The dog still wanted more, so she took him to another shop and pecked down some more for him. When he had eaten that, the sparrow asked whether he’d had enough yet. “Yes,” he said, “and now let’s take a walk out of town for a bit.” So they went out together onto the high road. But the weather was warm, and they hadn’t gone far when the dog said, “I’m very tired—I’d like to take a nap.” “All right,” said the sparrow, “go ahead. Meanwhile I’ll sit in that bush.” So the dog stretched out on the road and fell fast asleep. While he slept, a carter came along with a cart drawn by three horses and loaded with two barrels of wine. The sparrow saw that the carter wasn’t going to steer aside, but meant to keep to the rut where the dog lay and drive right over him. She called out, “Stop! Stop, Mr Carter, or you’ll be sorry!” But the carter muttered, “Sorry, indeed! What could you do to me?” He cracked his whip and drove the cart over the poor dog, and the wheels crushed him to death. “There,” cried the sparrow, “you cruel villain, you’ve killed my friend the dog. Now listen to what I say. This deed will cost you everything you own.” “Do your worst, and welcome,” said the brute. “What harm can you do me?” And he drove on. But the sparrow crept in under the cover of the cart and pecked at the bung of one of the barrels until she had worked it loose, and all the wine ran out without the carter noticing. At last he looked back and saw the cart dripping and the barrel completely empty. “What an unlucky wretch I am!” he cried. “Not wretched enough yet!” said the sparrow. She landed on the head of one of the horses and pecked at him until he reared up and kicked. When the carter saw this, he pulled out his hatchet and swung at the sparrow, meaning to kill her. She flew away, and the blow fell on the poor horse’s head with such force that he dropped dead. “What an unlucky wretch I am!” he cried. “Not wretched enough yet!” said the sparrow. The carter went on with the two remaining horses, and she crept under the cover of the cart again and pecked out the bung of the second barrel, so that all the wine ran out. When the carter saw it, he cried out again, “What a miserable wretch I am!” But the sparrow answered, “Not wretched enough yet!” and landed on the head of the second horse and pecked at him too. The carter ran up and struck at her with his hatchet again. Away she flew, and the blow fell on the second horse and killed him on the spot. “What an unlucky wretch I am!” he said. “Not wretched enough yet!” said the sparrow, and she settled on the third horse and began pecking at him as well. The carter was wild with fury. Without looking or thinking what he was doing, he struck at the sparrow once more, and killed his third horse just as he had the other two. “Alas, what a miserable wretch I am!” he cried. “Not wretched enough yet!” answered the sparrow as she flew off. “Now I’ll plague and punish you at your own house.” The carter had no choice but to leave his cart standing where it was and go home, bursting with rage and bitterness. “Oh,” he said to his wife, “what bad luck has struck me! My wine is all spilled, and all three of my horses are dead.” “Oh, husband,” she replied, “and a wicked bird has come into the house, and I’m sure she has brought every bird in the world along with her. They’ve fallen on our corn in the loft and are eating it up at a terrible rate!” The husband ran upstairs and saw thousands of birds sitting on the floor eating his corn, with the sparrow in the middle of them. “What an unlucky wretch I am!” cried the carter, for he saw that almost all the corn was gone. “Not wretched enough yet!” said the sparrow. “Your cruelty will cost you your life yet!” And away she flew.

The carter had now lost everything he owned. He went down to his kitchen, still not sorry for what he had done, and sat angrily and sullenly in the chimney corner. But the sparrow perched outside the window and cried, “Carter! Your cruelty will cost you your life!” He leapt up in a rage, grabbed his hatchet and hurled it at the sparrow. It missed her and only smashed the window. The sparrow hopped inside, landed on the window seat and cried, “Carter! It will cost you your life!” Now he was blind and mad with rage, and he struck the window seat so hard that he split it in two. As the sparrow flew from place to place, the carter and his wife grew so furious that they smashed all their furniture—mirrors, chairs, benches, the table, and finally even the walls—without ever touching the bird. In the end, though, they caught her. “Shall I kill her right now?” said the wife. “No,” he cried, “that would be letting her off too lightly. She’ll die a much crueler death. I’m going to eat her.” But the sparrow began to flutter about and stretch out her neck, and she cried, “Carter! It will cost you your life yet!” At that he could wait no longer. He handed his wife the hatchet and cried, “Wife, strike the bird and kill her right here in my hand.” The wife struck, but she missed her aim and hit her husband on the head, and he fell down dead. And the sparrow flew peacefully home to her nest.

chapters.title: The Twelve Dancing Princesses
paragraphs: A king had twelve beautiful daughters. They slept in twelve beds in a single room, and at bedtime the doors were shut and locked. Yet every morning their shoes were found worn right through, as if they had been dancing in them all night. Nobody could work out how it happened, or where the princesses had been.

So the king announced throughout the land that anyone who could solve the mystery and discover where the princesses danced at night would be allowed to marry the one he liked best and would become king after the king’s death. But anyone who tried and failed, after three days and nights, would be put to death.

Before long a king’s son arrived. He was treated well, and in the evening he was led to the room next to the one where the princesses lay in their twelve beds. There he was to sit and watch to see where they went to dance, and so that nothing could happen without his hearing it, the door of his room was left open. But the king’s son soon fell asleep, and when he woke in the morning he found that the princesses had been dancing after all, because the soles of their shoes were full of holes. The same thing happened on the second and third nights, and so the king ordered his head cut off. Several others came after him, but they all had the same luck and lost their lives the same way.

Now it happened that an old soldier, who had been wounded in battle and could no longer fight, was passing through the country where this king ruled. As he traveled through a wood, he met an old woman, who asked him where he was headed. “I hardly know where I’m going, or what I ought to do,” said the soldier. “But I think I’d like to find out where the princesses go to dance, and then in time I might be a king.” “Well,” said the old woman, “that’s not so hard. Just be careful not to drink any of the wine one of the princesses will bring you in the evening, and as soon as she leaves, pretend to be fast asleep.”

Then she gave him a cloak and said, “The moment you put this on, you’ll be invisible, and you’ll be able to follow the princesses wherever they go.” The soldier took all this good advice to heart and decided to try his luck. He went to the king and said he was willing to take on the task.

He was welcomed just as the others had been, and the king had fine royal robes given to him. When evening came, he was led to the outer room. Just as he was about to lie down, the eldest princess brought him a cup of wine. The soldier secretly poured it all away, careful not to swallow a drop. Then he lay down on his bed and, after a little while, began to snore loudly, as if he were fast asleep. When the twelve princesses heard this, they laughed heartily, and the eldest said, “This fellow could have done something wiser than throw his life away like this!” Then they got up, opened their drawers and boxes, took out all their finest clothes, dressed in front of the mirror, and skipped about as if they couldn’t wait to start dancing. But the youngest said, “I don’t know why, but while you’re all so happy I feel very uneasy. I’m sure something bad is going to happen to us.” “You silly thing,” said the eldest, “you’re always afraid. Have you forgotten how many kings’ sons have already kept watch for nothing? And as for this soldier, even if I hadn’t given him the sleeping draft, he’d have slept soundly enough.”

When they were all ready, they went to look at the soldier, but he went on snoring and didn’t move a hand or foot. So they thought they were perfectly safe. The eldest went to her own bed and clapped her hands, and the bed sank into the floor and a trapdoor flew open. The soldier watched them go down through the trapdoor one after another, the eldest in front. Thinking he had no time to lose, he jumped up, put on the cloak the old woman had given him, and followed them. But halfway down the stairs he stepped on the youngest princess’s gown, and she cried out to her sisters, “Something is wrong! Someone grabbed my gown.” “Don’t be so silly,” said the eldest. “It’s only a nail in the wall.” So down they all went, and at the bottom they found themselves in a lovely grove of trees where all the leaves were silver, glittering and sparkling beautifully. The soldier wanted to take some token of the place away with him, so he broke off a small branch, and a loud noise came from the tree. The youngest said again, “I’m sure something is wrong—didn’t you hear that noise? That has never happened before.” But the eldest said, “It’s only our princes, shouting for joy because we’re near.”

Next they came to another grove, where all the leaves were gold, and then to a third, where the leaves were glittering diamonds. The soldier broke off a branch from each, and every time there was a loud noise that made the youngest sister tremble with fear. But the eldest kept saying it was only the princes, crying out for joy. They went on until they reached a great lake. At the water’s edge lay twelve little boats, and in them sat twelve handsome princes, who seemed to be waiting for the princesses.

One princess climbed into each boat, and the soldier got into the same boat as the youngest. As they rowed across the lake, the prince in the boat with the youngest princess and the soldier said, “I don’t know why, but I’m rowing with all my strength and we’re not getting along as fast as usual. I’m worn out. The boat feels very heavy today.” “It’s only the hot weather,” said the princess. “I feel very warm too.”

On the far side of the lake stood a splendid castle, brightly lit, with the cheerful sound of horns and trumpets drifting out of it. They all landed and went inside, and each prince danced with his princess. The soldier, invisible the whole time, danced with them too. Whenever one of the princesses had a cup of wine set down beside her, he drank it all, so that when she lifted the cup to her lips it was empty. This frightened the youngest sister terribly, but the eldest always hushed her. They danced until three in the morning, by which time all their shoes were worn out and they had to stop. The princes rowed them back across the lake (this time the soldier took a seat in the boat with the eldest princess), and on the opposite shore they said goodbye, the princesses promising to return the next night.

When they reached the stairs, the soldier ran ahead of the princesses and lay down in his bed. As the twelve sisters came slowly up, very tired, they heard him snoring, and they said, “Now we’re quite safe.” Then they undressed, put away their fine clothes, took off their shoes, and went to bed. In the morning the soldier said nothing about what had happened, but decided to see more of this strange adventure, and he went again on the second and third nights. Everything happened just as before: each time the princesses danced until their shoes were worn to pieces and then went home. On the third night, however, the soldier carried off one of the golden cups as proof of where he had been.

When the day came for him to reveal the secret, he was brought before the king with the three branches and the golden cup, while the twelve princesses stood behind the door, listening for what he would say. The king asked him, “Where do my twelve daughters dance at night?” He answered, “With twelve princes, in a castle underground.” Then he told the king everything that had happened, and showed him the three branches and the golden cup he had carried away. The king summoned the princesses and asked whether the soldier was telling the truth. They saw that they had been found out and that denying it would do no good, so they confessed everything. Then the king asked the soldier which of them he wanted for his wife. “I’m not very young,” he said, “so I’ll take the eldest.” They were married that same day, and the soldier was named the king’s heir.

chapters.title: The Fisherman and His Wife
paragraphs: Once there was a fisherman who lived with his wife in a pigsty by the sea. He fished all day long, and one day he was sitting on the shore with his rod, gazing at the glittering water and watching his line, when suddenly the float was yanked down deep under the surface. When he hauled it up, he had caught a huge fish. But the fish said, “Please, let me live! I’m not really a fish. I’m an enchanted prince. Put me back in the water and let me go!” “Oh, come now,” said the man, “there’s no need for all these words. I want nothing to do with a fish that can talk. Swim off, sir, whenever you like!” And he put the fish back in the water, and it shot straight down to the bottom, leaving a long streak of blood behind it in the waves.

The fisherman went home to his wife in the pigsty and told her how he had caught a big fish, how the fish had said it was an enchanted prince, and how he had let it go again as soon as he heard it speak. “Didn’t you ask it for anything?” said his wife. “We live miserably here, in this filthy pigsty. Go back and tell the fish we want a snug little cottage.”
The fisherman wasn’t happy about it, but he went down to the sea anyway, and when he got there the water had turned yellow and green. He stood at the water’s edge and said:

“O man of the sea,
Come listen to me!
My wife, Ilsabill,
Will have her own will,
And she’s sent me to beg a favor of you!”

The fish came swimming up to him and said, “Well, what does she want? What is it your wife is asking for?” “Ah,” said the fisherman, “she says that when I caught you I should have asked for something before letting you go. She can’t stand living in the pigsty any longer, and she wants a snug little cottage.” “Go home,” said the fish. “She’s in the cottage already!” So the man went home and found his wife standing at the door of a neat, pretty cottage. “Come in, come in!” she said. “Isn’t this much better than that filthy pigsty we had?” Inside there was a parlor, a bedroom and a kitchen. Behind the cottage lay a little garden planted with every kind of flower and fruit tree, and beyond it a yard full of ducks and chickens. “Ah,” said the fisherman, “how happy we’ll be now!” “We’ll try to be, at any rate,” said his wife.

All went well for a week or two. Then Dame Ilsabill said, “Husband, this cottage is nowhere near big enough for us, and the yard and garden are far too small. I want a big stone castle to live in. Go back to the fish and tell him to give us a castle.” “Wife,” said the fisherman, “I don’t want to go to him again. He might get angry. We ought to be content with this lovely cottage.” “Nonsense!” said the wife. “He’ll do it gladly, I know he will. Go on, try!”
The fisherman went, but his heart was heavy. When he reached the sea it looked blue and gloomy, though it was perfectly calm. He walked right up to the edge of the waves and said:

“O man of the sea,
Come listen to me!
My wife, Ilsabill,
Will have her own will,
And she’s sent me to beg a favor of you!”

“Well, what does she want now?” said the fish. “Ah,” said the man miserably, “my wife wants to live in a stone castle.” “Go home,” said the fish. “She’s standing at its gate already.” So the fisherman hurried back and found his wife standing before the gate of a huge castle. “Look,” she said, “isn’t it grand?” They went inside together and found a great many servants, and rooms richly furnished and full of golden chairs and tables. Behind the castle was a garden, and around it a park half a mile long, full of sheep, goats, hares and deer, and in the courtyard there were stables and cowsheds. “Well,” said the man, “now we can live cheerfully and happily in this beautiful castle for the rest of our lives.” “Perhaps,” said the wife, “but let’s sleep on it before we decide.” And they went to bed.

The next morning Dame Ilsabill woke when it was broad daylight, poked the fisherman with her elbow and said, “Get up, husband, and get moving, because we have to be king of all the land.” “Wife, wife,” said the man, “why would we want to be king? I won’t be king.” “Then I will,” she said. “But wife,” said the fisherman, “how can you be king? The fish can’t make you a king.” “Husband,” she said, “not another word. Go and try! I will be king.” So the man set off, quite sorrowful that his wife wanted to be king. This time the sea was a dark gray, covered with rolling waves and ridges of foam, as he called out:

“O man of the sea,
Come listen to me!
My wife, Ilsabill,
Will have her own will,
And she’s sent me to beg a favor of you!”
“Well, what does she want now?” said the fish. “Alas,” said the poor man, “my wife wants to be king.” “Go home,” said the fish. “She is king already.”

The fisherman went home, and as he came near the palace he saw a troop of soldiers and heard drums and trumpets. Inside, he found his wife sitting on a throne of gold and diamonds with a golden crown on her head, and on each side of her stood six beautiful maidens, each one a head taller than the one before. “Well, wife,” said the fisherman, “are you king?” “Yes,” she said, “I am king.” He looked at her for a long while, and then he said, “Ah, wife, what a fine thing it is to be king! Now we’ll never have anything left to wish for as long as we live.” “I don’t know about that,” she said. “‘Never’ is a long time. I am king, it’s true, but I’m beginning to tire of it, and I think I’d like to be emperor.” “Alas, wife, why would you want to be emperor?” said the fisherman. “Husband,” she said, “go to the fish! I tell you, I will be emperor.” “Ah, wife,” replied the fisherman, “I’m sure the fish can’t make an emperor, and I wouldn’t like to ask him for such a thing.” “I am king,” said Ilsabill, “and you are my slave, so go at once!”

So the fisherman had to go, and as he trudged along he muttered, “This will end badly. It’s too much to ask. The fish will get tired of us in the end, and then we’ll be sorry for what we’ve done.” Soon he reached the shore. The water was black and muddy, and a mighty whirlwind swept over the waves and tossed them about, but he went as close to the water as he could and said:

“O man of the sea,
Come listen to me!
My wife, Ilsabill,
Will have her own will,
And she’s sent me to beg a favor of you!”
“What does she want now?” said the fish. “Ah,” said the fisherman, “she wants to be emperor.” “Go home,” said the fish. “She is emperor already.”

So he went home again, and as he approached he saw his wife Ilsabill sitting on a very high throne of solid gold, with an enormous crown on her head, fully two yards tall. On either side of her stood her guards and attendants in a row, each smaller than the one before, from the tallest giant down to a dwarf no bigger than my finger. Before her stood princes, dukes and earls. The fisherman walked up to her and said, “Wife, are you emperor?” “Yes,” she said, “I am emperor.” “Ah,” said the man, gazing at her, “what a fine thing it is to be emperor!” “Husband,” she said, “why should we stop at emperor? Next I will be pope.” “Oh wife, wife,” he said, “how can you be pope? There is only one pope at a time in Christendom.” “Husband,” she said, “I will be pope this very day.” “But,” replied the husband, “the fish can’t make you pope.” “What nonsense!” she said. “If he can make an emperor, he can make a pope. Go and try him.”

So the fisherman went. But when he reached the shore the wind was roaring and the sea heaved and boiled with waves, and the ships were in trouble, pitching wildly on the swells. In the middle of the sky there was one small patch of blue, but toward the south everything was red, as if a terrible storm were rising. The sight filled the fisherman with dread, and he shook so hard that his knees knocked together. Still, he went down close to the shore and said:

“O man of the sea,
Come listen to me!
My wife, Ilsabill,
Will have her own will,
And she’s sent me to beg a favor of you!”
“What does she want now?” said the fish. “Ah,” said the fisherman, “my wife wants to be pope.” “Go home,” said the fish. “She is pope already.”

The fisherman went home and found Ilsabill sitting on a throne two miles high. She wore three great crowns, and around her stood all the pomp and power of the Church. On either side of her were two rows of burning lights, of every size, the biggest as huge as the tallest tower in the world and the smallest no bigger than a little rushlight. “Wife,” said the fisherman, looking at all this splendor, “are you pope?” “Yes,” she said, “I am pope.” “Well, wife,” he replied, “it’s a grand thing to be pope, and now you must be content, because you can’t be anything greater.” “I’ll think about that,” said the wife. Then they went to bed, but Dame Ilsabill lay awake all night, thinking about what she should be next. At last, just as she was dozing off, morning came and the sun rose. “Ha!” she thought, waking and looking at it through the window. “After all, I can’t stop the sun from rising.” This thought made her furious. She woke her husband and said, “Husband, go to the fish and tell him I must be lord of the sun and moon.” The fisherman was half asleep, but the idea frightened him so much that he jerked up and fell out of bed. “Alas, wife,” he said, “can’t you be content with being pope?” “No,” she said, “I can’t rest as long as the sun and moon rise without my permission. Go to the fish at once!”

The man set off, shivering with fear, and as he went down to the shore a terrible storm broke, so that the trees and even the rocks shook. The whole sky turned black with storm clouds, lightning flashed and thunder rolled, and in the sea you could have seen great black waves heaving up like mountains, each with a crown of white foam on its head. The fisherman crept toward the water and cried out as best he could:

“O man of the sea,
Come listen to me!
My wife, Ilsabill,
Will have her own will,
And she’s sent me to beg a favor of you!”
“What does she want now?” said the fish. “Ah,” said he, “she wants to be lord of the sun and moon.” “Go home,” said the fish, “back to your pigsty.”
And there they are living to this very day.

chapters.title: The Willow-Wren and the Bear
paragraphs: One summer the bear and the wolf were walking in the forest when the bear heard a bird singing so beautifully that he said, “Brother wolf, what kind of bird sings so well?” “That is the King of the birds,” said the wolf, “and we must bow down to him.” In fact the bird was the willow-wren. “If that’s so,” said the bear, “I’d very much like to see his royal palace. Come, take me there.” “It isn’t done as simply as you seem to think,” said the wolf. “You have to wait until the Queen arrives.” Soon afterward the Queen came with some food in her beak, and the lord King came too, and they began to feed their young. The bear wanted to go in at once, but the wolf held him back by the sleeve and said, “No, you must wait until the lord and lady Queen have gone away again.” So they noted the hole where the nest lay and trotted off. The bear, however, couldn’t rest until he had seen the royal palace, and after a short while he went back. The King and Queen had just flown out, so he peeked in and saw five or six young ones lying there. “Is this the royal palace?” cried the bear. “What a wretched palace! And you aren’t King’s children, you’re disreputable brats!” When the young wrens heard this, they were furiously angry and screamed, “No, we are not! Our parents are honest people! Bear, you’ll pay for that!”

The bear and the wolf grew uneasy, turned back and went into their dens. The young willow-wrens, though, kept on crying and screaming, and when their parents came again with food they said, “We won’t so much as touch a fly’s leg, not even if we’re starving, until you have settled whether we are respectable children or not. The bear has been here and insulted us!” Then the old King said, “Calm down, he will be punished.” He flew straight off with the Queen to the bear’s cave and called in, “Old Growler, why have you insulted my children? You will suffer for it. We will punish you with a bloody war.” So war was declared on the Bear, and all the four-footed animals were called up to fight in it: oxen, asses, cows, deer, and every other animal the earth held. And the willow-wren called up everything that flew in the air, not only birds large and small, but midges too, and hornets, bees and flies.

When the day of the war drew near, the willow-wren sent out scouts to find out who would command the enemy. The gnat, the sneakiest of them all, flew into the forest where the enemy had gathered and hid under a leaf on the very tree where the password was to be given out. There stood the bear. He called the fox over and said, “Fox, you’re the cleverest animal there is. You’ll be our general and lead us.” “Very well,” said the fox, “but what signal should we agree on?” Nobody had an answer, so the fox said, “I have a fine long bushy tail that looks almost like a plume of red feathers. When I hold my tail up high, things are going well, and you should charge. But if I let it hang down, run for your lives.” Once the gnat had heard this, she flew back and told the willow-wren everything, down to the smallest detail. At daybreak, when the battle was about to begin, all the four-footed animals came racing up so noisily that the ground shook. The willow-wren and his army came flying through the air as well, humming and whirring and swarming so loudly that everyone grew uneasy and afraid, and the two sides advanced on each other. But the willow-wren sent the hornet down with orders to settle under the fox’s tail and sting with all his strength. At the first sting the fox flinched and lifted one leg in pain, but he bore it and kept his tail high in the air. At the second sting he had to lower it for a moment. At the third he could stand it no longer: he screamed and tucked his tail between his legs. When the animals saw that, they thought everything was lost and fled, each to his own hole, and the birds won the battle.

Then the King and Queen flew home to their children and called out, “Children, be glad! Eat and drink as much as you like. We’ve won the battle!” But the young wrens said, “We won’t eat yet. First the bear has to come to the nest, beg our pardon and say that we are honorable children. Only then will we eat.” So the willow-wren flew to the bear’s hole and shouted, “Growler, you must come to the nest, to my children, and beg their pardon, or every rib in your body will be broken.” The bear crept over, terrified, and begged their pardon. Only then were the young wrens satisfied. They sat down together, ate and drank, and made merry until late into the night.

chapters.title: The Frog-Prince
paragraphs: One fine evening a young princess put on her bonnet and clogs and went out for a walk alone in a wood. When she came to a cool spring of water that bubbled up in the middle of it, she sat down to rest for a while. In her hand she held a golden ball, her favorite plaything, and she kept tossing it up in the air and catching it again as it came down. After a while she threw it so high that she missed it. The ball bounced away and rolled along the ground until at last it dropped into the spring.
