The princess peered into the water after her ball, but the spring was so deep that she could not see the bottom. Then she began to lament her loss, saying, “Oh, if only I could have my ball back! I would give all my fine clothes and jewels and everything I own in the world.”

While she was speaking, a frog stuck his head out of the water and said, “Princess, why are you crying so bitterly?” “Oh,” she said, “what could you do for me, you nasty frog? My golden ball has fallen into the spring.” The frog said, “I don’t want your pearls or jewels or fine clothes. But if you will love me, and let me live with you, and eat from your golden plate, and sleep in your bed, then I will bring you your ball.” “What nonsense this silly frog is talking,” thought the princess. “He can never even get out of the spring to visit me, though he may be able to fetch my ball. So I’ll tell him he can have what he asks.” And she said to the frog, “All right. If you bring me my ball, I’ll do everything you ask.” The frog ducked his head and dived deep under the water. After a little while he came up again with the ball in his mouth and tossed it onto the edge of the spring. The moment the young princess saw her ball, she ran to pick it up, and she was so delighted to hold it again that she never thought of the frog and ran home with it as fast as she could. The frog called after her, “Wait, princess, and take me with you as you promised!” But she did not stop to hear a word.

The next day, just as the princess sat down to dinner, she heard a strange sound—tap, tap, plash, plash—as if something were climbing the marble staircase. Soon there was a soft knock at the door, and a little voice called out:

“Open the door, my princess dear,
Open the door, your true love’s here!
Remember the words that you and I said
By the cool spring in the greenwood shade.”

The princess ran to the door and opened it, and there was the frog, whom she had completely forgotten. She was badly frightened. She slammed the door shut as fast as she could and went back to her seat. The king, her father, saw that something had scared her and asked what was the matter. “There’s a nasty frog at the door,” she said. “He fetched my ball out of the spring for me this morning. I told him he could live with me here, because I thought he could never get out of the spring. But now he’s at the door, and he wants to come in.”
While she was speaking, the frog knocked at the door again and called:

“Open the door, my princess dear,
Open the door, your true love’s here!
Remember the words that you and I said
By the cool spring in the greenwood shade.”

Then the king said to the young princess, “You gave your word, so you must keep it. Go and let him in.” She did, and the frog hopped into the room and then straight across it—tap, tap, plash, plash—from one end to the other, until he reached the table where the princess sat. “Please lift me onto a chair,” he said to the princess, “and let me sit next to you.” As soon as she had done so, the frog said, “Push your plate closer so I can eat from it.” She did that too, and when he had eaten all he could, he said, “Now I’m tired. Carry me upstairs and put me in your bed.” The princess, though very unwilling, picked him up in her hand and set him on the pillow of her own bed, where he slept all night. As soon as it was light, he jumped up, hopped downstairs and left the house. “Well,” thought the princess, “at last he’s gone, and he won’t trouble me any more.”
But she was wrong. When night came again, she heard the same tapping at the door, and the frog was back, calling:

“Open the door, my princess dear,
Open the door, your true love’s here!
Remember the words that you and I said
By the cool spring in the greenwood shade.”

When the princess opened the door, the frog came in and slept on her pillow as before, until morning. On the third night he did the same. But when the princess woke the next morning, she was astonished to find, in place of the frog, a handsome prince standing at the head of her bed and gazing at her with the most beautiful eyes she had ever seen.

He told her that a spiteful fairy had enchanted him and turned him into a frog, and that he was doomed to stay that way until some princess lifted him out of the spring, let him eat from her plate and let him sleep on her bed for three nights. “You,” said the prince, “have broken the fairy’s cruel spell, and now I wish for nothing more than that you come with me to my father’s kingdom, where I will marry you and love you as long as you live.”

The young princess, as you can imagine, was quick to say “Yes” to all this. As they were speaking, a splendid coach drove up, drawn by eight beautiful horses with plumes of feathers on their heads and golden harness. Behind the coach rode the prince’s servant, faithful Heinrich, who had grieved so long and so bitterly over his dear master’s misfortune during the enchantment that his heart had nearly burst.

They said goodbye to the king and climbed into the coach with the eight horses, and all set off, full of joy and merriment, for the prince’s kingdom. They arrived safely, and there they lived happily for many years.

chapters.title: Cat and Mouse in Partnership
paragraphs: A certain cat had made friends with a mouse, and had told her so often how much love and friendship she felt for her that in the end the mouse agreed to live and keep house with her. “But we must lay in a supply for the winter, or we’ll go hungry,” said the cat. “And you, little mouse, can’t go poking about everywhere, or you’ll end up in a trap some day.” They took this good advice and bought a pot of fat, but they couldn’t decide where to put it. After thinking it over for a long time, the cat said, “I can’t think of a better place to keep it than the church, because nobody dares steal anything from there. We’ll tuck it under the altar and not touch it until we really need it.” So the pot was put away safely, but before long the cat was longing for it, and she said to the mouse, “I have something to tell you, little mouse. My cousin has had a baby boy and has asked me to be his godmother. He’s white with brown spots, and I’m to hold him over the font at the christening. Let me go out today, and you look after the house by yourself.” “Yes, yes,” answered the mouse, “by all means go. And if you get anything really good to eat, think of me. I’d love a drop of that sweet red christening wine myself.” None of it was true, though. The cat had no cousin and had not been asked to be anyone’s godmother. She went straight to the church, crept up to the pot of fat, started licking, and licked off the top layer. Then she strolled over the rooftops of the town, looked out for chances, stretched out in the sun, and licked her lips whenever she thought of the pot of fat. She did not come home until evening. “Well, there you are again,” said the mouse. “I’m sure you’ve had a lovely day.” “It all went well,” said the cat. “What did they name the child?” “Top-off!” said the cat, perfectly calm. “Top-off!” cried the mouse. “That’s a very strange and unusual name. Is it common in your family?” “What does it matter?” said the cat. “It’s no worse than Crumb-stealer, which is what your godchildren are called.”

Before long the cat was seized by another fit of longing. She said to the mouse, “You’ll have to do me a favor and run the house alone for another day. I’ve been asked to be godmother again, and since the child has a white ring around its neck, I can’t say no.” The good mouse agreed, but the cat sneaked along behind the town walls to the church and ate up half the pot of fat. “Nothing tastes as good as what you keep to yourself,” she said, and she was thoroughly pleased with her day’s work. When she got home, the mouse asked, “And what was this child christened?” “Half-done,” answered the cat. “Half-done! What are you saying? I’ve never heard that name in my life. I’ll bet you anything it isn’t in the calendar!”

The cat’s mouth soon began to water for more licking. “All good things come in threes,” she said. “I’ve been asked to be godmother again. The child is jet black, with only white paws, and not one other white hair on its whole body. That happens only once every few years. You’ll let me go, won’t you?” “Top-off! Half-done!” answered the mouse. “Such strange names. They make me think.” “That’s because you sit at home in your dark-gray fur coat and your long tail,” said the cat, “and fill your head with fancies. It comes of never going out in the daytime.” While the cat was away, the mouse cleaned the house and put it in order, but the greedy cat emptied the pot of fat completely. “Once everything is eaten up, a body gets some peace,” she told herself, and she came home only at nightfall, well fed and plump. The mouse asked at once what the third child had been named. “You won’t like it any better than the others,” said the cat. “He’s called All-gone.” “All-gone!” cried the mouse. “That is the most suspicious name of all! I’ve never seen it in print. All-gone. What can that mean?” She shook her head, curled up and went to sleep.

From then on nobody invited the cat to be a godmother. But when winter came and there was nothing left to find outside, the mouse remembered their store and said, “Come, cat, let’s go to our pot of fat that we put away for ourselves. We’ll enjoy that.” “Yes,” answered the cat, “you’ll enjoy it about as much as sticking that dainty tongue of yours out of the window.” They set off, and when they got there, the pot of fat was indeed still in its place, but it was empty. “Oh no,” said the mouse, “now I see what happened. Now it comes out! You’re a fine friend! You ate it all while you were off being godmother. First top-off, then half-done, then—” “Hold your tongue,” cried the cat, “or say one more word and I’ll eat you too.” “All-gone” was already on the poor mouse’s lips. She had barely said it when the cat sprang on her, seized her and swallowed her down. That, truly, is the way of the world.

chapters.title: The Goose-Girl
paragraphs: A king who ruled a great country died, leaving his queen alone with their only child, a daughter of rare beauty. Her mother loved her dearly and treated her with great tenderness. There was also a kindly fairy who was fond of the princess and helped the queen look after her. When the girl was grown, she was promised in marriage to a prince who lived far away, and as the wedding day came close, she prepared to travel to his country. The queen, her mother, packed a great many costly things: jewels, gold and silver, ornaments, fine gowns, and in short everything a royal bride ought to have. She also sent along a waiting-maid, who was to ride with the princess and hand her over to the bridegroom, and each of them had a horse for the journey. The princess’s horse was a gift from the fairy. Its name was Falada, and it could speak.

When the time came to leave, the fairy went to her bedroom, took a little knife and cut a lock of her own hair. She gave it to the princess and said, “Keep this safe, dear child, because it is a charm, and it may help you on the road.” Then everyone said a sad goodbye to the princess. She tucked the lock of hair inside her dress, climbed onto her horse and rode off toward her bridegroom’s kingdom.

One day they were riding beside a brook, and the princess grew very thirsty. She said to her maid, “Please get down and bring me some water from that brook in my golden cup, because I want a drink.” “No,” said the maid. “If you’re thirsty, get down yourself, bend down to the water and drink. I’m not going to be your servant any longer.” The princess was so thirsty that she climbed down and knelt over the little brook to drink. She was afraid, and did not dare to take out her golden cup. She wept and said, “Alas, what will become of me?” And the lock of hair answered her:

“Alas, alas, if your mother knew,
Bitterly, bitterly she would rue.”
But the princess was gentle and meek, so she said nothing about her maid’s bad behavior and simply got back on her horse.

They rode on for a good while, until the day turned so hot and the sun so fierce that the bride grew thirsty again. At last they came to a river, and, forgetting how rudely her maid had spoken before, she said, “Please get down and bring me some water in my golden cup.” But the maid answered even more arrogantly than before: “Drink if you want to, but I won’t be your servant.” The princess was so thirsty that she got off her horse, lay down and bent her head over the flowing water. She cried and said, “What will become of me?” And the lock of hair answered her once more:

“Alas, alas, if your mother knew,
Bitterly, bitterly she would rue.”

As she leaned down to drink, the lock of hair slipped out of her dress and floated off on the water. She was too frightened to notice, but the maid saw it and was delighted, because she knew about the charm. She could see that, with the hair gone, the poor bride would be in her power. So when the bride had finished drinking and was about to mount Falada again, the maid said, “I’ll ride Falada now, and you can have my horse.” The princess had to give up her horse, and soon after that she was made to take off her royal clothes and put on her maid’s shabby ones.

Finally, as they came near the end of the journey, the treacherous servant threatened to kill her mistress if she ever told anyone what had happened. But Falada had seen everything, and he took careful note of it.

Then the maid mounted Falada, the real bride took the other horse, and they rode on like that until they reached the royal court. Their arrival was greeted with great joy. The prince rushed out to meet them and lifted the maid down from her horse, believing she was the one he was to marry. She was led upstairs to the royal chamber, while the true princess was told to wait down in the courtyard.

It happened that the old king had nothing to do just then, so he sat at his kitchen window, watching what went on outside, and he noticed her standing in the courtyard. She was pretty, and far too delicate-looking for a waiting-maid, so he went up to the royal chamber and asked the bride who the girl was that she had brought with her and left standing below. “I brought her along to keep me company on the road,” said the bride. “Please give the girl some work, so she isn’t idle.” For a while the old king could think of no work for her, but finally he said, “I have a boy who looks after my geese. She can go and help him.” The boy’s name, the one the real bride was to help with the king’s geese, was Curdken.

Soon afterward the false bride said to the prince, “Dear husband, please do me a favor.” “Gladly,” said the prince. “Then have one of your butchers cut off the head of the horse I rode here, because it was wild and gave me a great deal of trouble on the road.” The truth was that she was terrified Falada might one day speak and tell everything she had done to the princess. She got her way, and faithful Falada was killed. When the true princess heard of it, she wept, and she begged the man to nail Falada’s head up on a large dark gate of the city, which she had to pass through every morning and evening, so that she could still see him now and then. The butcher said he would do as she asked, and he cut off the head and nailed it up beneath the dark gate.
At dawn, when she and Curdken passed through the gate, she spoke sorrowfully:
“Falada, Falada, there you hang!”
and the head answered:

“Bride, bride, there you go!
Alas, alas, if your mother knew,
Bitterly, bitterly she would rue.”

Then they went out of the city and drove the geese along. When she reached the meadow she sat down on a grassy bank and let down her wavy hair, which was pure silver. Curdken saw it glittering in the sun and ran over, wanting to pull out a few strands, but she cried:

“Blow, breezes, blow!
Let Curdken’s hat go!
Blow, breezes, blow!
Let him after it go!
Over hills, dales and rocks,
Away may it whirl,
Till my silver locks
Are all combed and curled!”

A wind came up, so strong that it blew Curdken’s hat right off, and away it flew over the hills. He had to turn and run after it, and by the time he got back she had finished combing and curling her hair and had pinned it up safely again. He was angry and sulky and would not say a word to her. They watched the geese until it grew dark in the evening, and then drove them home.
On the following morning, when they came to the dark gate again, the poor girl glanced up at Falada’s head and called out:
“Falada, Falada, there you hang!”
and the head answered:

“Bride, bride, there you go!
Alas, alas, if your mother knew,
Bitterly, bitterly she would rue.”
Then she drove the geese on, sat down in the meadow again and began to comb out her hair as before. Curdken ran up and tried to grab it, but she called out quickly:

“Blow, breezes, blow!
Let Curdken’s hat go!
Blow, breezes, blow!
Let him after it go!
Over hills, dales and rocks,
Away may it whirl,
Till my silver locks
Are all combed and curled!”

Then the wind came and blew his hat off, and it flew a long way, over the hills and far away, so that he had to run after it. When he came back, she had tied up her hair again, and everything was safe. So they watched the geese until dark.

That evening, after they got home, Curdken went to the old king and said, “I don’t want that strange girl helping me with the geese any more.” “Why not?” asked the king. “Because she does no good at all. She just teases me all day long.” The king made him explain what had happened, and Curdken said, “When we go through the dark gate in the morning with our flock of geese, she cries out and talks to the head of a horse that hangs on the wall. She says:
“Falada, Falada, there you hang!”
and the head answers:

“Bride, bride, there you go!
Alas, alas, if your mother knew,
Bitterly, bitterly she would rue.”

And Curdken went on to tell the king what happened in the meadow where the geese grazed: how his hat was blown away, and how he had to run after it and leave his flock to look after itself. But the old king told the boy to go out again the next day. When morning came, the king stood hidden behind the dark gate and heard how she spoke to Falada and how Falada answered. Then he went out to the field and hid in a bush at the edge of the meadow. Before long he saw with his own eyes how they drove the geese along and how, after a little while, she let down her hair, glittering in the sun. And then he heard her say:

“Blow, breezes, blow!
Let Curdken’s hat go!
Blow, breezes, blow!
Let him after it go!
Over hills, dales and rocks,
Away may it whirl,
Till my silver locks
Are all combed and curled!”

Straight away a gust of wind came and carried off Curdken’s hat, and Curdken ran after it, while the girl went on combing and curling her hair. The old king saw all of this. He went home without being seen, and when the little goose-girl came back in the evening, he called her aside and asked why she did these things. But she burst into tears and said, “I must not tell you, or any man, or I will lose my life.”

But the old king begged and pleaded so hard that she had no peace until she had told him the whole tale, from beginning to end, word for word. It was lucky for her that she did, because when she finished, the king had royal clothes put on her and stared at her in wonder, she was so beautiful. Then he called his son and told him that he had only a false bride, a mere waiting-maid, while the true bride was standing right there. The young king was overjoyed when he saw her beauty and heard how meek and patient she had been. Without a word to the false bride, the king ordered a great feast to be prepared for the whole court. The bridegroom sat at the head of the table, with the false princess on one side and the true one on the other. Nobody recognized her, because her beauty dazzled their eyes, and in her brilliant dress she looked nothing like the little goose-girl.

When they had eaten and drunk and were in high spirits, the old king said he would tell them a story. He began, and told the whole tale of the princess as though he had heard it somewhere long ago. Then he asked the true princess’s waiting-maid what she thought should be done to anyone who behaved like that. “Nothing better,” said the false bride, “than to put her in a barrel studded with sharp nails, harness two white horses to it, and have them drag it from street to street until she is dead.” “You are the one!” said the old king. “You have passed judgment on yourself, and so it shall be done to you.” Then the young king married his true wife, and they ruled the kingdom in peace and happiness for the rest of their lives. The good fairy came to visit them, and she brought faithful Falada back to life.

chapters.title: Chanticleer and Partlet: How They Went to the Mountains to Eat Nuts
paragraphs: “The nuts are ripe now,” Chanticleer said to his wife Partlet. “Let’s go up to the mountains together and eat as many as we can, before the squirrel carries them all off.” “Gladly,” said Partlet. “Let’s make a holiday of it.”

So they went up to the mountains, and since it was a lovely day, they stayed until evening. Whether they had eaten so many nuts that they couldn’t walk, or whether they were simply lazy and didn’t want to, I don’t know. In any case, they decided it was beneath them to go home on foot. So Chanticleer started building a little carriage out of nutshells. When it was finished, Partlet hopped in and sat down, and told Chanticleer to harness himself to it and pull her home. “That’s a good joke!” said Chanticleer. “No, that won’t do at all. I’d much rather walk home. I’ll sit up on the box and be the coachman, if you like, but I won’t do the pulling.” While they were arguing, a duck came quacking up and cried, “You thieving vagabonds, what are you doing on my land? I’ll teach you a lesson for your insolence!” And with that she attacked Chanticleer with all her might. But Chanticleer was no coward, and he hit back at the duck with his sharp spurs so fiercely that she was soon crying for mercy. He would grant it only on one condition: that she pull the carriage home for them. She agreed, and Chanticleer climbed onto the box and drove, crying, “Now, duck, get going as fast as you can.” And off they went at a fairly good pace.

After they had gone a little way, they met a needle and a pin walking along the road together. The needle called out, “Stop, stop!” He said it was so dark that they could hardly see where they were going, and the mud was so bad that they couldn’t get along at all. He explained that he and his friend the pin had been at an inn a few miles back and had sat drinking until they forgot how late it was. So he asked whether the travelers would be kind enough to give them a ride in their carriage. Chanticleer saw that they were only thin fellows who wouldn’t take up much room. He told them they could ride, but made them promise not to dirty the wheels as they climbed in, and not to step on Partlet’s toes.

Late at night they reached an inn. Traveling in the dark was difficult, and the duck seemed very tired and kept waddling from side to side, so they decided to stay there. The landlord was unwilling at first and said his house was full, because he thought they might not be respectable company. But they spoke politely to him, and they gave him the egg Partlet had laid along the way, and said they would also give him the duck, who laid one every day. So in the end he let them in, and they ordered a fine supper and spent the evening very merrily.

Before it was properly light, while everyone at the inn was still asleep, Chanticleer woke his wife. He fetched the egg, and the two of them pecked a hole in it, ate it up, and tossed the shells into the fireplace. Then they went over to the pin and the needle, who were sound asleep, grabbed them by the head, and pushed one into the landlord’s armchair and the other into his handkerchief. That done, they tiptoed away as quietly as they could. The duck, though, slept outdoors in the yard. She heard them coming, jumped into the brook that ran right beside the inn, and swam off out of their reach.

An hour or two later the landlord got up and reached for his handkerchief to wipe his face, but the pin stabbed him. He went to the kitchen to light his pipe at the fire, and when he stirred the embers, the eggshells flew up into his eyes and nearly blinded him. “Goodness me!” he said. “It seems the whole world has it in for my head this morning.” And with that he flung himself crossly into his armchair. But oh dear! The needle went into him, and this time it was not his head that hurt. He flew into a terrible rage. He suspected the guests who had arrived the night before and went to look for them, but they had all gone. He swore he would never again take in a gang of vagabonds who ate heartily, paid nothing, and gave him no thanks for his trouble except their monkey tricks.

chapters.title: Chanticleer and Partlet: How Chanticleer and Partlet Went to Visit Mr Korbes
paragraphs: On another day Chanticleer and Partlet decided to go out for a ride together. Chanticleer built a handsome carriage with four red wheels and hitched six mice to it, and then he and Partlet climbed in and off they drove. Before long a cat met them and asked, “Where are you off to?” And Chanticleer answered,

“We’re on our way
A visit to pay
To Mr Korbes, the fox, today.”
Then the cat said, “Take me with you.” “Gladly,” said Chanticleer. “Climb up on the back, and make sure you don’t fall off.”

“Look after this fine coach of mine,
And keep my pretty red wheels clean!
Now, mice, get ready,
And, wheels, roll steady!
For we’re on our way a visit to pay
To Mr Korbes, the fox, today.”
Soon a millstone, an egg, a duck and a pin came along, and Chanticleer let them all climb into the carriage and ride with them.

When they got to Mr Korbes’s house, he was not at home. So the mice pulled the carriage into the coach-house, Chanticleer and Partlet flew up onto a beam, the cat settled down in the fireplace, the duck climbed into the washing tub, the pin stuck himself into the bed pillow, the millstone lay down across the top of the front door, and the egg rolled itself up in the towel.

When Mr Korbes came home, he went to the fireplace to build a fire, but the cat threw all the ashes in his eyes. He ran to the kitchen to wash, but there the duck splashed water all over his face. When he tried to dry himself, the egg broke to pieces in the towel, all over his face and eyes. Now he was very angry, and he went to bed without any supper. But when he laid his head on the pillow, the pin stabbed his cheek. At that he was absolutely furious, and he jumped up and would have run out of the house. But when he reached the door, the millstone fell on his head and killed him on the spot.

chapters.title: Chanticleer and Partlet: How Partlet Died and Was Buried, and How Chanticleer Died of Grief
paragraphs: On another day Chanticleer and Partlet agreed to go up into the mountains again to eat nuts, and they settled that any nuts they found would be shared equally. Partlet found a very large nut, but she said nothing to Chanticleer about it and kept it all for herself. It was so big, though, that she could not swallow it, and it stuck in her throat. She was terrified and cried out to Chanticleer, “Please run as fast as you can and fetch me some water, or I will choke!” Chanticleer ran as fast as he could to the river and said, “River, give me some water, because Partlet is lying on the mountain and will choke on a big nut.” The river answered, “First run to the bride and ask her for a silken cord to draw the water up.” Chanticleer ran to the bride and said, “Bride, you must give me a silken cord, because then the river will give me water, and I will carry the water to Partlet, who is lying on the mountain and will choke on a big nut.” But the bride said, “First run and bring me my garland, which is hanging on a willow in the garden.” So Chanticleer ran to the garden, took the garland from the branch where it hung, and brought it to the bride. Then the bride gave him the silken cord, and he took the silken cord to the river, and the river gave him water, and he carried the water to Partlet. But in the meantime she had choked on the big nut, and she lay quite dead and never moved again.

Chanticleer was heartbroken and cried bitterly, and all the animals came and wept with him over poor Partlet. Six mice built a little hearse to carry her to her grave, and when it was finished they harnessed themselves to the front of it, and Chanticleer drove them. On the way they met the fox. “Where are you going, Chanticleer?” he asked. “To bury my Partlet,” said Chanticleer. “May I come with you?” asked the fox. “Yes, but you must climb up on the back, or my horses won’t be able to pull you.” So the fox climbed up on the back, and soon the wolf, the bear, the goat and all the other animals of the wood came and climbed onto the hearse as well.

So they went on until they came to a fast stream. “How will we get across?” said Chanticleer. A straw said, “I will lay myself across, and you can cross over on me.” But as the mice were crossing, the straw slid away and fell into the water, and all six mice fell in and drowned. What was to be done? Then a big log came and said, “I am large enough. I will lay myself across the stream, and you can cross over on me.” So he lay down across it, but they went about it so clumsily that the log fell in and was swept away by the current. Then a stone, who had seen what happened, came over and kindly offered to help poor Chanticleer by lying across the stream. This time Chanticleer got safely to the other side with the hearse and managed to pull Partlet out of it. But the fox and the other mourners, who were sitting at the back, were too heavy. They fell back into the water and were all swept away and drowned.

So Chanticleer was left alone with his dead Partlet. He dug a grave for her, laid her in it, and heaped a little mound over her. Then he sat down beside the grave and wept and mourned until at last he died too. And so everyone was dead.

chapters.title: Rapunzel
paragraphs: Once there was a man and a woman who had wished for a child for a long time, without success. At last the woman began to hope that God was about to grant her wish. At the back of their house they had a little window that looked out on a splendid garden, full of the loveliest flowers and herbs. A high wall surrounded it, and no one dared to enter, because it belonged to an enchantress who had great power and was feared by everyone. One day the woman was standing at this window, looking down into the garden, when she noticed a bed planted with the most beautiful rampion (rapunzel). It looked so fresh and green that she longed for some. She wanted it so much that she pined away and grew pale and miserable. Her husband became alarmed and asked, “What is wrong, dear wife?” “Oh,” she answered, “if I can’t eat some of that rampion from the garden behind our house, I will die.” The man loved her, and he thought, “Rather than let my wife die, I will fetch her some of that rampion, whatever it costs.” At twilight he climbed over the wall into the enchantress’s garden, hurriedly snatched a handful of rampion, and took it to his wife. She made a salad of it at once and ate it greedily. It tasted so good to her, so very good, that the next day she wanted it three times as much as before. If he was ever to have any peace, her husband would have to go down into the garden once more. So in the gloom of evening he lowered himself down again. But when he had climbed down the wall he was terrified, for there stood the enchantress right in front of him. “How dare you,” she said, with an angry look, “climb into my garden and steal my rampion like a thief? You will pay for this!” “Oh,” he answered, “let mercy win out over justice. I only did it because I had to. My wife saw your rampion from the window and wanted it so badly that she would have died if she hadn’t had some to eat.” Then the enchantress let her anger cool and said to him, “If it is as you say, I will let you take as much rampion as you like. But I have one condition: you must give me the child your wife will bring into the world. It will be well treated, and I will look after it like a mother.” In his terror the man agreed to everything. When the woman gave birth, the enchantress appeared at once, named the child Rapunzel, and took her away.

Rapunzel grew up to be the most beautiful child under the sun. When she was twelve years old, the enchantress shut her up in a tower in a forest. It had no stairs and no door, only a little window right at the top. When the enchantress wanted to go in, she stood beneath the window and called:

“Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
Let down your hair to me.”

Rapunzel had magnificent long hair, as fine as spun gold. When she heard the enchantress’s voice, she undid her braids, wound them around one of the window hooks, and let them fall twenty ells to the ground, and the enchantress climbed up by them.

A year or two later, the king’s son happened to ride through the forest and past the tower. He heard singing so lovely that he stopped to listen. It was Rapunzel, who passed the time in her loneliness by letting her sweet voice ring out. The king’s son wanted to climb up to her and looked for a door into the tower, but there was none. He rode home, but the singing had touched his heart so deeply that he went out into the forest every day to listen to it. One day, as he stood behind a tree, he saw an enchantress arrive, and he heard her call out:

“Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
Let down your hair to me.”

Then Rapunzel let down her braids, and the enchantress climbed up to her. “If that is the ladder people climb up by, then I will try my luck too,” he said. The next day, as it began to get dark, he went to the tower and called:

“Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
Let down your hair to me.”
At once the hair fell down, and the king’s son climbed up.

At first Rapunzel was terribly frightened when a man came in, for her eyes had never seen one before. But the king’s son talked to her like a friend. He told her that his heart had been so stirred that he could find no rest and had been forced to see her. Then Rapunzel lost her fear. When he asked whether she would take him as her husband, and she saw that he was young and handsome, she thought, “He will love me more than old Dame Gothel does.” So she said yes and put her hand in his. She said, “I would gladly go away with you, but I don’t know how to get down. Every time you come, bring a skein of silk, and I will weave a ladder from it. When it is finished, I will climb down, and you can take me away on your horse.” They agreed that until then he would come to her every evening, since the old woman came during the day. The enchantress noticed nothing, until one day Rapunzel said to her, “Tell me, Dame Gothel, how is it that you are so much heavier to pull up than the young king’s son? He is up here in a moment.” “Oh, you wicked child!” cried the enchantress. “What do I hear you say? I thought I had cut you off from the whole world, and still you have deceived me!” In her rage she seized Rapunzel’s beautiful hair, wrapped it twice around her left hand, took a pair of scissors in her right, and snip, snap, the hair was cut off and the lovely braids lay on the ground. And she was so merciless that she took poor Rapunzel to a wilderness, where she had to live in great sorrow and misery.
On the same day that she cast Rapunzel out, the enchantress fastened the braids she had cut off to the window hook. When the king’s son came and called:

“Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
Let down your hair to me.”

she let the hair down. The king’s son climbed up, but instead of finding his dear Rapunzel, he found the enchantress, who stared at him with wicked, venomous eyes. “Aha!” she cried mockingly. “You came to fetch your darling, but the beautiful bird no longer sits singing in her nest. The cat has got her, and it will scratch out your eyes as well. Rapunzel is lost to you. You will never see her again.” The king’s son was beside himself with grief, and in his despair he leapt from the tower. He escaped with his life, but the thorns he fell into pierced his eyes. Then he wandered blind through the forest, eating nothing but roots and berries, and did nothing but lament and weep over the loss of his dearest wife. He roamed in misery like this for some years, and at last he came to the wilderness where Rapunzel lived in wretchedness with the twins she had given birth to, a boy and a girl. He heard a voice, and it seemed so familiar that he walked toward it. When he came close, Rapunzel recognized him, threw her arms around his neck and wept. Two of her tears fell on his eyes, and they grew clear again, and he could see as well as before. He took her to his kingdom, where he was welcomed with joy, and they lived happily and contentedly for a long time after.

chapters.title: Fundevogel
paragraphs: Once there was a forester who went into the forest to hunt. As he entered it, he heard screaming, as if a little child were there. He followed the sound and at last came to a tall tree. At the top of it sat a little child. The mother had fallen asleep under the tree with the child in her arms, and a bird of prey had seen it, swooped down, snatched it away, and set it on the high tree.

The forester climbed the tree, lifted the child down, and thought to himself, “I’ll take him home and raise him alongside my Lina.” So he carried the baby home, and the two children grew up side by side. The one he had found in the tree was named Fundevogel, since a bird had carried him off. Fundevogel and Lina were so fond of each other that whenever they were apart, they were miserable.

The forester had an old cook. One evening she picked up two pails and started fetching water from the spring, and she didn’t make just one trip but many. Lina noticed and asked, “Tell me, old Sanna, why are you carrying so much water?” “I’ll tell you, if you swear never to repeat it to anyone.” Lina promised that she would never tell a soul, and the cook said, “Early tomorrow morning, as soon as the forester has gone hunting, I’m going to heat up the water. When it’s boiling in the kettle, I’ll throw Fundevogel in and boil him.”

Early the next morning the forester got up and went off hunting. While he was away, the children were still lying in bed. Lina said to Fundevogel, “If you promise never to leave me, I’ll never leave you either.” Fundevogel answered, “I won’t leave you, now or ever.” Then Lina said, “Then I’ll tell you. Last night old Sanna hauled bucket after bucket of water into the house, so I asked her why. She said she would tell me if I promised not to repeat it to anyone. Then she told me that early tomorrow morning, when Father is out hunting, she will fill the kettle, throw you in and boil you. But let’s get up quickly, get dressed and run away together.”

So the two children got up, dressed in a hurry and left. When the water in the kettle was bubbling, the cook went to the bedroom to fetch Fundevogel and throw him in. But when she walked in and reached the beds, both children had vanished. She was horrified and said to herself, “What am I going to tell the forester when he comes home and finds the children gone? They have to be chased right now and brought back.”

The cook sent three servants to chase the children and catch them. But the children were sitting at the edge of the forest, and when they saw the three servants running toward them from far off, Lina said to Fundevogel, “Never leave me, and I’ll never leave you.” Fundevogel said, “Not now, not ever.” Then Lina said, “You turn into a rose-bush, and I’ll be the rose on it.” When the three servants reached the forest, there was nothing there but a rose-bush with one rose on it, and no sign of the children. “There’s nothing for us here,” they said, and they went home and told the cook that they had seen nothing in the forest except a little rose-bush with a single rose. The old cook scolded them. “You idiots! You should have cut the rose-bush in half, snapped off the rose and brought it back with you. Go and do it, now.” So they had to go out and search a second time. But the children saw them coming from a long way off. Lina said, “Fundevogel, never leave me, and I’ll never leave you.” Fundevogel said, “Not now, not ever.” Lina said, “Then you turn into a church, and I’ll be the chandelier inside it.” When the three servants arrived, there was nothing but a church with a chandelier in it. They said to each other, “What can we do here? Let’s go home.” When they got back, the cook asked whether they had found the children, and they said no, they had found nothing but a church with a chandelier inside. The cook scolded them again. “You fools! Why didn’t you tear the church down and bring the chandelier home?” This time the old cook got to her feet herself and set off with the three servants after the children. Once more the children saw, far off, the three servants coming and the cook waddling along behind them. Lina said, “Fundevogel, never leave me, and I’ll never leave you.” Fundevogel said, “Not now, not ever.” Lina said, “Then be a fishpond, and I’ll be the duck swimming on it.” The cook came up to them, and when she saw the pond, she lay down beside it and started to drink it dry. But the duck swam over fast, grabbed her head in its beak and pulled her into the water, and the old witch drowned there. Then the children went home together, very happy, and if they haven’t died, they’re still alive today.

chapters.title: The Valiant Little Tailor
paragraphs: One summer morning a little tailor was sitting on his table by the window in a cheerful mood, sewing with all his might. A peasant woman came down the street calling, “Good jam for sale, cheap! Good jam, cheap!” That sounded lovely to the tailor. He poked his dainty head out of the window and called, “Come up here, my good woman. You’ll sell your goods here.” The woman climbed the three steps to the tailor with her heavy basket, and he had her unpack every one of her pots. He looked over each one, held it up, sniffed it, and finally said, “This jam seems good to me. Weigh me out four ounces, my good woman, and if it comes to a quarter pound, that’s no matter.” The woman, who had hoped for a good sale, gave him what he asked for, but she left angry and muttering. “May God bless this jam,” cried the little tailor, “and give me health and strength!” Then he took the bread out of the cupboard, cut a slice straight across the whole loaf and spread the jam on it. “This won’t taste bitter,” he said, “but first I’ll finish the jacket before I take a bite.” He set the bread down next to him and went on sewing, and in his happiness he made his stitches bigger and bigger. Meanwhile the smell of the sweet jam drifted up to where a great many flies were sitting, and it drew them in, and they came down on the bread in swarms. “Hey! Who invited you?” said the little tailor, and shooed away the uninvited guests. But the flies understood no German and wouldn’t be driven off. They kept coming back in bigger and bigger crowds. At last the little tailor lost his patience. He pulled a piece of cloth out of the hole under his worktable and said, “Wait, I’ll give you something!” and he brought it down on them without mercy. When he lifted it and counted, no fewer than seven lay in front of him, dead, with their legs stretched out. “So you’re that sort of fellow?” he said, and he couldn’t help admiring his own courage. “The whole town has to hear about this!” And the little tailor quickly cut himself a belt, stitched it up, and embroidered on it in big letters: “Seven at one stroke!” “The town, did I say?” he went on. “The whole world will hear of it!” And his heart wagged with joy like a lamb’s tail. The tailor put on the belt and decided to go out into the world, because he thought his workshop was too small for his bravery. Before leaving, he searched the house for something to take along, but he found nothing except an old cheese, and he put that in his pocket. In front of the door he noticed a bird that had got itself caught in the bushes. It went into his pocket with the cheese. Then he set off boldly down the road, and since he was light and quick on his feet, he never felt tired. The road led up a mountain, and when he reached the top, a mighty giant was sitting there, calmly looking out over the land. The little tailor walked up bravely, spoke to him, and said, “Good day, comrade! So you’re sitting up here looking out over the wide world! I’m on my way out there myself to try my luck. Do you feel like coming along?” The giant gave the tailor a scornful look and said, “You scruffy little wretch! You miserable creature!”

“Is that so?” answered the little tailor. He unbuttoned his coat and showed the giant his belt. “Read that, and see what kind of man I am!” The giant read “Seven at one stroke,” and assumed they were men the tailor had killed, and he began to feel some respect for the tiny fellow. Still, he wanted to test him first. He picked up a stone and squeezed it until water dripped out of it. “Do that too,” said the giant, “if you’re strong enough.” “Is that all?” said the tailor. “That’s child’s play for us!” He reached into his pocket, took out the soft cheese and squeezed it until the liquid ran out. “There,” he said, “that was a little better, wasn’t it?” The giant didn’t know what to say, and he couldn’t believe it of such a little man. Then the giant picked up a stone and threw it so high that the eye could hardly follow it. “Now, you little scrap of a man, do that too.” “Nice throw,” said the tailor, “but in the end the stone fell back to earth. I’ll throw you one that never comes back at all.” He put his hand in his pocket, took out the bird and tossed it into the air. The bird, delighted to be free, soared up, flew off and never returned. “How do you like that throw, comrade?” asked the tailor. “You can certainly throw,” said the giant, “but now let’s see whether you can carry a load properly.” He led the little tailor to a huge oak lying felled on the ground and said, “If you’re strong enough, help me carry this tree out of the forest.” “Gladly,” answered the little man. “You take the trunk on your shoulders, and I’ll lift the branches and twigs. They’re the heaviest part, after all.” The giant hoisted the trunk onto his shoulder, but the tailor sat down on a branch. The giant couldn’t look back, so he had to carry the whole tree, with the little tailor on top of it as well. Back there, the tailor was merry and content, whistling the song “Three tailors rode out of the gate,” as if carrying a tree were child’s play. After dragging the heavy burden some of the way, the giant couldn’t go on, and he cried, “Listen, I’m going to have to drop the tree!” The tailor sprang nimbly down, grabbed the tree with both arms as if he had been carrying it all along, and said to the giant, “A big fellow like you, and you can’t even carry a tree!”

They went on together, and as they passed a cherry tree, the giant took hold of the top, where the ripest fruit hung, bent it down, put it in the tailor’s hand and told him to eat. But the little tailor was far too weak to hold the tree, and when the giant let go, it snapped back up and swung the tailor into the air with it. He came down again unhurt, and the giant said, “What’s this? Don’t you have the strength to hold a weak little twig?” “I have plenty of strength,” answered the little tailor. “Do you think that would be anything to a man who has struck down seven at one blow? I jumped over the tree because the huntsmen are shooting down there in the bushes. Jump the way I did, if you can.” The giant tried, but he couldn’t get over the tree and stayed hanging in the branches. So in this contest too, the tailor came out on top.

The giant said, “If you’re such a brave fellow, come with me to our cave and spend the night with us.” The little tailor agreed and followed him. When they entered the cave, other giants were sitting around the fire, each holding a roasted sheep and eating it. The little tailor looked around and thought, “It’s a lot roomier in here than in my workshop.” The giant showed him a bed and told him to lie down and sleep. But the bed was too big for the little tailor. He didn’t lie down in it, and curled up in a corner instead. At midnight, when the giant thought the little tailor was fast asleep, he got up, took a great iron bar, and smashed it through the bed in one blow, thinking he had finished off the grasshopper for good. At first light the giants went off into the forest, having completely forgotten the little tailor, when suddenly he came strolling up to them, cheerful and bold. The giants were terrified. They were afraid he would strike them all dead, and they ran off as fast as they could.

The little tailor walked on, always following his own pointed nose. After a long walk, he came to the courtyard of a royal palace, and since he felt tired, he lay down on the grass and fell asleep. While he lay there, people came and looked him over from every side, and they read on his belt: “Seven at one stroke.” “Ah,” they said, “what is a great warrior doing here in the middle of peacetime? He must be a mighty lord.” They went and reported him to the king, and they gave their opinion that if war broke out, this would be an important and useful man, and that on no account should he be allowed to leave. The advice pleased the king, and he sent one of his courtiers to the little tailor, to offer him military service as soon as he woke up. The messenger stood beside the sleeper, waited until he stretched his limbs and opened his eyes, and then gave him the offer. “That is exactly why I came here,” the tailor replied. “I’m ready to enter the king’s service.” So he was received with honor, and a special residence was set aside for him.

The soldiers, though, had turned against the little tailor and wished him a thousand miles away. “Where is this going to end?” they muttered to one another. “If we pick a fight with him and he lashes out, seven of us will drop with every blow. None of us can stand up to him.” So they made up their minds, went to the king as a group, and asked to be released from service. “We can’t stay,” they told him, “with a man who kills seven at a single stroke.” The king was distressed that he might lose all his loyal men because of one person. He wished he had never laid eyes on the tailor, and would gladly have been rid of him. But he didn’t dare dismiss him, since he feared the tailor might strike him and all his people dead and seize the throne for himself. He turned it over in his mind for a long while, and at last he hit on a plan. He sent word to the little tailor that, since he was such a great warrior, the king had a favor to ask of him. Two giants lived in a forest in his land, and they did terrible damage with their robbing, murdering, plundering and burning. No one could go near them without risking death. If the tailor defeated and killed these two giants, the king would give him his only daughter as his wife and half his kingdom as her dowry, and a hundred horsemen would ride with him to help. “Now that would be a fine thing for a man like me!” thought the little tailor. “You don’t get offered a beautiful princess and half a kingdom every day of your life!” “Oh, yes,” he answered, “I’ll deal with the giants soon enough, and I don’t need the hundred horsemen for it. A man who can hit seven with one blow has nothing to fear from two.”

The little tailor set off, and the hundred horsemen rode after him. At the edge of the forest he told his escort, “Just wait here. I’ll finish off the giants on my own.” Then he leapt into the forest and looked around him, left and right. Before long he spotted both giants. They were lying asleep under a tree, snoring so loudly that the branches rose and fell. The little tailor, who was no idler, filled two pockets with stones and climbed up the tree. Halfway up, he slid out along a branch until he was sitting right above the sleepers, and then he began dropping stones, one after another, onto the chest of one giant. For a long time the giant felt nothing, but at last he woke, shoved his companion, and said, “Why are you hitting me?” “You must be dreaming,” said the other. “I’m not hitting you.” They lay down to sleep again, and then the tailor dropped a stone on the second one. “What is this?” he cried. “Why are you pelting me?” “I’m not pelting you,” the first answered with a growl. They argued about it for a while, but they were tired, so they let it drop and their eyes closed again. The little tailor started his game over, chose the biggest stone he had, and hurled it with all his strength onto the first giant’s chest. “That’s too much!” the giant shouted, and he jumped up like a madman and slammed his companion against the tree until it shook. The other paid him back in kind, and they flew into such a rage that they ripped up trees and beat each other with them, until finally both fell dead on the ground at the same moment. Then the little tailor jumped down. “It’s lucky,” he said, “that they didn’t pull up the tree I was sitting in, or I’d have had to dash off to another one like a squirrel. But we tailors are nimble.” He drew his sword and stabbed each of them a couple of times in the chest, then went out to the horsemen and said, “It’s done. I’ve finished them both, but it was hard work! In their desperation they tore up trees and fought back with them, but that does them no good when a man like me turns up, one who can kill seven at one blow.” “But aren’t you wounded?” asked the horsemen. “Don’t trouble yourself about that,” the tailor replied. “They haven’t bent a single hair on my head.” The horsemen didn’t believe him and rode into the forest. There they found the giants swimming in their own blood, and all around them the uprooted trees.

The little tailor asked the king for the reward he had promised. But the king regretted his promise and started thinking again about how to get rid of the hero. “Before you get my daughter and half my kingdom,” he told him, “you must do one more heroic deed. A unicorn is roaming the forest and doing great harm, and you must catch it first.” “I fear one unicorn even less than two giants. Seven at one blow is my sort of business.” He took a rope and an axe, went out into the forest, and once again told the men sent with him to wait outside. He didn’t have to search long. The unicorn soon came toward him and charged straight at the tailor, ready to gore him with its horn without further ado. “Easy, easy, it can’t be done that quickly,” he said. He stood still and waited until the animal was very close, then jumped nimbly behind the tree. The unicorn crashed into the tree with all its force, and its horn stuck so fast in the trunk that it hadn’t the strength to pull it out again, and so it was caught. “Now I’ve got my bird,” said the tailor. He came out from behind the tree, put the rope around its neck, and chopped the horn out of the trunk with his axe. When everything was ready, he led the beast away and brought it to the king.

Still the king would not hand over the promised reward, and he made a third demand. Before the wedding, the tailor was to catch a wild boar that was wreaking havoc in the forest, and the huntsmen would help him. “Gladly,” said the tailor. “That’s child’s play!” He didn’t take the huntsmen into the forest with him, and they were quite happy about that, because the boar had received them so roughly on several earlier occasions that they had no wish to lie in wait for it. When the boar saw the tailor, it rushed at him with foaming mouth and sharpened tusks, meaning to knock him down. But the hero ran, sprang into a chapel nearby, went straight up to the window, and in one bound was out again. The boar charged in after him, but the tailor ran around the outside and shut the door behind it. The raging beast, far too heavy and clumsy to jump out of the window, was trapped. The little tailor called the huntsmen over so they could see the prisoner with their own eyes. The hero then went to the king, who now had to keep his promise whether he liked it or not, and give him his daughter and half his kingdom. If the king had known that the man standing before him was no warrior hero but only a little tailor, it would have wounded him even more than it did. The wedding was held with great splendor and little joy, and a tailor was made into a king.

Some time later the young queen heard her husband talking in his sleep one night. “Boy, make me the doublet and patch the pantaloons, or I’ll rap the yardstick over your ears.” That is how she learned what station in life the young lord had been born to. The next morning she took her complaint to her father and begged him to help her get rid of her husband, who was nothing but a tailor. The king comforted her and said, “Leave your bedroom door open tonight. My servants will wait outside, and when he has fallen asleep they’ll go in, tie him up, and carry him onto a ship that will take him out into the wide world.” The woman was content with this. But the king’s armor-bearer had overheard everything. He was friendly with the young lord and told him the whole plot. “I’ll put a stop to that business,” said the little tailor. At night he went to bed with his wife at the usual time, and when she thought he had fallen asleep, she got up, opened the door, and lay down again. The little tailor, who was only pretending to sleep, began to call out in a clear voice, “Boy, make me the doublet and patch me the pantaloons, or I’ll rap the yardstick over your ears. I struck seven with one blow. I killed two giants, I brought in a unicorn, and I caught a wild boar. And am I supposed to be afraid of the men standing outside this room?” When those men heard the tailor speak like that, a great dread came over them, and they ran as though the wild huntsman were at their heels. None of them dared try anything further against him. So the little tailor was a king, and stayed a king, for the rest of his life.

chapters.title: Hansel and Gretel
paragraphs: Near a great forest lived a poor woodcutter with his wife and his two children. The boy was called Hansel and the girl Gretel. He had hardly anything to eat, and when a great famine struck the land, he couldn’t even get their daily bread any more. One night he lay in bed worrying about this, tossing and turning in his anxiety, and he groaned and said to his wife, “What is going to become of us? How can we feed our poor children, when we have nothing left even for ourselves?” “I’ll tell you what, husband,” the woman answered. “Early tomorrow morning we’ll take the children out into the forest, to the thickest part. We’ll light a fire for them there and give each of them one more piece of bread, and then we’ll go off to our work and leave them alone. They won’t find their way home again, and we’ll be rid of them.” “No, wife,” said the man, “I won’t do that. How could I bring myself to leave my children alone in the forest? The wild animals would soon come and tear them apart.” “Oh, you fool!” she said. “Then all four of us will starve to death, and you may as well start planing the boards for our coffins.” She gave him no peace until he agreed. “But I still feel sorry for the poor children,” said the man.

The two children hadn’t been able to sleep either, from hunger, and they had heard what their stepmother said to their father. Gretel wept bitter tears and said to Hansel, “It’s all over for us now.” “Hush, Gretel,” said Hansel. “Don’t upset yourself. I’ll find a way to help us.” When the old people had fallen asleep, he got up, put on his little coat, opened the door downstairs, and crept outside. The moon was shining brightly, and the white pebbles lying in front of the house glittered like silver coins. Hansel bent down and stuffed his coat pocket with as many as it would hold. Then he went back in and said to Gretel, “Take comfort, dear little sister, and sleep in peace. God won’t abandon us.” And he lay down in his bed again. At daybreak, before the sun had risen, the woman came and woke the two children. “Get up, you lazybones! We’re going into the forest to fetch wood.” She gave each of them a small piece of bread and said, “That’s for your midday meal, but don’t eat it before then, because you’ll get nothing else.” Gretel put the bread under her apron, since Hansel had the pebbles in his pocket. Then they all set out together for the forest. After they had walked a little way, Hansel stopped and looked back at the house, and he did this again and again. His father said, “Hansel, what are you staring at, and why do you keep lagging behind? Pay attention, and don’t forget how to use your legs.” “Oh, Father,” said Hansel, “I’m looking at my little white cat. She’s sitting up on the roof and wants to say goodbye to me.” The woman said, “Fool, that isn’t your cat. That’s the morning sun shining on the chimneys.” But Hansel hadn’t been looking at any cat. He had been taking one white pebble after another out of his pocket and dropping it on the road.

When they reached the middle of the forest, the father said, “Now, children, gather some wood, and I’ll make a fire so that you won’t be cold.” Hansel and Gretel collected brushwood and piled it as high as a small hill. The brushwood was lit, and when the flames were leaping high, the woman said, “Now, children, lie down by the fire and rest. We’re going into the forest to cut wood. When we’re finished, we’ll come back and get you.”

Hansel and Gretel sat by the fire, and at noon each of them ate a small piece of bread. Hearing the sound of an axe, they believed their father was close by. But it wasn’t an axe. It was a branch that he had tied to a dead tree, and the wind was swinging it back and forth. They had been sitting there so long that their eyes closed from tiredness, and they fell fast asleep. When they finally woke, it was already dark night. Gretel started to cry and said, “How are we ever going to get out of the forest?” But Hansel comforted her. “Just wait a little while, until the moon has risen, and then we’ll find the way easily.” And when the full moon had risen, Hansel took his little sister by the hand and followed the pebbles, which shone like freshly minted silver coins and showed them the way.

They walked all night long, and at daybreak they came back to their father’s house. They knocked at the door, and when the woman opened it and saw that it was Hansel and Gretel, she said, “You wicked children, why did you sleep so long in the forest? We thought you weren’t coming back at all!” The father, though, was overjoyed, because it had broken his heart to leave them behind alone.

Not long afterward there was great famine in the land once more, and the children heard their mother say to their father one night, “We’ve eaten everything again. We have half a loaf left, and then that’s the end. The children have to go. We’ll take them deeper into the woods, so they can’t find their way out again. There is no other way to save ourselves!” The man’s heart was heavy, and he thought, “It would be better to share our last mouthful with the children.” But the woman wouldn’t listen to anything he had to say. She scolded him and heaped reproaches on him. Whoever says A must say B too, and since he had given in the first time, he had to give in the second time as well.

But the children were still awake and had heard the conversation. When the old people were asleep, Hansel got up again and wanted to go out and gather pebbles as he had before. But the woman had locked the door, and Hansel couldn’t get out. Even so, he comforted his little sister and said, “Don’t cry, Gretel. Go to sleep quietly. The good God will help us.”

The woman came at dawn and pulled the children out of bed. They were handed their bread, but this time the piece was smaller still. As they walked into the forest, Hansel broke his up in his pocket, and kept stopping to drop a crumb on the ground. “Hansel, why do you keep stopping and looking back?” said the father. “Come along.” “I’m looking at my little pigeon sitting on the roof. It wants to say goodbye to me,” Hansel answered. “Fool!” said the woman. “That isn’t your pigeon. It’s the morning sun shining on the chimney.” But bit by bit, Hansel went on throwing every crumb onto the path.

The woman took the children even deeper into the forest, to a place they had never been in all their lives. Once more a big fire was lit, and the mother said: “Sit down here, children, and if you get tired you can sleep for a while. We’re going into the forest to chop wood. When we’ve finished this evening, we’ll come back and collect you.” At noon Gretel shared her bread with Hansel, since he had scattered his along the way. Then they fell asleep, and the evening went by, but nobody came for the poor children. They woke only when the night was pitch dark, and Hansel comforted his little sister. “Wait till the moon comes up, Gretel,” he said. “Then we’ll see the crumbs I dropped, and they’ll show us the way home.” When the moon rose, they set off, but there were no crumbs to be seen, because the thousands of birds that fly around the woods and fields had pecked up every one. Hansel said to Gretel, “We’ll find the way soon,” but they never did. They walked all night and the whole of the next day, from morning until evening, and still they couldn’t get out of the forest. They were very hungry, since all they had to eat was a few berries growing on the ground. And when they were so tired that their legs would not carry them any further, they lay down under a tree and fell asleep.

Three mornings had now passed since they left their father’s house. They started walking again, but they only went deeper into the forest, and unless help came soon, they would die of hunger and exhaustion. At midday they saw a beautiful snow-white bird perched on a branch. It sang so sweetly that they stopped and listened. When its song ended, it spread its wings and flew off ahead of them, and they followed it until they came to a little house. The bird landed on the roof, and as the children came closer they saw that the house was made of bread and covered with cakes, and that its windows were clear sugar. “Let’s get started on this,” said Hansel, “and have a proper meal. I’ll eat a piece of the roof, Gretel, and you can eat some of the window. It will taste sweet.” Hansel reached up and broke off a bit of the roof to see what it tasted like, while Gretel leaned against the window and nibbled at the panes. Then a soft voice called out from inside the room:

“Nibble, nibble, gnaw,
Who is nibbling at my little house?”
The children answered:

“The wind, the wind,
The child of heaven, the wind,”

and they carried on eating, not bothered in the least. Hansel liked the taste of the roof so much that he tore off a huge piece, and Gretel pushed out an entire round windowpane, sat down, and enjoyed it. All at once the door opened, and out crept a woman as old as the hills, leaning on crutches. Hansel and Gretel were so badly frightened that they dropped everything they were holding. The old woman only nodded her head and said, “Oh, dear children, who brought you here? Come inside and stay with me. No harm will come to you.” She took them both by the hand and led them into her little house. Then she put a good meal in front of them: milk and pancakes with sugar, apples, and nuts. Afterwards she made up two pretty little beds with clean white sheets, and Hansel and Gretel lay down in them and felt as if they were in heaven.

The old woman had only pretended to be kind. In truth she was a wicked witch who lay in wait for children, and she had built her little bread house just to lure them in. When a child fell into her hands, she killed it, cooked it and ate it, and for her that was a feast day. Witches have red eyes and can’t see far, but they have a sharp sense of smell, like animals, and know when people are near. As Hansel and Gretel came close to her house, she gave a nasty laugh and said with a sneer, “I’ve got them! They won’t get away from me this time!” She was up early in the morning, before the children woke, and when she saw the two of them asleep, looking so lovely with their plump rosy cheeks, she muttered to herself, “What a tasty bite that will be!” Then she grabbed Hansel with her bony hand, carried him to a little stable, and locked him in behind a barred door. He could scream all he liked; it did him no good. Then she went to Gretel, shook her awake, and shouted, “Get up, you lazy thing! Fetch some water and cook something good for your brother. He’s in the stable outside, and he’s going to be fattened up. When he’s fat, I’ll eat him.” Gretel began to cry bitterly, but it was no use. She had to do whatever the wicked witch told her.

So the finest food was cooked for poor Hansel, while Gretel got nothing but crab shells. Every morning the old woman crept out to the little stable and called, “Hansel, stick out your finger, so I can feel whether you’re getting fat.” But Hansel held out a small bone instead. The old woman had weak eyes and couldn’t see it. She thought it was Hansel’s finger, and she was amazed that he didn’t get any fatter. After four weeks had passed and Hansel was still thin, she lost patience and refused to wait any longer. “Now then, Gretel,” she shouted at the girl, “get moving and bring some water. Fat or thin, tomorrow I’ll kill Hansel and cook him.” Oh, how the poor little sister wept as she carried the water, and how the tears ran down her cheeks! “Dear God, please help us,” she cried. “If only the wild animals in the forest had eaten us, at least we would have died together.” “Save your whining,” said the old woman. “It won’t do you any good.”

Early in the morning, Gretel had to go out, hang the cauldron of water over the fire, and light it. “First we’ll bake,” said the old woman. “I’ve already heated the oven and kneaded the dough.” She shoved poor Gretel toward the oven, where flames were already leaping out. “Crawl in,” said the witch, “and check whether it’s hot enough for us to put the bread in.” Her plan was to shut the oven once Gretel was inside, and bake her in it, and then eat her too. But Gretel saw what she was up to, and said, “I don’t know how to do it. How do I get in?” “Stupid goose,” said the old woman. “The opening is big enough. Look, I could get in myself!” And she scrambled up and stuck her head into the oven. Then Gretel gave her a shove that sent her flying right inside, slammed the iron door, and slid the bolt across. Oh! The witch began to howl horribly, but Gretel ran off, and the godless witch burned to a miserable death.

Gretel ran to Hansel as fast as lightning, opened his little stable, and cried, “Hansel, we’re saved! The old witch is dead!” Hansel leaped out like a bird from a cage when the door is opened. How they cheered, and hugged, and danced around, and kissed each other! Now that they had nothing to fear from her, they went into the witch’s house, and in every corner stood chests full of pearls and jewels. “These are much better than pebbles!” said Hansel, and he stuffed his pockets with as much as they would hold. Gretel said, “I’ll take something home too,” and filled her apron to the top. “But now we have to go,” said Hansel, “so we can get out of the witch’s forest.”

After they had walked for two hours, they came to a wide stretch of water. “We can’t get across,” said Hansel. “I can’t see a plank or a bridge anywhere.” “There’s no ferry either,” Gretel answered, “but there’s a white duck swimming over there. If I ask her, she’ll help us across.” Then she called out:

“Little duck, little duck, do you see
Hansel and Gretel, who are waiting for you?
There is no plank and no bridge in sight,
Carry us over on your back so white.”

The duck swam over to them, and Hansel sat down on her back and told his sister to sit beside him. “No,” Gretel replied, “that would be too heavy for the little duck. She should take us across one at a time.” The kind little duck did just that. Once they were safely over and had walked on a little way, the forest began to look more and more familiar, and at last they saw their father’s house in the distance. Then they started to run, burst into the room, and threw their arms around their father’s neck. The man had not had one happy hour since he left the children in the forest, and the woman was dead. Gretel shook out her apron until pearls and precious stones rolled across the floor, and Hansel tossed down one handful after another from his pocket to add to them. All their worries were over, and they lived together in perfect happiness. My tale is done; see, a mouse is running by. Whoever catches it can make himself a big fur cap out of it.

chapters.title: The Mouse, the Bird, and the Sausage
paragraphs: Once upon a time a mouse, a bird and a sausage went into partnership and set up house together. For a long while everything went well. They lived comfortably and did so well that their stores grew considerably. The bird’s job was to fly into the woods every day and bring back firewood. The mouse fetched the water, and the sausage did the cooking.

When people are too well off, they always start longing for something new. So it happened that the bird, out one day, met another bird and boasted to him at length about how well their household was run. But the other bird sneered at him for being a poor fool who did all the hard work while the other two stayed home and had an easy time. After all, once the mouse had lit the fire and fetched the water, she could retire to her little room and rest until it was time to lay the table. The sausage only had to watch the pot and make sure the food was cooking properly, and when dinnertime was near, he would throw himself into the broth, or roll in and out among the vegetables three or four times, and there they were, buttered and salted and ready to serve. Then, when the bird came home and put down his load, they sat down to eat, and when the meal was over they could sleep as much as they liked until the next morning. It really was a very pleasant life.

Swayed by these remarks, the bird refused the next morning to bring in the wood. He told the others that he had been their servant long enough, and a fool besides, and that it was time for a change, to try arranging the work some other way. The mouse and the sausage begged and pleaded, but it did no good. The bird stayed firm, and the experiment had to be made. So they drew lots, and it fell to the sausage to bring the wood, to the mouse to cook, and to the bird to fetch the water.

And what happened then? The sausage set off to look for wood, the bird made the fire, and the mouse put the pot on, and the two of them waited for the sausage to come back with fuel for the next day. But the sausage stayed away so long that they grew worried, and the bird flew out to meet him. He hadn’t flown far when he came upon a dog. The dog had met the sausage, taken him for fair game, and seized him and swallowed him. The bird complained to the dog about this barefaced robbery, but nothing he said made any difference. The dog replied that he had found forged papers on the sausage, and that was why he had forfeited his life.
The bird picked up the wood and flew home sadly, and told the mouse everything he had seen and heard. They were both very unhappy, but they agreed to make the best of it and stay together.

So now the bird laid the table, and the mouse looked after the food. Wanting to prepare it the way the sausage had, by rolling in and out among the vegetables to salt and butter them, she jumped into the pot. But she stopped short long before she reached the bottom, having already lost not just her skin and hair, but her life as well.

Soon the bird came in, ready to serve the dinner, but he couldn’t find the cook anywhere. In his alarm and confusion he flung the wood about the floor, calling and searching, but no cook was to be found. Then some of the wood he had carelessly thrown down caught fire and began to blaze. The bird rushed to fetch water, but his bucket fell into the well, and he fell in after it, and since he could not get himself out, he drowned.

chapters.title: Mother Holle
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a widow who had two daughters. One was beautiful and hard-working, the other ugly and lazy. But the mother loved the ugly, lazy one best, because she was her own daughter. So the other girl, who was only a stepdaughter, had to do all the housework and was treated just like Cinderella. Every day her stepmother sent her to sit by the well on the high road and spin until her fingers bled. Then one day it happened that some blood dropped onto the spindle, and as the girl bent over the well to wash it off, the spindle suddenly jumped out of her hand and fell into the well. She ran home in tears to tell about her misfortune, but her stepmother spoke harshly to her and, after giving her a fierce scolding, said coldly, “Since you let the spindle fall into the well, you can go and get it out yourself.”
Not knowing what else to do, the girl returned to the well, and in her despair she jumped into the water after the spindle.
The next thing she knew, she was waking up in a lovely meadow, bright with sunshine, where flowers by the thousand bloomed on every side.

She walked across the meadow, and soon she came to a baker’s oven full of bread, and the loaves called out to her, “Take us out, take us out, or we’ll burn to a cinder! We were baked through long ago.” So she took the bread shovel and pulled them all out.

Farther on she came to a tree loaded with apples. “Shake me, shake me, please,” the tree called out. “All my apples are ripe.” So she shook the tree, and the apples rained down on her. She kept shaking until not one apple was left on the branches. Then she stacked them neatly in a pile and went on her way.

The next thing she reached was a small house. An old woman was looking out of the window, and her teeth were so huge that the girl was terrified and started to run. But the old woman called after her, “Why are you afraid, dear child? Stay with me. If you do my housework properly, things will go very well for you. Just be sure to make my bed the right way: shake it hard, until the feathers fly. Down in the world, people say it is snowing when I do that, because I am Mother Holle.” She spoke so kindly that the girl found her courage and agreed to work for her.

She did everything exactly as the old woman asked, and each time she made the bed she shook it as hard as she could, so the feathers swirled around like snowflakes. The old woman kept her promise. She never raised her voice to the girl, and every day she served her roasted and boiled meat.

She stayed with Mother Holle for a good while, and then she grew unhappy. At first she could not say why she felt so low. Eventually she realized she was homesick, though she was a thousand times better off here than with her mother and sister. After a time she went to Mother Holle and said, “I miss home so much that I can’t stay with you any longer. I’m very happy here, but I have to go back to my own people.”
Mother Holle answered, “I’m glad you want to go back to your family. You have served me so faithfully and well that I will take you home myself.”
