With that she took the girl by the hand and led her up to a wide gateway. The gate swung open, and as the girl walked through, a shower of gold poured down over her. The gold stuck to her, until she was covered in it from head to toe.
“This is your reward for working so hard,” said Mother Holle, and she gave her the spindle that had fallen into the well.
Then the gate closed, and the girl found herself back in the ordinary world, close to her mother’s house. As she came into the yard, the rooster sitting on the well crowed:

“Cock-a-doodle-doo!
Your golden daughter’s come back to you.”

She went in to her mother and sister, and since she was covered in gold, they welcomed her warmly. She told them everything that had happened to her. When the mother heard how she had come by such wealth, she wanted her own ugly, lazy daughter to go and try for the same luck. So she made that daughter sit by the well and spin. To get blood on her spindle, the girl pricked her finger and pushed her hand into a thorn-bush. Then she threw the spindle into the well and jumped in after it.

Like her sister, she woke up in the beautiful meadow and walked across it until she reached the oven. “Take us out, take us out, or we’ll burn to cinders! We were baked long ago,” cried the loaves, just as before. But the lazy girl answered, “Do you think I’m going to get my hands dirty for you?” and walked on.
Soon she came to the apple tree. “Shake me, shake me, please. All my apples are ripe,” it cried. But she only said, “What a thing to ask of me! An apple might fall on my head,” and went on.
At last she reached Mother Holle’s house. Her sister had told her all about the big teeth, so she was not afraid of them, and she hired herself out to the old woman right away.

On the first day she was obedient and hardworking, putting in great effort to please Mother Holle, because she was thinking of the gold she would get. On the second day she began to slack off, and on the third she was lazier still. After that she started lying in bed in the mornings and refusing to get up. Worse, she failed to make the old woman’s bed properly and forgot to shake it so that the feathers would fly. Before long Mother Holle was fed up with her and told her she could go. The lazy girl was delighted, and thought to herself, “The gold will soon be mine.” Mother Holle led her to the wide gateway, just as she had led her sister. But as the girl passed through, instead of a shower of gold, a huge bucketful of pitch poured down on her.
“That is what you have earned,” said the old woman, and she shut the gate.
So the lazy girl had to walk home covered in pitch, and when the rooster on the well saw her, he crowed:

“Cock-a-doodle-doo!
Your dirty daughter’s come back to you.”
No matter how she tried, she could not get the pitch off, and it stayed on her for the rest of her life.

chapters.title: Little Red-Cap (Little Red Riding Hood)
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a sweet little girl whom everyone loved on sight, and her grandmother loved her most of all. There was nothing the old woman would not have given the child. One time she gave her a little cap of red velvet, and it suited her so well that she refused to wear anything else. From then on everybody called her “Little Red-Cap.”

One day her mother said to her, “Come here, Little Red-Cap. Here is a piece of cake and a bottle of wine. Take them to your grandmother, since she is ill and weak, and they will do her good. Leave before it gets hot. On the way, walk politely and calmly, and don’t stray from the path. Otherwise you might fall and break the bottle, and then your grandmother would get nothing. And when you step into her room, remember to say ‘Good morning,’ and don’t go looking into every corner first.”
“I’ll be very careful,” Little Red-Cap told her mother, and she shook on it.

The grandmother lived out in the woods, half a league from the village. Just as Little Red-Cap reached the edge of the woods, a wolf came up to her. She had no idea what a wicked creature he was, so she wasn’t afraid of him at all.
“Good day, Little Red-Cap,” he said.
“Thank you, wolf.”
“Where are you off to so early, Little Red-Cap?”
“To my grandmother’s.”
“And what do you have in your apron?”
“Cake and wine. We baked yesterday, so my poor sick grandmother is going to have something nice to make her stronger.”
“And where does your grandmother live, Little Red-Cap?”
“Another good quarter of a league into the woods. Her house stands under the three big oak trees, with the nut trees just below. You must know it,” answered Little Red-Cap.

The wolf thought to himself, “What a tender young thing. What a nice plump mouthful—she’ll taste better than the old woman. I have to be clever about this, so that I get both of them.” So he walked beside Little Red-Cap for a while, and then he said, “Look at the lovely flowers all around us, Little Red-Cap. Why don’t you look about you? And I don’t think you can even hear how sweetly the little birds are singing. You plod along as if you were on your way to school, while everything else out here in the woods is cheerful.”

Little Red-Cap looked up. She saw the sunbeams dancing through the trees and pretty flowers growing everywhere, and she thought, “If I brought grandmother a fresh bunch of flowers, she would like that too. It’s still early, so I’ll get there in plenty of time.” And she left the path and ran into the woods to look for flowers. Each time she picked one, she imagined she could see a prettier one a little farther on, and she ran after it. In this way she wandered deeper and deeper into the woods.
In the meantime the wolf hurried directly to the grandmother’s house, where he rapped on the door.
“Who’s there?”
“Little Red-Cap,” answered the wolf. “She’s bringing cake and wine. Open the door.”
“Just lift the latch,” called the grandmother. “I’m too weak to get up.”

The wolf lifted the latch and the door swung open. Without a word he went straight to the grandmother’s bed and gobbled her up. Then he put on her clothes and her cap, lay down in her bed and drew the curtains.
Little Red-Cap, meanwhile, had been running around picking flowers. When she had so many that she couldn’t carry any more, she remembered her grandmother and set off for her house.

She was surprised to find the cottage door standing open. When she walked into the room, she felt so strange that she said to herself, “Oh dear, I feel so uneasy today, and usually I love being at grandmother’s.” She called out, “Good morning,” but got no answer. So she went over to the bed and pulled back the curtains. There lay her grandmother, with her cap pulled down low over her face, looking very odd.
“Oh, grandmother,” she said, “what big ears you have!”
“All the better to hear you with, my child,” came the answer.
“But grandmother, what big eyes you have!” she said.
“All the better to see you with, my dear.”
“But grandmother, what large hands you have!”
“All the better to hug you with.”
“Oh, but grandmother, what a terribly big mouth you have!”
“All the better to eat you with!”
The wolf had barely finished speaking when he leapt out of bed in a single bound and swallowed Red-Cap whole.

Once the wolf had satisfied his hunger, he lay back down in the bed, fell asleep and began to snore very loudly. A huntsman happened to be walking past the house, and he thought, “How loudly the old woman is snoring! I had better check whether she needs anything.” So he stepped into the room, and when he reached the bed he saw the wolf lying in it. “So here you are, you old sinner!” he said. “I’ve been looking for you for a long time!” He was just about to shoot, when it struck him that the wolf might have eaten the grandmother and that she might still be saved. So he didn’t fire. Instead he took a pair of scissors and began to cut open the sleeping wolf’s belly. After two snips he saw Little Red-Cap shining, and after two more the girl sprang out, crying, “Oh, I was so scared! It was so dark inside the wolf!” Then the old grandmother climbed out alive too, though she could hardly breathe. Red-Cap quickly fetched big stones and they filled the wolf’s belly with them. When he woke up he tried to run off, but the stones were so heavy that his legs gave way at once and he dropped dead.

All three of them were delighted. The huntsman skinned the wolf and took the pelt home. The grandmother ate the cake and drank the wine that Red-Cap had brought, and she recovered. But Red-Cap thought to herself, “As long as I live, I will never again leave the path and run off into the woods on my own when my mother has forbidden it.”

They also tell how, another time when Red-Cap was taking cakes to her old grandmother, a second wolf spoke to her and tried to lure her off the path. But Red-Cap was on her guard. She kept straight on her way, and told her grandmother that she had met a wolf, and that he had wished her good morning, but with such a wicked look in his eyes that, if they had not been on the public road, she was sure he would have eaten her. “Well then,” said the grandmother, “we’ll lock the door so he can’t get in.” Soon afterward the wolf knocked and called, “Open the door, grandmother, it’s Little Red-Cap, I’ve brought you some cakes.” But the two of them stayed silent and did not open the door. So the gray-beard slunk around the house two or three times, and finally jumped up on the roof. He meant to wait until Red-Cap went home in the evening, then creep after her and devour her in the dark. But the grandmother could tell what he was thinking. In front of the house stood a big stone trough, and she said to the child, “Take the pail, Red-Cap. I made sausages yesterday, so carry the water I boiled them in over to the trough.” Red-Cap carried water until the big trough was completely full. Then the smell of sausages reached the wolf. He sniffed and peered down, and finally stretched his neck out so far that he lost his footing. He began to slide, slid right off the roof into the big trough, and drowned. But Red-Cap went happily home, and nobody ever did her any harm again.

chapters.title: The Robber Bridegroom
paragraphs: A miller once had one beautiful daughter, and when she was grown he wanted to see her married well and taken care of. He told himself, “I will give her to the first suitable man who comes and asks for her.” Not long afterward a suitor turned up. He seemed very rich, and the miller could find nothing to object to in him, so he promised his daughter to the man. But the girl did not feel for him what a girl should feel for the man she is going to marry. She did not trust him, and she could not look at him or think of him without a shiver. One day he said to her, “You still haven’t visited me, though we have been engaged for some time.” “I don’t know where your house is,” she answered. “My house is out there in the dark forest,” he said. She tried to get out of it by saying she would never find the way there. Her fiancé only replied, “You must come and see me next Sunday. I have already invited guests for that day, and so that you don’t lose your way, I will scatter ashes along the path.”

When Sunday came and it was time for the girl to set out, a dread she couldn’t explain came over her. So that she could find her way back again, she filled her pockets with peas and lentils to scatter on the ground as she went. At the edge of the forest she found the path strewn with ashes, and she followed them, tossing a few peas to either side with every step. She walked all day, until she came to the deepest, darkest part of the forest. There she saw a lonely house that looked so grim and mysterious that she did not like it at all. She went inside, but there was not a soul to be seen, and a deep silence hung over everything. Suddenly a voice cried:

“Turn back, turn back, young maiden fair,
Don’t stay in this murderers’ lair.”
Looking up, the girl saw that a bird in a cage on the wall had spoken. It called out once more:

“Turn back, turn back, young maiden fair,
Don’t stay in this murderers’ lair.”

The girl kept going, walking from room to room through the house, but every room was empty and she still saw nobody. Finally she reached the cellar. There sat an extremely old woman whose head shook constantly. “Can you tell me,” the girl asked, “whether my betrothed lives here?”

“Oh, you poor child,” the old woman replied, “what a place you have walked into! This is a den of murderers. You believe you are a bride-to-be and that your wedding is near, but the feast you will keep is with death. Look, do you see that big cauldron of water I have to keep heated over the fire? Once they have you in their hands, they will kill you without mercy, then cook you and eat you, for they eat human flesh. If I didn’t take pity on you and rescue you, you would be lost.”

With that, the old woman took her behind a large cask that hid her completely. “Stay as quiet as a mouse,” she said. “Don’t move and don’t speak, or you are finished. Tonight, when the robbers are all asleep, we will run away together. I have been waiting a long time for a chance to get out.”

She had barely finished speaking when the godless gang came back, hauling another young girl with them. They were all drunk and ignored her screams and her weeping. They made her drink wine, three full glasses: one of white, one of red and one of yellow. At that her heart burst and she died. Then they ripped off her fine clothes, laid her on a table, chopped her lovely body into pieces and sprinkled salt over it.

Behind the cask, the poor betrothed girl crouched shaking and shuddering, for she now saw the dreadful fate the robbers had planned for her. One of them noticed a gold ring still on the dead girl’s little finger. It would not come off easily, so he picked up a hatchet and chopped the finger off. But the finger flew up into the air and dropped behind the cask, right into the lap of the girl hiding there. The robber took a lamp and searched for it, but he could not find it. “Did you look behind the big cask?” asked one of the others. But the old woman called out, “Come and eat your supper, and leave the thing until tomorrow. The finger isn’t going to run away.”
“The old woman’s right,” said the robbers. They gave up the search for the finger and sat down.

The old woman then stirred a sleeping potion into their wine, and before long they were all stretched out on the cellar floor, sound asleep and snoring. Once the girl was sure of it, she came out from behind the cask. She had to step over the sleeping men, who lay packed close together, and with every step she was gripped by fresh terror that she might wake one of them. But God helped her, and she got across safely. Then she and the old woman went upstairs, opened the door and hurried away from the murderers’ den as fast as they could. The wind had blown the ashes away, but the peas and lentils had sprouted and grown far enough above the ground to show them the path in the moonlight. They walked all night, and it was morning when they reached the mill. There the girl told her father everything that had happened.

The day fixed for the wedding arrived. The bridegroom came, along with a big crowd of guests, for the miller had been careful to invite all his friends and relatives. While they sat at the feast, each guest in turn was asked to tell a story. The bride sat quietly and said nothing.
“And you, my love,” said the bridegroom, turning to her, “don’t you know a story? Tell us something.”

“Then I’ll tell you a dream,” said the bride. “I was walking alone through a forest, and at last I came to a house. I could not find a living soul inside, but a bird hanging in a cage on the wall cried out:

“Turn back, turn back, young maiden fair,
Don’t stay in this murderers” lair.’
and it said those words a second time.”
“My darling, it’s only a dream.”

“I went on through the house, from room to room, but they were all empty, and everything felt grim and strange. Finally I went down to the cellar, and there sat a very, very old woman whose head would not stay still. I asked her whether my betrothed lived here, and she answered, ‘Oh, you poor child, you have walked into a murderers’ den. Your betrothed does live here, but he will kill you without mercy, and then cook you and eat you.’”
“My darling, it’s only a dream.”

“The old woman hid me behind a big cask, and she had hardly done so when the robbers came home, hauling a young girl with them. They made her drink three kinds of wine, white, red and yellow, and at that she died.”
“My darling, it’s only a dream.”
“Then they ripped off her fine clothes, chopped her lovely body into pieces and sprinkled salt over it.”
“My darling, it’s only a dream.”

“And one of the robbers saw that she still had a gold ring on her finger, and since it was hard to pull off, he took a hatchet and chopped the finger off. But the finger flew up into the air and landed behind the big cask, in my lap. And here is the finger with the ring.” With these words the bride pulled out the finger and showed it to all the guests.

The bridegroom, who had turned deathly pale during her telling, jumped up and tried to escape, but the guests seized him and held him fast. They handed him over to the law, and he and his whole murderous band were sentenced to death for their wicked crimes.

chapters.title: Tom Thumb
paragraphs: One night a poor woodcutter was sitting in his cottage by the fire, smoking his pipe, while his wife sat beside him spinning. “How lonely it is, wife,” he said, blowing out a long curl of smoke, “for the two of us to sit here by ourselves, with no children running around to keep us entertained, while everyone else seems so happy and cheerful with theirs!” “That is perfectly true,” said his wife with a sigh, turning her wheel. “How happy I would be if I had just one child! Even if it were tiny—even if it were no bigger than my thumb—I would be very happy, and I would love it dearly.” Now, strange as it may sound, this good woman’s wish came true in exactly the way she had put it. Not long afterward she had a little boy who was perfectly healthy and strong, but hardly bigger than my thumb. So they said, “Well, we can’t claim we didn’t get what we wished for, and small as he is, we will love him dearly.” And they named him Thomas Thumb.

They fed him plenty, but whatever they did he never grew any bigger. He stayed exactly the size he had been when he was born. Still, his eyes were bright and sharp, and he soon proved to be a clever little fellow who always knew what he was doing.

One day the woodcutter was getting ready to go into the forest to cut firewood. “I wish I had someone to bring the cart along after me,” he said, “because I’m in a hurry.” “Oh, father,” cried Tom, “I’ll take care of that. The cart will be in the forest by the time you need it.” The woodcutter laughed. “How could that be?” he said. “You can’t even reach the horse’s bridle.” “Never mind that, father,” said Tom. “If Mother will just harness the horse, I’ll climb into his ear and tell him which way to go.” “Well,” said his father, “let’s try it once.”

When the time came, his mother harnessed the horse to the cart and put Tom in its ear. Sitting there, the little man told the animal where to go, calling “Giddy-up!” and “Whoa!” as he needed, and the horse went along just as well as if the woodcutter had driven it into the forest himself. It happened that the horse was going a bit too fast and Tom was shouting, “Easy! Easy!” when two strangers came along. “How strange!” said one. “There’s a cart rolling along and I can hear a driver talking to the horse, but I can’t see anyone.” “That is odd,” said the other. “Let’s follow the cart and see where it goes.” So they followed it into the forest until they reached the spot where the woodcutter was. Tom Thumb saw his father and called out, “Look, father, here I am with the cart, safe and sound! Now lift me down!” His father held the horse with one hand and with the other lifted his son out of the horse’s ear and set him on a piece of straw, where he sat as cheerful as could be.

All this time the two strangers had been watching, too amazed to speak. Finally one drew the other aside and said, “That little rascal could make our fortune if we got hold of him and took him from town to town as a show. We should buy him.” So they went up to the woodcutter and asked what he wanted for the little man. “He’ll be better off with us than with you,” they said. “I won’t sell him at all,” said the father. “My own flesh and blood is worth more to me than all the silver and gold in the world.” But Tom heard what kind of deal they were after, and he crept up his father’s coat to his shoulder and whispered in his ear, “Take the money, father, and let them have me. I’ll be back with you soon enough.”

In the end the woodcutter agreed to sell Tom to the strangers for a big piece of gold, and they paid the price. “Where would you like to sit?” one of them asked. “Oh, put me on the brim of your hat. That will make a fine balcony for me. I can walk around there and see the countryside as we go.” They did as he asked, and once Tom had said goodbye to his father, they took him away with them.

They traveled on until it began to get dark, and then the little man said, “Let me down, I’m tired.” The man took off his hat and set him on a clod of earth in a plowed field beside the road. But Tom ran about among the furrows and finally slipped into an old mouse hole. “Good night, gentlemen!” he said. “I’m off! Watch me more carefully next time.” They rushed over and poked the ends of their sticks into the mouse hole, but it was no use. Tom only crawled farther and farther in, and soon it was completely dark, so they had to go on their way without their prize, as sulky as could be.

When Tom was sure they had gone, he came out of his hiding place. “How dangerous it is to walk in this plowed field!” he said. “If I fell off one of these huge clods, I would certainly break my neck.” By good luck he finally found a large empty snail shell. “That’s lucky,” he said. “I can sleep here quite comfortably.” And in he crept.

He was just dropping off to sleep when he heard two men go by, chatting. One of them said to the other, “How can we rob that rich parson’s house of its silver and gold?” “I’ll tell you!” cried Tom. “What was that noise?” said the thief, startled. “I’m sure I heard someone speak.” They stood still and listened, and Tom said, “Take me with you, and I’ll soon show you how to get the parson’s money.” “But where are you?” they asked. “Look around on the ground,” he answered, “and listen for where the voice comes from.” At last the thieves found him and picked him up in their hands. “You little rascal!” they said. “What could you do for us?” “Why, I can squeeze between the iron bars of the parson’s window and throw out to you whatever you want.” “Good idea,” said the thieves. “Come along, and we’ll see what you can do.”

When they reached the parson’s house, Tom slipped between the window bars into the room and then shouted at the top of his lungs, “Do you want everything that’s in here?” The thieves were terrified and said, “Quietly, quietly! Speak softly, so you don’t wake anyone.” But Tom acted as if he didn’t understand and bellowed again, “How much do you want? Shall I throw it all out?” The cook was lying in the next room, and hearing the noise she sat up in bed and listened. Meanwhile the thieves, frightened, had run off a short distance, but at last they got their nerve back and said, “The little rascal is only trying to make fools of us.” So they came back and whispered to him, “Now, no more of your cheeky jokes. Just throw us out some of the money.” Then Tom shouted as loudly as he could, “All right! Hold out your hands! Here it comes.”

The cook heard this quite clearly, so she jumped out of bed and ran to open the door. The thieves bolted as if a wolf were at their heels. The maid groped around, found nothing, and went off to fetch a light. By the time she came back, Tom had slipped away into the barn. She looked in every hole and corner and found nobody, so she went back to bed, thinking she must have been dreaming with her eyes open.

The little man crawled around the hayloft and finally found a cozy spot to finish his night’s rest. He lay down, meaning to sleep until daylight and then find his way home to his father and mother. But alas, how dreadfully things went wrong for him! What troubles and sorrows we all meet in this world! The cook got up early, before daybreak, to feed the cows. She went straight to the hayloft and carried off a large bundle of hay with the little man in the middle of it, fast asleep. He kept on sleeping and did not wake until he found himself in the cow’s mouth, for the cook had put the hay in the cow’s rack and the cow had picked Tom up in one mouthful. “Good heavens!” he said. “How did I end up in the mill?” But he soon realized where he really was, and he had to keep all his wits about him so that he would not get between the cow’s teeth and be crushed to death. At last down he went into her stomach. “It’s rather dark,” he said. “They forgot to put windows in this room to let the sun in. A candle wouldn’t be a bad idea.”

He made the best of his bad luck, but he did not like it in there one bit. Worst of all, hay kept tumbling down in ever greater amounts, and the room left for him shrank and shrank. Finally he yelled at the top of his voice, “Don’t bring me any more hay! Don’t bring me any more hay!”

The maid was milking the cow at that very moment. She heard someone speak but could see nobody, and she was sure it was the same voice she had heard in the night. She was so terrified that she toppled off her stool and spilled the milk-pail. Once she had scrambled up out of the dirt, she raced to her master the parson and cried, “Sir, sir, the cow is talking!” “Woman, you must be out of your mind!” said the parson. All the same, he went with her to the cow-house to find out what was going on.

They had barely stepped through the doorway when Tom shouted, “Don’t bring me any more hay!” Now the parson was frightened too. He decided the cow must be bewitched and ordered his man to kill her right then and there. So the cow was slaughtered and cut open, and the stomach with Tom inside it was tossed onto a dunghill.

Tom set about trying to get free, which was no easy job. He had just managed to push his head out when more bad luck struck. A hungry wolf leapt up and gulped down the whole stomach, Tom and all, in a single swallow, then ran off.

Even so, Tom did not lose heart. It occurred to him that the wolf might enjoy a bit of conversation on the way, so he called out, “My good friend, I can show you a wonderful feast.” “Where?” asked the wolf. “At such and such a house,” said Tom, describing his own father’s house. “You can squeeze through the drain into the kitchen and on into the pantry, and there you’ll find cakes, ham, beef, cold chicken, roast pig, apple-dumplings, and anything else your heart desires.”

The wolf needed no second invitation. That same night he went to the house, squeezed through the drain into the kitchen and then the pantry, and ate and drank there until he was full. When he had had enough he wanted to leave, but he had stuffed himself so much that he could not fit out the way he had come in.

This was exactly what Tom had been counting on. He started shouting at the top of his voice, making as much noise as he could. “Will you be quiet?” said the wolf. “You’ll wake everyone in the house with all this racket.” “What do I care?” said the little man. “You’ve had your fun, and now I feel like enjoying myself.” And he began to sing and shout as loudly as he could.

The woodman and his wife woke at the noise and peeked through a crack in the door. When they saw a wolf in there, you can imagine how badly they were frightened. The woodman ran for his axe and handed his wife a scythe. “You stay back,” said the woodman, “and when I’ve struck him on the head, you must slash him open with the scythe.” Tom heard every word and cried out, “Father, father! I’m here, the wolf has swallowed me.” “Heaven be praised!” said his father. “We’ve found our dear child again.” He told his wife not to use the scythe, in case she hurt the boy. Then he swung hard, hit the wolf on the head, and killed him on the spot. When the wolf was dead they cut open his body and set Tommy free. “Ah,” said the father, “how afraid we have been for you!” “Yes, father,” he answered, “I think I’ve traveled all over the world, one way or another, since we parted, and now I’m very glad to be home and breathing fresh air again.” “Why, where have you been?” asked his father. “I’ve been in a mouse-hole—and in a snail-shell—and down a cow’s throat—and in the wolf’s belly. And yet here I am again, safe and sound.”
“Well,” they said, “you’re back now, and we will never sell you again, not for all the riches in the world.”

Then they hugged and kissed their dear little son and gave him plenty to eat and drink, because he was very hungry. They fetched him new clothes as well, since his old ones had been ruined on his journey. So Master Thumb stayed at home in peace with his father and mother. He had been a great traveler and had done and seen many fine things, and he liked telling the whole story, but he always agreed that, after all, there’s no place like HOME!

chapters.title: Rumpelstiltskin
paragraphs: Beside a wood, in a country far away, a fine stream flowed, and on the stream stood a mill. The miller’s house was close by, and the miller, as you should know, had a very beautiful daughter. She was also sharp and clever, and the miller was so proud of her that one day he told the king of that land, who often came to hunt in the wood, that his daughter could spin straw into gold. Now this king loved money, and when he heard the miller’s boast, his greed was stirred and he had the girl brought to him. He led her to a room in his palace that held a huge heap of straw, gave her a spinning-wheel, and said, “All of this must be spun into gold by morning, if you value your life.” The poor girl pleaded that it was only a foolish boast of her father’s and that she could do no such thing as spin straw into gold. It made no difference: the door was locked, and she was left alone.

She sat down in a corner of the room and began to lament her cruel fate. Suddenly the door opened and a comical little man hobbled in. “Good morning to you, my girl,” he said. “Why are you crying?” “Oh,” she said, “I have to spin this straw into gold, and I don’t know how.” “What will you give me,” said the hobgoblin, “if I do it for you?” “My necklace,” the girl replied. He took her up on it, sat down at the wheel, and whistled and sang:

“Round about, round about,
Lo and behold!
Reel away, reel away,
Straw into gold!”
And the wheel went merrily round and round. The work was soon finished, and all the straw was spun into gold.

When the king came and saw it, he was amazed and delighted, but it only made him hungrier for gold. He shut the miller’s poor daughter in again with a new task. She had no idea what to do and sat down to weep once more, but soon the dwarf opened the door and said, “What will you give me to do your task?” “The ring on my finger,” she said. So her little friend took the ring and set to work at the wheel again, whistling and singing:

“Turn and turn, turn and turn,
Watch it now unfold!
Spin away, spin away,
Straw becomes gold!”
until, well before morning, everything was done again.

The king was overjoyed to see all that glittering treasure, but he still wanted more. He took the miller’s daughter to an even bigger heap and said, “All this must be spun tonight, and if it is, you will be my queen.” As soon as she was alone, the dwarf came in and said, “What will you give me to spin gold for you this third time?” “I have nothing left,” she said. “Then promise me,” said the little man, “that you will give me the first child you have once you are queen.” “That may never happen,” thought the miller’s daughter, and since she knew no other way to get the task done, she promised what he asked. Round went the wheel again to the same old song, and the manikin once more spun the heap into gold. In the morning the king came and found everything he wanted. He had to keep his word, so he married the miller’s daughter, and she truly became queen.

When her first child was born she was very happy, and she forgot all about the dwarf and what she had promised. But one day he came into her room, where she sat playing with her baby, and reminded her. She was bitterly distressed and offered him all the wealth of the kingdom if he would release her, but it was no use. At last her tears softened him, and he said, “I will give you three days. If you can tell me my name in that time, you may keep your child.”

The queen lay awake all that night, thinking of every odd name she had ever heard, and she sent messengers all over the land to find new ones. The next day the little man came, and she started with TIMOTHY, ICHABOD, BENJAMIN, JEREMIAH, and every other name she could remember. To each and every one he replied, “Madam, that is not my name.”

On the second day she began with all the funny names she could find, BANDY-LEGS, HUNCHBACK, CROOK-SHANKS, and so on. But the little gentleman still answered every one of them, “Madam, that is not my name.”

On the third day one of the messengers came back and said, “I have traveled for two days without hearing of any other names. But yesterday, as I was climbing a high hill, in the forest where the fox and the hare say good night to each other, I saw a little hut. In front of the hut a fire was burning, and around the fire a funny little dwarf was dancing on one leg and singing:

“Merrily the feast I’ll make.
Today I’ll brew, tomorrow bake;
Merrily I’ll dance and sing,
For the next day a stranger will bring.
Little does my lady dream
Rumpelstiltskin is my name!”

When the queen heard this she jumped for joy. As soon as her little friend arrived, she sat on her throne and called her whole court around to enjoy the fun. The nurse stood beside her with the baby in her arms, as though it were all ready to be handed over. The little man began to chuckle at the thought of taking the poor child home to his hut in the woods, and he cried, “Now, lady, what is my name?” “Is it JOHN?” she asked. “No, madam!” “Is it TOM?” “No, madam!” “Is it JEMMY?” “It is not.” “Could your name be RUMPELSTILTSKIN?” said the lady slyly. “A witch told you that!—a witch told you that!” shrieked the little man, and in his rage he stamped his right foot so deep into the floor that he had to grab it with both hands to pull it out.

Then he made off as fast as he could, while the nurse laughed and the baby crowed. The whole court jeered at him for going to so much trouble for nothing, and called, “We wish you a very good morning and a merry feast, Mr RUMPLESTILTSKIN!”

chapters.title: Clever Gretel
paragraphs: There was once a cook named Gretel, who wore shoes with red heels. When she went out in them she twisted this way and that, feeling very happy, and thought, “You really are a pretty girl!” When she came home, she was so cheerful that she drank a cup of wine, and since wine makes you hungry, she tasted the best of whatever she was cooking until she was full, saying, “The cook must know what the food tastes like.”

One day the master said to her, “Gretel, a guest is coming this evening. Prepare two fowls for me, and do it nicely.” “I’ll see to it, master,” answered Gretel. She killed two fowls, scalded and plucked them, put them on the spit, and toward evening set them in front of the fire to roast. The fowls began to turn brown and were nearly done, but the guest had still not arrived. Then Gretel called to her master, “If the guest doesn’t come, I’ll have to take the fowls off the fire, but it will be a sin and a shame if they aren’t eaten the moment they’re at their juiciest.” The master said, “I’ll run and fetch the guest myself.” As soon as his back was turned, Gretel laid the spit with the fowls to one side and thought, “Standing by the fire so long makes a person sweat and get thirsty. Who knows when they’ll turn up? In the meantime I’ll run down to the cellar and have a drink.” She ran down, set a jug under the tap, said, “God bless it for you, Gretel,” and took a good drink. Then she thought that wine ought to keep flowing and not be interrupted, and she took another hearty swig.

Then she went and put the fowls back to the fire, basted them, and turned the spit briskly. But the roasting meat smelled so good that Gretel thought, “Something might be wrong with it. It ought to be tasted!” She touched it with her finger and said, “Ah, how good fowls are! It’s certainly a sin and a shame that they aren’t eaten at the right time!” She ran to the window to see whether the master was coming with his guest, but she saw no one. She went back to the fowls and thought, “One of the wings is burning! I’d better take it off and eat it.” So she cut it off, ate it, and enjoyed it, and when she had finished she thought, “The other one must go too, or else master will notice something is missing.” When both wings were eaten, she went to look for her master and could not see him. Suddenly it occurred to her, “Who knows? Maybe they aren’t coming at all, and have stopped somewhere else.” Then she said, “Well, Gretel, enjoy yourself. One fowl has been cut into, so take another drink and eat it up completely. When it’s gone you’ll have some peace. Why should God’s good gifts go to waste?” So she ran down to the cellar again, took an enormous drink, and ate up the one chicken with great glee. When the first chicken was swallowed and her master still had not come, Gretel looked at the other one and said, “Where one goes, the other should follow, since the two belong together. What’s right for one is right for the other. I think another drink wouldn’t do me any harm.” So she took another hearty drink and let the second chicken follow the first.

While she was busy enjoying herself, her master came in and called out, “Hurry up, Gretel, the guest will be here right behind me!” “Yes, sir, I’ll be serving very soon,” Gretel answered. Meanwhile the master checked that the table was properly set, took the big knife he meant to carve the chickens with, and sharpened it on the steps. Soon the guest arrived and knocked at the front door, politely and courteously. Gretel ran to see who it was, and when she saw the guest, she held a finger to her lips and said, “Hush, hush! Get away from here as fast as you can. If my master catches you, you’ll be sorry. He did invite you to supper, but what he really wants is to cut off both your ears. Listen to him sharpening the knife for it!” The guest heard the scraping and hurried back down the steps as fast as his legs would carry him. Gretel didn’t waste a moment. She ran screaming to her master and cried, “A fine guest you’ve invited!” “Why, Gretel? What do you mean?” “Well,” she said, “he snatched the chickens off the dish, the very ones I was about to serve, and ran off with them!” “What a dirty trick!” said her master, mourning the lost chickens. “If only he’d left me one, so I had something to eat.” He shouted after him to stop, but the guest acted as though he hadn’t heard. So the master ran after him with the knife still in his hand, yelling, “Just one, just one!” He meant that the guest should leave him one chicken and not take both. The guest, though, understood only that he was being asked for one of his ears, and he ran as if the ground were on fire beneath him, so that he would get away with both of them.

chapters.title: The Old Man and His Grandson
paragraphs: Once there was a very old man. His eyes had grown dim and his hearing was dull, his knees shook, and at the table he could barely hold his spoon. He spilled soup on the tablecloth, or it dribbled out of his mouth. His son and his son’s wife found this disgusting, and in the end the old grandfather was made to sit in the corner behind the stove. They gave him his food in a clay bowl, and not even enough of it. He would look over toward the table with his eyes full of tears. Once his shaking hands couldn’t keep hold of the bowl, and it dropped to the floor and smashed. The young wife scolded him, but he said nothing and only sighed. Then they bought him a wooden bowl for a few pennies, and he had to eat out of that.

They were sitting like this one day when their little grandson, who was four years old, started gathering scraps of wood on the floor. “What are you doing?” asked his father. “I’m making a little trough,” the child answered, “for you and Mother to eat out of when I’m grown up.”

The man and his wife stared at each other for a while, and then they began to cry. They led the old grandfather to the table, and from then on they always let him eat with them, and they said nothing even when he spilled a little.

chapters.title: The Little Peasant
paragraphs: There was once a village where nobody lived but very rich peasants, and one poor man, whom they called the little peasant. He didn’t even own a cow, and had still less money to buy one, yet he and his wife longed to have one. One day he said to her, “Listen, I have a good idea. Our friend the carpenter can make us a wooden calf and paint it brown so that it looks like any other. In time it will surely grow up and be a cow.” His wife liked the idea too, and their friend the carpenter sawed and planed the calf, painted it the way it should be, and gave it a lowered head, as if it were grazing.

The next morning, when the cows were being driven out, the little peasant called the cowherd in and said, “Look, I have a little calf here, but it’s still small and needs to be carried.” “All right,” said the cowherd. He took it in his arms, carried it to the pasture and set it down in the grass. The little calf just kept standing there as if it were eating, and the cowherd said, “It’ll be running on its own soon. Look how it’s eating already!” In the evening, when he was about to drive the herd home, he said to the calf, “If you can stand there and eat your fill, you can walk home on your own four legs. I’m not going to carry you back in my arms.” But the little peasant was standing at his door, waiting for his calf. When the cowherd drove the cows through the village and the calf wasn’t among them, he asked where it was. The cowherd answered, “It’s still out there eating. It wouldn’t stop and come with us.” But the little peasant said, “Oh no, I must have my animal back.” So they went back to the meadow together, but someone had stolen the calf, and it was gone. The cowherd said, “It must have run away.” “Don’t tell me that,” said the peasant, and he took the cowherd before the mayor. The mayor found him guilty of carelessness and ordered him to give the peasant a cow in place of the calf that had run away.

So now the little peasant and his wife had the cow they had wanted for so long, and they were overjoyed. But they had no fodder and nothing to feed it, so before long it had to be slaughtered. They salted the meat, and the peasant went into town to sell the hide, meaning to buy a new calf with the money. On the way he passed a mill, and there sat a raven with broken wings. Out of pity he picked it up and wrapped it in the hide. But the weather turned so bad, with a storm of rain and wind, that he couldn’t go any farther, so he went back to the mill and asked for shelter. The miller’s wife was alone in the house. She said to the peasant, “Lie down on the straw over there,” and gave him a slice of bread and cheese. The peasant ate it and lay down with his hide beside him, and the woman thought, “He’s tired and has fallen asleep.” Meanwhile the parson arrived. The miller’s wife welcomed him warmly and said, “My husband is out, so we’ll have a feast.” The peasant listened, and when he heard them talk of a feast he was annoyed that he’d had to make do with a slice of bread and cheese. Then the woman served four different dishes: roast meat, salad, cakes and wine.

They were just about to sit down and eat when there was a knock at the door. The woman said, “Oh, heavens! It’s my husband!” She quickly hid the roast meat in the tiled stove, the wine under the pillow, the salad on the bed and the cakes under the bed, and the parson in the cupboard on the porch. Then she opened the door for her husband and said, “Thank heaven you’re back again! What a storm, it looks as if the world is coming to an end.” The miller saw the peasant lying on the straw and asked, “What’s that fellow doing there?” “Oh,” said the wife, “the poor wretch came in out of the storm and rain and begged for shelter, so I gave him some bread and cheese and showed him where the straw was.” The man said, “I don’t mind, but hurry up and get me something to eat.” The woman said, “But I have nothing except bread and cheese.” “I’ll take anything,” said her husband. “As far as I’m concerned, bread and cheese will do.” He looked at the peasant and said, “Come and eat some more with me.” The peasant didn’t need to be asked twice. He got up and ate. After that the miller noticed the hide with the raven in it, lying on the floor, and asked, “What have you got there?” The peasant answered, “I have a soothsayer inside it.” “Can he foretell something for me?” said the miller. “Why not?” answered the peasant. “But he only says four things, and the fifth he keeps to himself.” The miller was curious and said, “Let him prophesy something, just once.” Then the peasant pinched the raven’s head so that it croaked and made a noise like krr, krr. The miller said, “What did he say?” The peasant answered, “First, he says there’s some wine hidden under the pillow.” “Bless me!” cried the miller, and he went over and found the wine. “Go on,” he said. The peasant made the raven croak again and said, “Second, he says there’s some roast meat in the tiled stove.” “Well, I never!” cried the miller, and he went over and found the roast meat. The peasant made the raven prophesy some more and said, “Third, he says there’s some salad on the bed.” “Now that is something!” cried the miller, and he went over and found the salad. Finally the peasant pinched the raven once more until it croaked, and said, “Fourth, he says there are some cakes under the bed.” “Now that is something!” cried the miller, and he looked, and found the cakes.

Now the two of them sat down at the table together, but the miller’s wife was scared half to death. She went to bed and took all the keys with her. The miller was very eager to hear the fifth thing, but the little peasant said, “First let’s eat the four things quickly, because the fifth is something bad.” So they ate, and afterward they haggled over how much the miller should pay for the fifth prophecy, until they settled on three hundred talers. Then the peasant pinched the raven’s head once more until it croaked loudly. The miller asked, “What did he say?” The peasant replied, “He says the Devil is hiding out there in the cupboard on the porch.” The miller said, “Then the Devil has to come out,” and he opened the front door. The woman was forced to hand over the keys, and the peasant opened the cupboard. The parson ran out as fast as he could, and the miller said, “It’s true. I saw the black rascal with my own eyes.” The peasant, for his part, slipped away at daybreak the next morning with the three hundred talers.

Back home, the little peasant slowly began to spend more freely. He built a beautiful house, and the other peasants said, “The little peasant must have been to the place where golden snow falls and people carry the gold home by the shovelful.” Then he was brought before the mayor and told to say where his wealth came from. He answered, “I sold my cow’s hide in town for three hundred talers.” When the peasants heard that, they wanted a share of this great profit too. They ran home, killed all their cows and stripped off the hides to sell in town for the best price. But the mayor said, “My servant must go first.” When she came to the merchant in town, he gave her no more than two talers for a hide, and when the others came, he gave them even less, and said, “What am I supposed to do with all these hides?”

The peasants were furious that the little peasant had made fools of them like this. They wanted revenge, and they accused him of fraud before the mayor. The innocent little peasant was sentenced to death by unanimous vote: he was to be rolled into the water in a barrel full of holes. He was led out, and a priest was brought to say a mass for his soul. Everyone else had to stand back at a distance, and when the peasant looked at the priest, he recognized the man who had been with the miller’s wife. He said to him, “I let you out of the cupboard, now let me out of the barrel.” Just then a shepherd came along with a flock of sheep, the very man the peasant knew had long been wishing to be mayor. So the peasant shouted with all his might, “No, I won’t do it! Not even if the whole world demands it, I won’t!” Hearing this, the shepherd came up to him and asked, “What’s going on? What is it you won’t do?” The peasant said, “They want to make me mayor if I’ll just get into the barrel, but I won’t do it.” The shepherd said, “If that’s all it takes to be mayor, I’d climb into the barrel right now.” The peasant said, “If you get in, you’ll be mayor.” The shepherd was willing and got in, and the peasant fastened the lid on top of him. Then he took the shepherd’s flock for himself and drove it away. The parson went to the crowd and announced that the mass had been said. Then they came and rolled the barrel toward the water. As the barrel started to roll, the shepherd cried, “I’m perfectly happy to be mayor!” They could only think it was the peasant speaking, and they answered, “That’s what we’re planning, but first you’re going to take a look around down there,” and they rolled the barrel into the water.

After that the peasants went home, and as they were walking into the village, the little peasant came in quietly too, driving a flock of sheep and looking perfectly content. The peasants were amazed and said, “Peasant, where have you come from? Did you come out of the water?” “Yes, indeed,” replied the peasant. “I sank deep, deep down until I reached the bottom. I pushed the bottom out of the barrel and crawled out, and there were lovely meadows with lots of lambs grazing on them, and that’s where I brought this flock from.” The peasants said, “Are there any more down there?” “Oh yes,” he said, “more than I could ever want.” So the peasants decided that they would fetch some sheep for themselves too, a flock apiece, but the mayor said, “I go first.” They went to the water together, and just then some of those small fluffy clouds that are called little lambs were drifting in the blue sky, and they were reflected in the water. The peasants cried, “We can already see the sheep down below!” The mayor pushed to the front and said, “I’ll go down first and look around, and if things look good I’ll call you.” So he jumped in. Splash! went the water, and it sounded as if he were calling them, and the whole crowd plunged in after him, all as one man. So the entire village died, and the little peasant, as the only heir, became a rich man.

chapters.title: Frederick and Catherine
paragraphs: There was once a man named Frederick, who had a wife called Catherine, and the two had only recently married. One day Frederick said, “Kate, I’m off to work in the fields. I’ll be hungry when I get back, so have something tasty cooked for me, and a good mug of ale.” “All right,” she said, “it’ll all be ready.” When dinner time was getting close, Catherine took a nice steak, the only meat she had in the house, and set it on the fire to fry. Soon the steak was turning brown and sizzling in the pan, and Catherine stood over it with a fork, turning it. Then she said to herself, “The steak is nearly done. I might as well fetch the ale from the cellar.” So she left the pan on the fire, picked up a big jug, went down to the cellar and tapped the ale cask. The beer poured into the jug while Catherine stood and watched. Then suddenly a thought struck her: “I never shut the dog in. He could be making off with the steak. Good thing I remembered!” So she dashed up the cellar steps, and sure enough, the thieving cur had the steak in his mouth and was trotting away with it.

Catherine tore off after him, and the dog tore off across the field, but he was faster than she was and kept a firm hold on the steak. “Well, it’s gone, and ‘what can’t be cured must be endured,’” said Catherine. She turned around, and since she had run a long way and was worn out, she strolled home slowly to cool off.

All this while the ale had been running too, because Catherine had not turned off the tap. When the jug was full, the beer spilled over onto the floor and kept going until the cask was empty. When she reached the cellar stairs, she saw what had happened. “Good heavens!” she said. “How am I going to hide this mess from Frederick?” She thought for a while, and finally remembered the sack of fine flour they had bought at the last fair. If she sprinkled that over the floor, it would soak up the ale nicely. “How lucky that we kept that flour,” she said. “Now it’s useful.” Off she went to fetch it, but she set it down right on top of the big jug of beer and knocked it over, so that all the ale she had saved went swimming across the floor as well. “Ah well,” she said, “if one goes, the other might as well follow.” Then she scattered the flour all over the cellar, delighted with her own cleverness, and said, “Doesn’t it look neat and clean!”

At noon Frederick came home. “Well, wife,” he called, “what’s for dinner?” “Oh, Frederick,” she answered, “I was frying you a steak, but while I went down to draw the ale, the dog ran off with it. While I was chasing him, the ale ran out, and when I tried to dry up the ale with the sack of flour we got at the fair, I knocked over the jug. But the cellar is nice and dry now, and it looks so clean!” “Kate, Kate,” he said, “how could you do all this? Why did you leave the steak frying and the ale running, and then ruin all the flour?” “Well, Frederick,” she said, “I didn’t know it was wrong. You should have told me before.”

The husband thought to himself, “If my wife runs things like this, I’d better keep a sharp eye out.” Now he had a good deal of gold in the house, so he said to Catherine, “What pretty yellow buttons these are! I’ll put them in a box and bury them in the garden. But mind you never go near them or touch them.” “No, Frederick,” she said, “I never will.” As soon as he had gone, some peddlers came by with earthenware plates and dishes and asked whether she wanted to buy any. “Oh dear, I’d love to buy some, but I have no money. If you had any use for yellow buttons, we might do business.” “Yellow buttons!” they said. “Let’s have a look at them.” “Go into the garden and dig where I tell you, and you’ll find the yellow buttons. I don’t dare go myself.” So the rogues went, and when they saw what these yellow buttons really were, they carried them all off and left her plenty of plates and dishes. She arranged them all around the house for show, and when Frederick came back, he cried, “Kate, what have you done?” “Look,” she said, “I bought all this with your yellow buttons. But I didn’t touch them myself. The peddlers went and dug them up on their own.” “Wife, wife,” said Frederick, “what a fine mess you’ve made! Those yellow buttons were all the money we had. How could you do such a thing?” “Well,” she answered, “I didn’t know there was any harm in it. You should have told me.”

Catherine stood thinking for a while, and then said to her husband, “Listen, Frederick, we’ll soon get the gold back. Let’s run after the thieves.” “All right, we’ll try,” he answered. “But take some butter and cheese with you, so we have something to eat on the way.” “Very well,” she said, and they set out. Frederick walked faster, and he left his wife some way behind. “It doesn’t matter,” she thought. “When we turn back, I’ll be that much closer to home than he is.”

Soon she came to the top of a hill. A road ran down its side, so narrow that the cart wheels always scraped the trees on either side as they went by. “Oh, look,” she said, “how they’ve bruised and hurt those poor trees. They’ll never heal.” She felt sorry for them, so she used the butter to grease every one of them, so the wheels wouldn’t hurt them so much. While she was busy with this kindly work, one of her cheeses dropped out of the basket and rolled down the hill. Catherine looked but couldn’t see where it had gone, so she said, “Well, I suppose the other one will go the same way and find you. It has younger legs than I do.” Then she rolled the other cheese after it, and off it went, nobody knows where, down the hill. But she said she supposed they knew the way and would follow her, and she couldn’t stand there all day waiting for them.

At last she caught up with Frederick, who asked her for something to eat. She gave him the dry bread. “Where are the butter and cheese?” he said. “Oh,” she answered, “I used the butter to grease those poor trees the wheels were scraping. And one of the cheeses ran away, so I sent the other after it to find it. I expect they’re both somewhere on the road together.” “What a goose you are, doing such silly things!” said her husband. “How can you say that?” she said. “I’m sure you never told me not to.”

They ate the dry bread together, and Frederick said, “Kate, I hope you locked the door properly when you left.” “No,” she answered, “you didn’t tell me to.” “Then go home and do it now, before we go any farther,” said Frederick, “and bring something to eat with you.”

Catherine did as he said, and on the way she thought to herself, “Frederick wants something to eat, but I don’t think he cares much for butter and cheese. I’ll bring him a bag of good nuts and the vinegar, since I’ve often seen him take some.”

When she got home, she bolted the back door, but the front door she lifted off its hinges, saying, “Frederick told me to lock the door, but surely it can’t be safer anywhere than with me.” So she took her time on the way back, and when she caught up with her husband she called out, “There you are, Frederick, there’s the door itself. You can guard it as carefully as you like.” “Good grief!” he said. “What a clever wife I have! I sent you to make the house secure, and you take the door away, so anyone can walk in and out as they please. Still, since you brought the door, you can carry it around with you for your trouble.” “Very well,” she answered, “I’ll carry the door, but I won’t carry the nuts and the vinegar bottle too. That would be too heavy a load. So if you don’t mind, I’ll tie them to the door.”

Frederick naturally had no objection to that, and they went into the wood to look for the thieves, but they couldn’t find them. When it got dark, they climbed a tree to spend the night. They had barely settled when who should come along but the very rogues they were hunting. They were real scoundrels, the kind of people who find things before they’re lost. They were tired, so they sat down and lit a fire right under the tree where Frederick and Catherine were. Frederick slid down the other side and picked up some stones. Then he climbed back up and tried to hit the thieves on the head with them, but all they said was, “It must be nearly morning, the wind’s knocking the fir cones down.”

Catherine, with the door on her shoulder, was getting very tired, but she thought it was the nuts on it that made it so heavy. So she said quietly, “Frederick, I’ll have to let the nuts go.” “No,” he answered, “not now, they’ll find us out.” “I can’t help it, they’ve got to go.” “Oh, all right, then hurry up and throw them down, if you must.” Away the nuts rattled down through the branches, and one of the thieves cried, “Good Lord, it’s hailing!”

A little while later, Catherine felt the door was still very heavy, so she whispered to Frederick, “I’ll have to pour the vinegar out.” “Please don’t,” he answered, “it will give us away.” “I can’t help it,” she said, “it has to go.” So she poured all the vinegar down, and the thieves said, “What a heavy dew there is!”

At last it dawned on Catherine that it was the door itself that had been so heavy all along. So she whispered, “Frederick, I’ll have to throw the door down soon.” But he begged and pleaded with her not to, sure that it would betray them. “Here it goes, anyway,” she said, and down went the door onto the thieves with such a crash that they screamed “Murder!” and, not knowing what was falling on them, ran off as fast as they could and left all the gold behind. So when Frederick and Catherine climbed down, they found all their money there, safe and sound.

chapters.title: Sweetheart Roland
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a woman who was a real witch and had two daughters. One was ugly and wicked, and she loved this one because she was her own daughter. The other was beautiful and good, and she hated this one because she was her stepdaughter. The stepdaughter once had a pretty apron, and the other girl liked it so much that she grew jealous and told her mother she must and would have that apron. “Hush, my child,” said the old woman, “you’ll have it. Your stepsister has deserved to die for a long time. Tonight, when she’s asleep, I’ll come and cut her head off. Just make sure you lie on the far side of the bed, and push her well to the front.” It would have been the end of the poor girl if she hadn’t been standing in a corner at that moment and heard every word. She didn’t dare leave the house all day, and when bedtime came, the witch’s daughter got into bed first, to lie on the far side. But once she was asleep, the other girl gently pushed her to the front and took the place at the back for herself, next to the wall. In the night the old woman came creeping in, an axe in her right hand, feeling with her left to check whether someone was lying on the outside. Then she gripped the axe with both hands and cut off her own child’s head.

When the witch had gone, the girl got up, went to her sweetheart, whose name was Roland, and knocked on his door. When he came out, she said to him, “Listen, dearest Roland, we have to flee at once. My stepmother wanted to kill me, but she has struck down her own child. When daylight comes and she sees what she’s done, we’ll be lost.” “But,” said Roland, “my advice is to take her magic wand first, or we can’t get away if she chases us.” The girl fetched the magic wand. Then she took the dead girl’s head and let three drops of blood fall on the ground, one in front of the bed, one in the kitchen and one on the stairs. Then she hurried off with her lover.

When the old witch got up the next morning, she called her daughter, meaning to give her the apron, but the girl didn’t come. So the witch cried, “Where are you?” “Here on the stairs, sweeping,” answered the first drop of blood. The old woman went out but saw no one on the stairs, and called again, “Where are you?” “Here in the kitchen, warming myself,” called the second drop of blood. She went into the kitchen but found no one. Then she called again, “Where are you?” “Ah, here in the bed, sleeping,” called the third drop of blood. She went into the room, up to the bed. What did she see? Her own child, whose head she had cut off, lying in her blood. The witch flew into a rage and sprang to the window, and since she could see a long way out over the world, she spotted her stepdaughter hurrying off with her sweetheart Roland. “That won’t save you,” she cried. “Even if you’ve gone a long way, you still won’t escape me.” She pulled on her many-league boots, which covered an hour’s walk with every step, and it wasn’t long before she caught up with them. But when the girl saw the old woman striding toward her, she used her magic wand to turn her sweetheart Roland into a lake and herself into a duck swimming in the middle of it. The witch stood on the shore, threw breadcrumbs in and went to endless trouble to lure the duck, but the duck wouldn’t be lured, and the old woman had to go home at nightfall just as she had come. Then the girl and her sweetheart Roland took their own shapes again, and they walked all night until daybreak. Then the girl turned herself into a beautiful flower growing in the middle of a briar hedge, and her sweetheart Roland into a fiddler. It wasn’t long before the witch came striding up and said to the musician, “Dear musician, may I pick that beautiful flower for myself?” “Oh yes,” he replied, “and I’ll play for you while you do it.” She was hurriedly creeping into the hedge and was just about to pluck the flower, knowing perfectly well who the flower was, when he began to play. Whether she wanted to or not, she was forced to dance, for it was a magic dance. The faster he played, the wilder the leaps she had to make, and the thorns tore the clothes from her body and pricked and wounded her until she bled. Since he never stopped, she had to dance until she lay dead on the ground.

Now that they were free, Roland said, “I’ll go to my father and arrange the wedding.” “Then I’ll stay here and wait for you,” said the girl, “and so that nobody recognizes me, I’ll turn myself into a red boundary stone.” So Roland left, and the girl stood in the field as a red boundary stone, waiting for her beloved. But when Roland reached home, he fell into another woman’s trap. She bewitched him so completely that he forgot the girl. The poor girl stayed there a long time, but in the end, when he never came back, she grew sad and turned herself into a flower, thinking, “Somebody is sure to walk by and trample me.”

It happened, though, that a shepherd was grazing his sheep in that field. He noticed the flower, and because it was so pretty he picked it, took it home and put it away in his chest. From then on, strange things went on in the shepherd’s house. Every morning when he got up, all the work was already finished: the room was swept, the table and benches were wiped clean, the fire was burning in the hearth, and the water was fetched. At noon, when he came home, the table was set and a good dinner was waiting. He could not understand how this came about, since he never saw a soul in his house, and nobody could have hidden in it. He was pleased enough with such good service, but in the end he grew so frightened that he went to a wise woman and asked her advice. The wise woman said, “There is some enchantment behind this. Some morning, listen very early for anything stirring in the room, and if you see something, whatever it is, throw a white cloth over it, and the magic will be broken.”

The shepherd did as she told him. The next morning, just as day was breaking, he saw the chest open and the flower step out. He leapt toward it quickly and threw a white cloth over it. At once the spell ended, and a beautiful girl stood in front of him. She told him she had been the flower and that until now she had been looking after his house. She told him her story, and since he liked her, he asked whether she would marry him. But she said “No,” because she wanted to stay true to her sweetheart Roland, even though he had abandoned her. Even so, she promised not to leave, and to go on keeping house for the shepherd.

Now the time came near for Roland’s wedding. According to an old custom of the country, it was proclaimed that all the girls must attend and sing in honor of the bride and groom. When the faithful girl heard this, she became so sad that she thought her heart would break, and she did not want to go there, but the other girls came and fetched her. When her turn to sing came, she kept stepping back until she was the only one left, and then she could not refuse. But as soon as she began her song and it reached Roland’s ears, he jumped up and cried, “I know that voice! That is the true bride, and I will have no other!” Everything he had forgotten, everything that had slipped from his mind, suddenly came back to his heart. Then the faithful girl married her sweetheart Roland, and sorrow ended and joy began.

chapters.title: Snowdrop
paragraphs: In the middle of winter, when broad snowflakes were drifting down all around, the queen of a country many thousands of miles away sat sewing at her window. The window frame was made of fine black ebony, and as she sat looking out at the snow, she pricked her finger, and three drops of blood fell on the wood. She gazed thoughtfully at the red drops on the white snow and said, “If only my little daughter could be as white as that snow, as red as that blood, and as black as this ebony frame!” And so the little girl did grow up with skin as white as snow, cheeks as rosy as blood, and hair as black as ebony, and she was named Snowdrop.

But this queen died, and before long the king married another wife. She became queen and was very beautiful, but so vain that she could not stand the thought of anyone being lovelier than she was. She owned a magic looking-glass, and she would go to it, gaze at herself, and say:

“Glass, tell me honestly,
Of all the ladies in the land,
Who is the fairest? Tell it to me.”
And the glass had always replied:
“You, my queen, are the fairest in all the land.”

But Snowdrop grew lovelier and lovelier, and by the time she was seven she was radiant as the day and more beautiful than the queen herself. So one day, when the queen went to consult the glass as usual, it replied:

“Fair are you, queen, and fine to see,
But Snowdrop is lovelier far than you!”

When the queen heard this, she turned pale with rage and jealousy. She called one of her servants and said, “Take Snowdrop out into the wide forest, so that I never have to see her again.” The servant led her away, but his heart softened when Snowdrop begged him to spare her life, and he said, “I won’t hurt you, you pretty child.” So he left her alone. He thought it very likely that the wild beasts would tear her to pieces, yet he felt a great weight lift from his heart once he had decided not to kill her but to leave her to her fate, in the hope that someone might find and save her.

Poor Snowdrop wandered through the forest in great fear, and the wild beasts roared around her, but none of them harmed her. In the evening she came to a cottage in the hills and went in to rest, because her little feet could carry her no further. Everything inside was neat and tidy. On the table a white cloth was spread, and there were seven little plates, seven little loaves and seven little glasses of wine, with seven knives and forks set out in order, and along the wall stood seven little beds. She was very hungry, so she nibbled a little from each loaf and drank a few drops from each glass, and then she decided to lie down and rest. She tried all the little beds, but one was too long and another too short, until at last the seventh fitted her, and there she lay down and fell asleep.

Soon afterwards the owners of the cottage came home. They were seven little dwarfs who lived in the mountains and dug and searched for gold. They lit their seven lamps and saw right away that something was wrong. The first said, “Who has been sitting on my stool?” The second said, “Who has been eating from my plate?” The third, “Who has been taking my bread?” The fourth, “Who has been messing with my spoon?” The fifth, “Who has been touching my fork?” The sixth, “Who has been cutting with my knife?” The seventh, “Who has been drinking my wine?” Then the first looked around and said, “Who has been lying in my bed?” The others came running to him, and each one cried out that someone had been in his bed. But the seventh saw Snowdrop and called all his brothers to come and look. They cried out in wonder and amazement, and fetched their lamps to look at her, and said, “Good heavens! What a lovely child she is!” They were delighted to see her and took care not to wake her, and the seventh dwarf slept an hour with each of the others in turn, until the night was over.

In the morning Snowdrop told them her whole story. They felt sorry for her and said that if she would keep everything in order, and cook, wash, knit and spin for them, she could stay where she was and they would take good care of her. Then they went off to work for the whole day, hunting for gold and silver in the mountains, while Snowdrop stayed at home. They warned her, saying, “The queen will soon find out where you are, so be careful and let no one in.”
But the queen, now that she believed Snowdrop was dead, was sure she must be the most beautiful lady in the land. She went to her glass and said:

“Glass, tell me honestly,
Of all the ladies in the land,
Who is the fairest? Tell it to me.”
And the glass replied:

“You, my queen, are the fairest in this land.
But over the hills, in the greenwood shade,
Where the seven dwarfs have made their home,
Snowdrop is hiding her head, and she
Is lovelier far, O queen, than you.”

The queen was terrified, for she knew the glass always told the truth, and she was certain the servant had betrayed her. She could not bear the thought that anyone alive was more beautiful than she was, so she disguised herself as an old pedlar and set off over the hills to the place where the dwarfs lived. She knocked at the door and called, “Fine wares for sale!” Snowdrop looked out of the window and said, “Good day, good woman! What have you got to sell?” “Good wares, fine wares,” said the queen, “laces and cords of every color.” “I can let this old lady in, she seems a perfectly decent person,” thought Snowdrop, and she ran down and unbolted the door. “Goodness me!” said the old woman. “Your bodice is laced so badly! Let me lace it up for you with one of my nice new laces.” Snowdrop suspected no harm, so she stood in front of the old woman. But the woman set to work so quickly and pulled the lace so tight that Snowdrop could not breathe, and she fell down as if dead. “That’s the end of your beauty,” said the spiteful queen, and she went home.

That evening the seven dwarfs came home, and I need hardly say how upset they were to find their faithful Snowdrop stretched out on the floor as if she were quite dead. They lifted her up, and when they saw what was wrong, they cut the lace. After a little while she began to breathe, and soon she came back to life. Then they said, “That old woman was the queen herself. Be careful next time, and let no one in while we are away.”
Back home, the queen hurried to her glass and put the same question to it, and to her bitter distress it gave the same answer:

“You, my queen, are the fairest in this land.
But over the hills, in the greenwood shade,
Where the seven dwarfs have made their home,
Snowdrop is hiding her head, and she
Is lovelier far, O queen, than you.”

Then the blood ran cold in her heart with spite and malice, because Snowdrop was still alive. She disguised herself again, in a quite different outfit from the first, and took a poisoned comb with her. When she reached the dwarfs’ cottage, she knocked at the door and called, “Fine wares for sale!” But Snowdrop said, “I mustn’t let anyone in.” Then the queen said, “Just look at my beautiful combs!” and handed her the poisoned one. It looked so pretty that Snowdrop picked it up and put it in her hair to try it, but the moment it touched her head the poison was so strong that she fell down unconscious. “There you can lie,” said the queen, and she went on her way. But luckily the dwarfs came home very early that evening. When they saw Snowdrop lying on the floor, they guessed what had happened and soon found the poisoned comb. As soon as they took it out she recovered, and she told them everything that had happened, and once more they warned her not to open the door to anyone.

Meanwhile the queen went home to her glass and shook with rage when she heard exactly the same answer as before. She said, “Snowdrop shall die, even if it costs me my own life.” So she went alone into her private room and prepared a poisoned apple. The outside looked rosy and tempting, but anyone who tasted it was sure to die. Then she disguised herself as a peasant’s wife, traveled over the hills to the dwarfs’ cottage and knocked at the door. But Snowdrop put her head out of the window and said, “I mustn’t let anyone in, because the dwarfs have forbidden it.” “As you like,” said the old woman, “but at least take this pretty apple. I’ll give it to you.” “No,” said Snowdrop, “I mustn’t take it.” “Silly girl!” the other replied. “What are you afraid of? Do you think it’s poisoned? Come now, you eat one half and I’ll eat the other.” The apple had been made so that one side was good and only the other side was poisoned. Snowdrop was greatly tempted to taste it, because the apple looked so delicious, and when she saw the old woman take a bite, she could wait no longer. But she had barely put the piece in her mouth when she fell to the ground dead. “This time nothing will save you,” said the queen. She went home to her glass, and at last it said:
“Queen, of all the fair, you are the fairest.”
At that her wicked heart rejoiced, as much as a heart like hers ever could.

When evening came and the dwarfs got home, they found Snowdrop lying on the ground. No breath came from her lips, and they were afraid she was truly dead. They lifted her up, combed her hair and washed her face with wine and water, but it was all in vain: the little girl seemed quite dead. So they laid her on a bier, and all seven sat by her and mourned her for three whole days. Then they thought they should bury her, but her cheeks were still rosy and her face looked just as it had when she was alive, so they said, “We will never bury her in the cold ground.” They made a glass coffin so that they could keep looking at her, and wrote on it in golden letters her name and the fact that she was a king’s daughter. The coffin was placed up in the hills, and one of the dwarfs always sat beside it keeping watch. The birds of the air came too and mourned for Snowdrop, first an owl, then a raven, and finally a dove, and they sat beside her.

And so Snowdrop lay for a long, long time, and she still looked as if she were only sleeping, for even now she was as white as snow, as red as blood and as black as ebony. At last a prince came by and called at the dwarfs’ house. He saw Snowdrop and read what was written in golden letters. He offered the dwarfs money and begged and pleaded with them to let him take her away, but they said, “We won’t give her up for all the gold in the world.” In the end, though, they took pity on him and gave him the coffin. But the moment he lifted it to carry it home, the piece of apple fell from between her lips, and Snowdrop woke up and said, “Where am I?” And the prince said, “You are perfectly safe with me.”

Then he told her everything that had happened. “I love you more than anything in the world,” he said. “Come with me to my father’s palace and be my wife.” Snowdrop agreed and went home with the prince, and the wedding was prepared with great pomp and splendor.
Among the guests invited to the feast was Snowdrop’s old enemy, the queen. While she was putting on her finest clothes, she stood before the glass and said:

“Glass, tell me honestly,
Of all the ladies in the land,
Who is the fairest? Tell it to me.”
And the glass replied:

“You, my lady, are fairest here, I know,
But the new-made queen is fairer still, and so.”
