When she heard this, she shook with rage. Yet she was so consumed with envy and curiosity that she could not stay away, and she set out to see the bride. But when she arrived and saw that the bride was none other than Snowdrop, whom she had believed dead for a long time, she choked with fury, fell to the ground and died. Snowdrop and the prince lived and ruled happily over that land for many, many years. Now and then they climbed up into the mountains to visit the little dwarfs, who had been so kind to Snowdrop when she was in need.

chapters.title: The Pink
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a queen to whom God had given no children. Every morning she went out into the garden and prayed to God in heaven to grant her a son or a daughter. One day an angel came down from heaven and said to her, “Be at peace. You will have a son who has the power of wishing, so that whatever he wishes for in the world, he will have.” She went to the king and told him the joyful news, and when the time came she gave birth to a son, and the king was filled with happiness.

Every morning she took the child with her to the garden where the wild animals were kept, and washed in a clear stream there. One day, when the child was a little older, it was lying in her arms and she fell asleep. The old cook, who knew the child had the power of wishing, came and stole it away. He killed a hen, cut it into pieces, and dripped some of its blood on the queen’s apron and dress. Then he carried the child off to a secret place, where a nurse was forced to nurse it, and ran to the king and accused the queen of letting wild animals take her child from her. When the king saw the blood on her apron, he believed it. He flew into such a rage that he ordered a high tower to be built, with no way for the sun or moon to shine in, and had his wife shut up inside and walled in. She was to stay there for seven years without food or drink, and starve to death. But God sent two angels from heaven in the shape of white doves, and they flew to her twice a day and brought her food until the seven years were over.

The cook, though, thought to himself, “If the child has the power of wishing and I stay here, he could easily bring trouble down on me.” So he left the palace and went to the boy, who was by now old enough to talk, and said to him, “Wish for a beautiful palace for yourself, with a garden and everything that goes with it.” The words were barely out of the boy’s mouth when everything he had wished for was there. After a while the cook said to him, “It isn’t good for you to be so alone. Wish for a pretty girl to keep you company.” So the king’s son wished for one, and she stood before him at once, more beautiful than any painter could have painted her. The two of them played together and loved each other with all their hearts, while the old cook went hunting like a nobleman. But then it occurred to him that the king’s son might one day wish to be with his father, and that this would put him in great danger. So he went out, took the girl aside, and said, “Tonight, when the boy is asleep, go to his bed and drive this knife into his heart. Bring me his heart and his tongue. If you don’t do it, you will lose your life.” Then he left, and when he came back the next day she had not done it. She said, “Why should I shed the blood of an innocent boy who has never harmed anyone?” The cook said again, “If you don’t do it, it will cost you your own life.” After he had gone, she had a young hind brought to her and ordered it killed. She took its heart and tongue and laid them on a plate, and when she saw the old man coming, she said to the boy, “Lie down in your bed and pull the covers over you.” Then the wicked man came in and said, “Where are the boy’s heart and tongue?” The girl handed him the plate, but the king’s son threw off the quilt and said, “You old sinner, why did you want to kill me? Now I pronounce your sentence. You will become a black poodle with a gold collar around your neck, and you will eat burning coals until flames burst from your throat.” As soon as he had spoken these words, the old man was turned into a poodle with a gold collar around his neck, and the cooks were told to bring live coals, and he ate them until flames shot out of his throat. The king’s son stayed there a little while longer, thinking of his mother and wondering whether she was still alive. At last he said to the girl, “I want to go home to my own country. If you come with me, I will look after you.” “Oh,” she answered, “it is such a long way, and what would I do in a strange land where nobody knows me?” She did not seem quite willing, and since they could not bear to be parted, he wished her into a beautiful pink and took her with him. Then he set off for his own country, with the poodle running behind him. He went to the tower where his mother was shut up, and since it was so high, he wished for a ladder that would reach all the way to the top. He climbed up, looked inside, and called, “Dearest mother, Lady Queen, are you still alive, or are you dead?” She answered, “I have just eaten, and I am still full,” for she thought the angels were there. He said, “I am your dear son, the one the wild animals were said to have torn from your arms. But I am still alive, and I will soon set you free.” Then he climbed down again, went to his father, and had himself announced as a stranger and a huntsman, and asked whether the king could use his services. The king said yes: if he was skillful and could bring in game, he could come into his service, but there had never been any deer in that district or anywhere in the country. The huntsman promised to supply as much game as the royal table could possibly use. He called all the huntsmen together and told them to come out into the forest with him. There he had them form a great circle, open at one end, and he stood in the opening and began to wish. More than two hundred deer came running into the circle at once, and the huntsmen shot them. They were loaded onto sixty country carts and driven home to the king, and for once he could load his table with game, after years without any.

The king was very pleased, and ordered his whole household to dine with him the next day, and held a great feast. When everyone had gathered, he said to the huntsman, “Since you are so clever, you will sit beside me.” The huntsman replied, “Lord King, Your Majesty must excuse me. I am only a poor huntsman.” But the king insisted, saying, “You will sit beside me,” until he did. As he sat there, he thought of his dearest mother, and wished that one of the king’s chief servants would speak of her and ask how the queen was doing in the tower, and whether she was still alive or had died. He had hardly made the wish when the marshal began, “Your Majesty, we live in joy here, but how does the queen fare in the tower? Is she still alive, or has she died?” But the king answered, “She let my dear son be torn to pieces by wild animals. I will not have her named.” Then the huntsman stood up and said, “Gracious lord father, she is still alive, and I am her son. I was not carried off by wild animals. It was that wretch, the old cook, who tore me from her arms while she slept and smeared her apron with the blood of a chicken.” Then he took the dog with the golden collar and said, “There is the wretch!” He had live coals brought, and the dog was forced to swallow them in front of everyone, until flames burst from its throat. The huntsman then asked the king whether he would like to see the dog in its true shape, and wished him back into the cook, who stood there at once in his white apron with his knife at his side. When the king saw him, he flew into a rage and ordered him thrown into the deepest dungeon. Then the huntsman went on, “Father, would you like to see the girl who raised me so tenderly, and who was later supposed to murder me, but did not, though her own life depended on it?” The king answered, “Yes, I would like to see her.” The son said, “Most gracious father, I will show her to you as a beautiful flower.” He put his hand in his pocket, took out the pink, and set it on the royal table, and it was so beautiful that the king had never seen one to match it. Then the son said, “Now I will show her to you in her own form,” and he wished her into a girl again, and she stood there, so beautiful that no painter could have made her more so.

The king sent two maids and two attendants to the tower to fetch the queen and bring her to the royal table. But when she was led in, she ate nothing. She said, “The gracious and merciful God who kept me alive in the tower will soon set me free.” She lived three days longer and then died a happy death. When she was buried, the two white doves that had brought her food in the tower, and were angels from heaven, followed her body and settled on her grave. The old king ordered the cook torn into four pieces, but grief ate away at the king’s own heart, and he soon died. His son married the beautiful girl he had carried with him as a flower in his pocket, and whether they are still alive or not, God knows.

chapters.title: Clever Elsie
paragraphs: There was once a man who had a daughter called Clever Elsie. When she had grown up, her father said, “We should get her married.” “Yes,” said the mother, “if only someone would turn up who wanted her.” At last a man came from far away to court her. His name was Hans, but he made one condition: Clever Elsie had to be truly smart. “Oh,” said the father, “she has plenty of good sense.” And the mother said, “Oh, she can see the wind coming up the street and hear the flies cough.” “Well,” said Hans, “if she isn’t really smart, I won’t have her.” When they were sitting at dinner and had finished eating, the mother said, “Elsie, go down to the cellar and fetch some beer.” Clever Elsie took the pitcher down from the wall and went to the cellar, tapping the lid briskly as she went, so the time would not seem long. Down below, she fetched a chair and set it in front of the barrel, so she would not have to bend over and hurt her back or give herself some unexpected injury. Then she set the can in front of her and turned the tap, and while the beer ran she would not let her eyes sit idle. She looked up at the wall, and after much peering this way and that, she saw a pick-axe right above her head, which the masons had left there by accident.

Clever Elsie started to cry. “Say I get Hans,” she said, “and we have a child, and he grows up, and we send him down to this cellar to draw beer. Then the pick-axe will fall on his head and kill him.” She sat there sobbing and wailing at the top of her voice over the terrible fate that lay ahead of her. Upstairs they were waiting for their drink, but Clever Elsie didn’t appear. At last the lady of the house said to the maid, “Go down to the cellar and see what’s keeping Elsie.” The maid went down and found her sitting in front of the barrel, screaming her head off. “Elsie, why are you crying?” asked the maid. “Oh,” said Elsie, “don’t I have good reason? If I get Hans, and we have a child, and he grows up and has to draw beer down here, the pick-axe might fall on his head and kill him.” “What a clever Elsie we have!” said the maid, and she sat down next to her and began to wail over the coming disaster too. After a while, when the maid didn’t return and the people upstairs were getting thirsty, the master said to the boy, “Go down to the cellar and see where Elsie and the girl have got to.” The boy went down, and there sat Clever Elsie and the maid, crying together. “Why are you crying?” he asked. “Oh,” said Elsie, “don’t I have good reason? If I get Hans, and we have a child, and he grows up and has to draw beer down here, the pick-axe will fall on his head and kill him.” “What a clever Elsie we have!” said the boy, and he sat down beside her and started howling as loudly as the others. Upstairs they waited for the boy, but when he didn’t come back either, the man said to his wife, “Go down to the cellar and see where Elsie is!” The woman went down and found all three in the middle of their lament. She asked what the matter was, and Elsie told her too: how her future child would be killed by the pick-axe when he was grown and had to draw beer, and the pick-axe fell. “What a clever Elsie we have!” said the mother, and she sat down and wept with them. The man upstairs waited a little while, but when his wife didn’t return and his thirst got worse and worse, he said, “I’ll have to go down to the cellar myself and see where Elsie is.” When he got there, they were all sitting together in tears. He heard the reason: that Elsie’s child was to blame, that Elsie might one day bring one into the world, and that it might be killed by the pick-axe if it happened to be sitting underneath, drawing beer, at the very moment the pick-axe fell. “Oh, what a clever Elsie!” he cried, and he sat down and wept with them. The bridegroom stayed upstairs alone for a long time. Then, since nobody came back, he thought, “They must be waiting for me down there. I’d better go and see what they’re up to.” When he got down, there were the five of them, shrieking and lamenting pitifully, each trying to outdo the others. “What’s the disaster, then?” he asked. “Oh, dear Hans,” said Elsie, “if we marry and have a child, and he grows up, and we happen to send him down here to draw something to drink, then the pick-axe that’s been left up there could fall and smash his brains out. Don’t we have good reason to weep?” “Well,” said Hans, “my household needs no more sense than that. Since you’re such a clever Elsie, I’ll have you.” He took her by the hand, led her upstairs, and married her.

Once Hans had had her for a while, he said, “Wife, I’m going out to work and earn us some money. You go to the field and cut the corn, so that we’ll have bread.” “Yes, dear Hans, I’ll do that.” When Hans had gone, she cooked herself a nice broth and took it with her to the field. When she got there, she said to herself, “What should I do? Cut first, or eat first? Oh, I’ll eat first.” So she drank her cup of broth, and when she was full she asked again, “What should I do? Cut first, or sleep first? I’ll sleep first.” She lay down in the corn and fell asleep. Hans had been home a long time, but Elsie didn’t come. “What a clever Elsie I have,” he said. “She’s so hardworking that she doesn’t even come home to eat.” But when evening fell and she still hadn’t come, Hans went out to see how much she had cut. Nothing was cut at all, and she was lying in the corn, fast asleep. Hans hurried home and fetched a bird-catcher’s net hung with little bells, and draped it all around her. She kept on sleeping. Then he ran home, shut the front door, sat down in his chair, and went on with his work. At last, when it was completely dark, Clever Elsie woke up. As she got to her feet, there was a jingling all around her, and the bells rang at every step she took. She was frightened, and she began to doubt whether she was really Clever Elsie or not. “Is it me, or isn’t it me?” she asked. She had no idea how to answer, and stood there uncertain for a while. Finally she thought, “I’ll go home and ask whether it’s me or not. They’re sure to know.” She ran to the door of her own house, but it was shut. So she knocked at the window and called, “Hans, is Elsie inside?” “Yes,” Hans answered, “she’s inside.” That terrified her. “Oh, heavens! Then it isn’t me,” she said, and she went to another door. But when the people there heard the jingling bells, they wouldn’t open up, and she couldn’t get in anywhere. So she ran out of the village, and nobody has seen her since.

chapters.title: The Miser in the Bush
paragraphs: A farmer had a loyal, hard-working servant who had labored for him for three years without ever being paid. At last it occurred to the man that he didn’t want to go on like this, working for nothing. He went to his master and said, “I’ve worked hard for you for a long time. I’ll trust you to give me whatever I’ve earned for my trouble.” The farmer was a wretched miser, and he knew his servant was very simple-minded. So he took out three pennies and gave him one for each year of service. The poor fellow thought this was a huge amount of money, and he said to himself, “Why should I keep slaving away and living on bad food here? Now I can go out into the wide world and enjoy myself.” He put the money in his purse and set off, wandering over hill and valley.

He was strolling across the fields, singing and dancing, when a little dwarf met him and asked what made him so cheerful. “Why would I be down in the mouth?” he said. “I’m healthy, my purse is full, and I haven’t a care. I’ve saved up three years’ wages, and it’s all safe in my pocket.” “How much is it?” asked the little man. “Three whole pennies,” said the countryman. “I wish you’d give them to me,” said the dwarf. “I’m very poor.” The man felt sorry for him and handed over everything he had. In return the dwarf said, “You have such a kind, honest heart that I’ll grant you three wishes, one for each penny. Choose whatever you like.” The countryman was delighted with his luck. “There are plenty of things I like better than money,” he said. “First, I’d like a bow that brings down everything I aim at. Second, a fiddle that makes everyone who hears it dance. And third, I’d like everyone to grant whatever I ask.” The dwarf said he should have all three wishes, and he gave him the bow and the fiddle and went on his way.

Our honest friend went on his way as well, and if he had been merry before, he was ten times merrier now. He hadn’t gone far when he met an old miser. Nearby stood a tree, and on its topmost twig a thrush was singing joyfully. “Oh, what a pretty bird!” said the miser. “I’d pay a lot of money to have one like that.” “If that’s all you want,” said the countryman, “I’ll have it down in no time.” He raised his bow, and the thrush dropped into the bushes at the foot of the tree. The miser crawled into the thicket to look for it. But as soon as he was in the middle, the countryman took up his fiddle and began to play, and the miser started to dance and leap about, jumping higher and higher in the air. The thorns soon tore his clothes until they hung from him in rags, and he was scratched and cut all over, so that the blood ran down. “Oh, for heaven’s sake!” cried the miser. “Master! Master! Please stop the fiddle! What have I done to deserve this?” “You’ve fleeced plenty of poor souls to the bone,” said the other. “You’re only getting what’s coming to you.” And he struck up another tune. Then the miser began to beg and make promises, and he offered money for his freedom. But for some time his offers fell short of the musician’s price, and the fiddler kept him dancing faster and faster while the miser bid higher and higher. At last he offered a full hundred florins that he had in his purse, money he had just got by cheating some poor fellow. When the countryman saw so much money, he said, “I accept your offer.” He took the purse, put away his fiddle, and traveled on, well pleased with his bargain.

Meanwhile the miser crawled out of the bush half-naked and in a sorry state, and began to think how he could get revenge and play a trick on the man he had just left. At last he went to the judge and complained that a rascal had robbed him of his money and beaten him as well. The man who did it, he said, carried a bow on his back and a fiddle slung round his neck. The judge sent his officers to bring in the accused wherever they found him, and before long the countryman was caught and brought in for trial.

The miser told his story, saying he had been robbed of his money. “No, you gave it to me for playing you a tune,” said the countryman. But the judge told him that was unlikely, and he cut the matter short by ordering him to the gallows.

So he was led away. But as he stood on the steps, he said, “My Lord Judge, grant me one last request.” “Anything except your life,” replied the judge. “No,” he said, “I’m not asking for my life. Only let me play my fiddle one last time.” The miser cried out, “Oh, no! No! For heaven’s sake, don’t listen to him! Don’t listen to him!” But the judge said, “It’s only this once. He’ll soon be done.” The truth was that he couldn’t refuse the request, because of the dwarf’s third gift.

Then the miser said, “Tie me up tight, tie me up tight, for pity’s sake!” But the countryman grabbed his fiddle and struck up a tune. At the very first note the judge, the clerks, and the jailer were all in motion. They began to caper about, and no one could hold on to the miser. At the second note the hangman let his prisoner go and started dancing too, and by the time the fiddler had played the first bar, everyone was dancing together: the judge, the court, the miser, and all the people who had followed to watch. At first it was merry and pleasant enough. But after a while, when there seemed to be no end to the playing or the dancing, they began to shout and beg him to stop. He didn’t stop one bit for all their pleading, until the judge not only gave him his life but also promised to return the hundred florins.

Then the countryman called to the miser. “Tell us now, you scoundrel, where you got that gold, or I’ll go on playing just for your amusement.” “I stole it,” said the miser in front of all the people. “I admit that I stole it, and that you earned it fairly.” Then the countryman stopped his fiddle and left the miser to take his place at the gallows.

chapters.title: Ashputtel
paragraphs: A rich man’s wife fell ill, and when she felt that her end was near, she called her only daughter to her bedside and said, “Always be a good girl, and I will look down from heaven and watch over you.” Soon afterwards she closed her eyes and died, and she was buried in the garden. The little girl went to her grave every day and wept, and she stayed good and kind to everyone around her. The snow fell and spread a lovely white blanket over the grave, but by the time spring came and the sun had melted it away again, her father had married a second wife. The new wife brought two daughters of her own into the house. They were fair of face but foul of heart, and it was a miserable time for the poor little girl. “What does this good-for-nothing want in the parlor?” they said. “Anyone who wants bread must earn it first. Away with the kitchen maid!” They took away her fine clothes, gave her an old gray dress to wear, laughed at her, and sent her off to the kitchen.

There she was made to do hard work. She had to get up before daybreak, carry the water, light the fire, cook, and wash. On top of that, the sisters tormented her in every way they could think of, and made fun of her. In the evening, when she was worn out, she had no bed to lie in, but had to sleep by the hearth among the ashes. Naturally this left her always dusty and dirty, so they called her Ashputtel.

Once, when the father was about to go to the fair, he asked his wife’s daughters what he should bring them. “Fine clothes,” said the first. “Pearls and diamonds,” said the second. “And you, child,” he said to his own daughter, “what would you like?” “The first twig that brushes against your hat on the way home, dear father,” she said. So he bought the first two the fine clothes, pearls, and diamonds they had asked for. On his way home, as he rode through a green thicket, a hazel twig brushed against him and nearly knocked his hat off. He broke it off and took it with him, and when he got home he gave it to his daughter. She took it to her mother’s grave and planted it there, and she cried so much that her tears watered it, and it grew into a fine tree. Three times a day she went to it and wept. Soon a little bird came and built its nest in the tree, and it talked with her, watched over her, and brought her whatever she wished for.

As it happened, the king of that country gave a feast that was to go on for three days, and his son was to pick a bride from among the guests. Ashputtel’s two stepsisters were invited. They called her over and said, “Comb our hair, brush our shoes, and fasten our sashes, because we’re going to dance at the king’s feast.” She did as she was told, but when everything was finished she couldn’t stop herself from crying, since she would have loved to go with them to the ball. In the end she begged her stepmother very hard to allow it. “You, Ashputtel?” the woman said. “You, with nothing to wear, not a single dress, and not even able to dance—you want to go to the ball?” But Ashputtel kept on begging, and at last, just to be rid of her, the stepmother said, “I’m going to tip this dishful of peas into the ash-heap. If you have picked them all out again within two hours, you may come to the feast too.”
She tipped the peas out among the ashes. The little maiden ran through the back door into the garden and called out:

“Come here, come here, through the sky,
Turtle-doves and linnets, fly!
Blackbird, thrush, and chaffinch, too,
Come here, come here, hurry through!
Every one of you, help me quick!
Hurry, hurry!—pick, pick, pick!”

First two white doves came flying in through the kitchen window, then two turtle-doves, and after them every little bird under heaven came chirping and fluttering in. They swooped down into the ashes, and the doves bent their heads and set to work, pick, pick, pick. Then the others started in, pick, pick, pick, and between them they soon had all the good grain sorted into the dish and left the ashes behind. The job was finished long before the hour was up, and the birds all flew out of the windows again.

Ashputtel carried the dish to her stepmother, overjoyed, thinking she would now be allowed to go to the ball. But the woman said, “No, no, you slut! You have no clothes and you can’t dance. You’re not going.” When Ashputtel begged hard to go all the same, she said, “If you can pick two whole dishes of peas out of the ashes in one hour, then you may come.” She thought that way she would be rid of the girl for good. And she shook two dishes of peas into the ashes.
But the little maiden went out into the garden behind the house and called out as she had before:

“Come here, come here, through the sky,
Turtle-doves and linnets, fly!
Blackbird, thrush, and chaffinch, too,
Come here, come here, hurry through!
Every one of you, help me quick!
Hurry, hurry!—pick, pick, pick!”

First two white doves came in through the kitchen window, then two turtle-doves, and after them every little bird under heaven, chirping and hopping about. They flew down into the ashes, and the doves lowered their heads and set to work, pick, pick, pick. The others began, pick, pick, pick, and they put all the good grain into the dishes and left every bit of ash. In less than half an hour it was all done, and out they flew. Ashputtel took the dishes to her stepmother, glad to think she could go to the ball now. But the woman said, “It’s no use. You can’t go. You have no clothes and you can’t dance, and you would only shame us.” And she left for the ball with her two daughters.
When they had all gone and nobody was left at home, Ashputtel went sadly out and sat down under the hazel-tree, and called out:

“Shake, shake, hazel-tree,
Gold and silver over me!”

Her friend the bird flew down out of the tree and brought her a dress of gold and silver, and slippers of spangled silk. She put them on and followed her sisters to the feast. They did not recognize her. They took her for some strange princess, she looked so fine and lovely in her rich clothes, and it never crossed their minds that it might be Ashputtel, whom they took to be safe at home in the dirt.

The king’s son came over to her at once, took her by the hand and danced with her, and with nobody else. He never let go of her hand, and whenever someone else came to ask her for a dance, he said, “This lady is dancing with me.”

They danced until late in the night. Then she wanted to go home, and the king’s son said, “I’ll go with you and see you safely there,” because he wanted to find out where the beautiful maiden lived. But she slipped away from him before he knew it and ran toward home. The prince followed, and she jumped up into the pigeon-house and shut the door behind her. He waited until her father came home and told him that the unknown maiden from the feast had hidden in the pigeon-house. They broke the door open and found nobody inside. When they came back into the house, there was Ashputtel lying in her dirty dress by the ashes, as she always did, with her dim little lamp burning in the chimney. She had run as fast as she could through the pigeon-house and on to the hazel-tree, where she had taken off her beautiful clothes and laid them under the tree for the bird to carry away, and then she had lain down again in the ashes in her little gray dress.
The next day, when the feast was held again and her father, stepmother and sisters had gone, Ashputtel went to the hazel-tree and said:

“Shake, shake, hazel-tree,
Gold and silver over me!”

The bird came and brought her a dress even finer than the one she had worn the day before. When she arrived in it at the ball, everyone marveled at her beauty. The king’s son had been waiting for her. He took her by the hand and danced with her, and when anyone asked her to dance, he said as before, “This lady is dancing with me.”

When night came she wanted to go home, and the king’s son followed her as before, to see which house she went into. But she bolted away from him all at once, into the garden behind her father’s house. In that garden stood a big, fine pear-tree heavy with ripe fruit. Ashputtel had nowhere else to hide, so she climbed up into it without being seen. The king’s son lost sight of her and could not find out where she had gone. He waited until her father came home and said to him, “The unknown lady who danced with me has slipped away, and I think she must have leapt into the pear-tree.” The father thought to himself, “Could it be Ashputtel?” He had an axe brought, and they cut the tree down, but there was no one in it. When they went back into the kitchen, there lay Ashputtel among the ashes. She had slid down the far side of the tree, carried her beautiful clothes back to the bird at the hazel-tree, and put on her little gray dress.
On the third day, when her father, stepmother and sisters had gone, she went into the garden again and said:

“Shake, shake, hazel-tree,
Gold and silver over me!”

Her kind friend the bird brought a dress finer than either of the others, and slippers made entirely of gold. When she came to the feast, nobody knew what to say, they were so amazed at her beauty. The king’s son danced with no one but her, and when anyone else asked her to dance, he said, “This lady is _my_ partner, sir.”

When night came she wanted to go home, and the king’s son said to himself, “I won’t lose her this time,” and meant to go with her. But once again she slipped away from him, and in such a hurry that she lost her left golden slipper on the stairs.

The next day the prince took the shoe to the king his father and said, “I will marry the lady whom this golden slipper fits.” Both sisters were delighted to hear it, because they had lovely feet and had no doubt they could wear the slipper. The elder went first into the room where the slipper lay, and tried to put it on, with her mother standing by. But her big toe would not go in, and the shoe was far too small for her. Then her mother handed her a knife and said, “Never mind, cut it off. Once you’re queen you won’t care about toes, because you’ll never need to walk.” The foolish girl cut off her big toe, squeezed her foot into the shoe, and went out to the king’s son. He accepted her as his bride, sat her beside him on his horse, and rode off with her toward home.
On the way they had to pass the hazel-tree that Ashputtel had planted, and on a branch sat a little dove, singing:

“Turn around! Turn around! Look at the shoe!
The shoe is too small, it was not made for you!
Prince, prince, go look again for your bride,
This is not the true one sitting at your side.”

The prince got down and looked at her foot, and by the blood streaming from it he saw the trick she had played on him. He turned his horse around, took the false bride back to her home and said, “This is not the right bride. Let the other sister try the slipper.” So the second sister went into the room and got her foot into the shoe, all but the heel, which was too big. Her mother squeezed it in until the blood came and took her out to the king’s son. He seated her beside him on his horse as his bride and rode away with her.
When they reached the hazel-tree, the little dove was still sitting there, and it sang:

“Turn around! Turn around! Look at the shoe!
The shoe is too small, it was not made for you!
Prince, prince, go look again for your bride,
This is not the true one sitting at your side.”

He looked down and saw that so much blood was pouring from the shoe that her white stockings had turned completely red. He turned his horse around and brought her back too. “This is not the true bride,” he said to the father. “Don’t you have another daughter?” “No,” said the father. “There is only a dirty little Ashputtel, the child of my first wife, and she can’t possibly be the bride.” The prince told him to send for her anyway. But the mother said, “No, no, she is much too dirty. She wouldn’t dare show herself.” The prince insisted, though, so Ashputtel washed her face and hands, went in and curtsied to him, and he held out the golden slipper. She took her clumsy shoe off her left foot and put on the golden slipper, and it fitted as if it had been made for her. When he came closer and looked at her face, he knew her and said, “This is the right bride.” The stepmother and both sisters were horrified and went pale with rage as he lifted Ashputtel onto his horse and rode away with her. When they came to the hazel-tree, the white dove sang:

“Home, home! Look at the shoe!
Princess, the shoe was made for you!
Prince, prince, take home your bride,
For she is the true one sitting at your side!”
When the dove had finished its song, it flew down and settled on her right shoulder, and so it went home with her.

chapters.title: The White Snake
paragraphs: Long ago there lived a king whose wisdom was famous throughout the land. Nothing was hidden from him, and it seemed that news of even the most secret matters was carried to him through the air. But he had a strange habit. Every day after dinner, when the table had been cleared and nobody else was there, a trusted servant had to bring him one more dish. It was covered, though, and the servant did not know what was in it, and neither did anyone else, since the king never lifted the cover and ate from the dish until he was completely alone.

This had gone on for a long time, when one day the servant who took the dish away was seized by such curiosity that he could not help carrying it to his own room. He locked the door carefully, lifted the cover, and saw a white snake lying on the dish. At the sight of it he could not resist tasting it, so he cut off a little piece and put it in his mouth. The moment it touched his tongue, he heard a strange whispering of tiny voices outside his window. He went and listened, and realized that it was the sparrows chattering, telling each other all the things they had seen in the fields and woods. Eating the snake had given him the power to understand the language of animals.

Now it happened that on that very day the queen lost her most beautiful ring, and suspicion fell on this trusted servant, who was allowed to go everywhere. The king had the man brought before him and angrily threatened that if he could not name the thief by the next morning, he himself would be held guilty and executed. The servant protested his innocence in vain, and was sent away with no better answer.

Worried and afraid, he went down into the courtyard and tried to think of a way out. Some ducks were sitting quietly together beside a brook, resting, and as they smoothed their feathers with their bills they were having a cozy chat. The servant stood nearby and listened. They were telling one another about all the places they had been waddling around that morning and the good food they had found. Then one of them said in a miserable voice, “Something sits heavy in my stomach. I was eating in such a hurry that I swallowed a ring that was lying under the queen’s window.” The servant grabbed her by the neck at once, carried her to the kitchen and said to the cook, “Here’s a fine duck. Please kill her.” “Yes,” said the cook, weighing her in his hand. “She has certainly gone to plenty of trouble to fatten herself up, and she’s been waiting to be roasted long enough.” He cut off her head, and as she was being prepared for the spit, the queen’s ring was found inside her.

Now the servant could easily prove his innocence. To make up for the wrong, the king allowed him to ask a favor and promised him the best position at court he could wish for. The servant turned down everything. He asked only for a horse and some money for traveling, because he wanted to see the world and wander about a little. When his request was granted, he set out, and one day he came to a pond where he saw three fish caught in the reeds, gasping for water. People say fish are dumb, yet he heard them lamenting that they would die such a wretched death. Since he had a kind heart, he got down from his horse and put the three prisoners back into the water. They leapt for joy, stuck their heads out, and cried to him, “We’ll remember you, and we’ll repay you for saving us!”

He rode on, and before long he thought he heard a small voice coming from the sand beneath him. He stopped to listen, and it was an ant-king complaining: “Why can’t people keep their clumsy animals off us? That stupid horse with his heavy hooves has been trampling my people without any mercy!” So the young man steered onto a side path, and the ant-king called after him: “We will remember you—one good turn deserves another!”

The path took him into a forest, where he saw two old ravens standing at their nest, shoving their young out of it. “Get out, you lazy good-for-nothings!” they screamed. “We can’t feed you anymore. You’re big enough to look after yourselves.” But the poor young ravens just lay on the ground, beating their wings and wailing: “Oh, what helpless chicks we are! We’re supposed to fend for ourselves, and we can’t even fly! What can we do except lie here and starve?” So the kind young man got down, killed his horse with his sword, and gave it to them to eat. They came hopping over, ate until they were full, and cried: “We will remember you—one good turn deserves another!”

Now he had to go on foot, and after walking a long way he reached a big city. The streets were crowded and noisy, and a man came riding up on a horse, shouting: “The king’s daughter wants a husband! But anyone who asks for her hand must complete a hard task, and if he fails, he will lose his life.” Many had tried already, and all in vain. Still, when the young man caught sight of the king’s daughter, her beauty overwhelmed him so completely that he forgot every danger, went to the king, and announced that he wished to court her.

He was taken out to the sea, and while he watched, a gold ring was thrown into the water. Then the king commanded him to bring the ring up from the sea floor, and added: “If you come back up without it, you will be thrown in again and again until you die in the waves.” Everyone felt sorry for the handsome young man. Then they all left, and he was alone by the sea.

He stood on the shore, wondering what to do, when all at once three fishes came swimming toward him. They were the very fishes whose lives he had saved. The one in the middle carried a mussel in its mouth and set it down on the shore at his feet. When he picked it up and opened it, the gold ring was lying inside the shell. Overjoyed, he carried it to the king, expecting to receive the reward he had been promised.

But the proud princess realized he was not her equal by birth. She looked down on him and demanded that he first complete another task. She went down into the garden and, with her own hands, scattered ten sacks of millet seed across the grass. Then she said: “Tomorrow morning, before sunrise, every one of these seeds must be picked up. Not a single grain may be missing.”

The young man sat down in the garden and tried to think how such a thing could be done. Nothing came to him, so he just sat there in misery, waiting for daybreak, when he would be led away to die. But as soon as the first rays of sun fell on the garden, he saw all ten sacks standing in a row, completely full, with not one grain missing. The ant-king had come during the night with thousands upon thousands of ants, and the grateful creatures had worked hard to gather all the millet seed and fill the sacks.

Soon the king’s daughter came down into the garden herself, and she was astonished to find that the young man had done what she asked. But her proud heart still would not give way. She said: “Even though he has passed both tasks, he will not be my husband until he brings me an apple from the Tree of Life.” The young man had no idea where the Tree of Life stood. Even so, he set off, ready to walk for as long as his legs would carry him, though he had no hope of finding it. He wandered through three kingdoms, and one evening he came to a forest and lay down under a tree to sleep. Then he heard a rustling in the branches, and a golden apple dropped into his hand. At the same moment three ravens flew down, settled on his knee, and said: “We are the three young ravens you saved from starving. When we had grown big and heard that you were looking for the Golden Apple, we flew across the sea to the end of the world, where the Tree of Life stands, and fetched the apple for you.” Overjoyed, the young man started for home and brought the Golden Apple to the king’s beautiful daughter, who now had no excuses left. They cut the Apple of Life in two and ate it together. Then her heart filled with love for him, and they lived in untroubled happiness until a great old age.

chapters.title: The Wolf and the Seven Little Kids
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was an old goat who had seven little kids, and she loved them as only a mother can. One day she needed to go into the forest to get food. She called all seven to her and said: “Dear children, I have to go into the forest. Watch out for the wolf. If he gets in, he will eat you all up—skin, hair and everything. The wretch often disguises himself, but you will know him at once by his rough voice and his black feet.” The kids answered: “Dear mother, we will take good care of ourselves. You can go without worrying.” So the old goat bleated and set off with an easy mind.

Before long, someone knocked at the door and called: “Open up, dear children! Your mother is here, and she has brought something for each of you.” But the little kids could tell by the rough voice that it was the wolf. “We won’t open the door,” they cried. “You are not our mother. She has a soft, sweet voice, and yours is rough. You are the wolf!” So the wolf went off to a shopkeeper and bought a big lump of chalk. He ate it, and it made his voice soft. Then he came back, knocked on the door, and called: “Open up, dear children, your mother is here and has brought something for each of you.” But the wolf had rested his black paws against the window, and the children saw them and cried: “We won’t open the door! Our mother doesn’t have black feet like yours. You are the wolf!” Next the wolf ran to a baker and said: “I’ve hurt my feet. Rub some dough over them for me.” When the baker had covered his feet with dough, the wolf ran to the miller and said: “Sprinkle some white flour on my feet for me.” The miller thought, “The wolf is planning to trick somebody,” and said no. But the wolf said: “If you don’t do it, I’ll eat you.” The miller got frightened and whitened his paws for him. That is just how people are.

So the wretch went to the door a third time, knocked, and said: “Open the door for me, children! Your dear little mother is home, and she has brought each of you something from the forest.” The little kids cried: “First show us your paws, so we can tell whether you are our dear little mother.” He pushed his paws in through the window, and when the kids saw that they were white, they believed everything he said and opened the door. And who walked in but the wolf! They were terrified and tried to hide. One jumped under the table, the second into the bed, the third into the stove, the fourth into the kitchen, the fifth into the cupboard, the sixth under the washbowl, and the seventh into the clock case. But the wolf found every one of them, and he did not stand on ceremony: one after another, he gulped them down his throat. Only the youngest, hiding in the clock case, he did not find. When the wolf had eaten his fill, he wandered off, lay down under a tree in the green meadow outside, and went to sleep. Soon afterward the old goat came back from the forest. Oh, what a sight she saw! The front door stood wide open. The table, chairs and benches were knocked over, the washbowl lay smashed to pieces, and the quilts and pillows had been dragged off the bed. She looked for her children, but they were nowhere. She called them by name, one after another, but nobody answered. At last, when she came to the youngest, a soft voice cried: “Dear mother, I’m in the clock case.” She lifted the kid out, and it told her that the wolf had come and eaten all the others. You can imagine how she wept over her poor children.

At last, in her grief, she went outside, and the youngest kid ran along with her. In the meadow they found the wolf lying by the tree, snoring so loudly that the branches shook. She looked him over from every side and saw that something was moving and struggling inside his bloated belly. “Oh, heavens,” she said, “could it be that my poor children, whom he swallowed for his supper, are still alive?” So the kid had to run home and fetch scissors, a needle and thread. The goat cut open the monster’s stomach, and she had hardly made the first cut when one little kid poked out its head. As she cut further, all six jumped out one after another. Every one was still alive and not hurt at all, because the monster had been so greedy that he had swallowed them whole. What joy there was! They hugged their dear mother and leaped about like a tailor at his wedding. But the mother said: “Now go and find some big stones, and we will fill the wicked beast’s belly with them while he is still asleep.” The seven kids dragged the stones over as fast as they could and stuffed as many into his belly as it would hold. Then the mother sewed him up again in a great hurry, so that he never noticed anything and never even stirred.

When the wolf had finally slept enough, he got to his feet. The stones in his belly had made him very thirsty, so he wanted to go to a well and drink. But as soon as he began to walk and move around, the stones in his belly knocked together and rattled. Then he cried:

“What’s rumbling and tumbling
Against my poor bones?
I thought it was six kids,
But it feels like big stones.”

And when he reached the well and bent over the water to drink, the heavy stones pulled him in, and he drowned miserably. When the seven kids saw it, they came running and shouted: “The wolf is dead! The wolf is dead!” And they danced for joy around the well with their mother.

chapters.title: The Queen Bee
paragraphs: Two kings’ sons once went out into the world to seek their fortunes, but they soon fell into a wasteful and foolish way of life and could not go home again. Then their brother, a small, unimportant dwarf, set out to look for them. When he found them, they only laughed at him. How could he, so young and simple, hope to get through the world, when they, who were so much cleverer, had not managed it? Still, the three of them traveled on together and eventually came to an anthill. The two elder brothers wanted to tear it down, just to watch the poor ants run around in terror, carrying off their eggs. But the little dwarf said: “Leave the poor creatures in peace. I won’t let you disturb them.”

They went on and came to a lake where lots of ducks were swimming. The two brothers wanted to catch a couple and roast them. But the dwarf said: “Leave the poor creatures in peace. You will not kill them.” Next they found a bees’ nest in a hollow tree, with so much honey that it ran down the trunk. The two brothers wanted to light a fire under the tree and kill the bees to get at the honey. But the dwarf held them back and said: “Leave the pretty insects in peace. I can’t let you burn them.”

At last the three brothers came to a castle. As they passed the stables, they saw fine horses standing there, but all of them were made of marble, and there was no one in sight. They walked through all the rooms until they reached a door with three locks. In the middle of the door was a small hatch, through which they could see into the next room. Inside, a little gray old man sat at a table. They called to him once or twice, but he did not hear. They called a third time, and then he got up and came out to them.
He said nothing. He took hold of them and led them to a lovely table loaded with all kinds of good food. When they had eaten and drunk, he showed each of them to a bedroom.

The next morning he came to the eldest brother and took him to a marble table, where three tablets lay, telling how the castle could be freed from its enchantment. The first tablet said: “In the forest, under the moss, lie the thousand pearls that belong to the king’s daughter. All of them must be found, and if even one is missing by sunset, whoever is searching will be turned to marble.”
The eldest brother went out and searched for the pearls all day long. But evening came, and he had not even found the first hundred. So he was turned to stone, just as the tablet had said.
The next day the second brother took up the task, but he did no better than the first. He found only the second hundred of the pearls, and so he too was turned to stone.

At last it was the little dwarf’s turn. He searched in the moss, but the pearls were so hard to find and the work was so tedious!—so he sat down on a stone and cried. And while he sat there, the king of the ants, whose life he had saved, came to help him with five thousand ants. It was not long before they had found all the pearls and piled them up in a heap.

The second tablet said: “The key to the princess’s bedroom must be fished out of the lake.” When the dwarf reached the edge of the water, he saw the two ducks whose lives he had saved paddling about. They dived down and soon brought up the key from the bottom.

The third task was the hardest of all: he had to choose the youngest and best of the king’s three daughters. All three were beautiful, and they looked exactly alike. The only clue he was given was that the eldest had eaten a piece of sugar, the second some sweet syrup, and the youngest a spoonful of honey. He had to work out which one had eaten the honey.

Then the queen of the bees arrived, whom the little dwarf had saved from the fire. She tested the lips of all three sisters, and in the end she settled on the lips of the one who had eaten the honey. That was how the dwarf knew which was the youngest. So the spell was broken, and everyone who had been turned to stone woke up and took their own shapes again. The dwarf married the youngest and best of the princesses, and after her father died he became king. His two brothers married the other two sisters.

chapters.title: The Elves and the Shoemaker
paragraphs: Once there was a shoemaker who worked hard and was perfectly honest, and still he could not earn enough to live on. Bit by bit everything he owned was gone, until all he had left was enough leather for a single pair of shoes.

That evening he cut the leather out and left it ready to sew the next day, planning to get up early and start work. His conscience was clear and his heart was light despite all his troubles, so he went calmly to bed, left his worries in God’s hands, and was soon asleep. In the morning, after saying his prayers, he sat down to work, and to his great astonishment the shoes were already made, standing on the table. The good man did not know what to say or think about such a strange thing. He examined the workmanship. There was not a single bad stitch anywhere, and it was all so neat and exact that it was a true masterpiece.

That same day a customer came in. The shoes fitted him so well that he gladly paid more than the usual price, and with the money the poor shoemaker bought enough leather for two more pairs. In the evening he cut them out and went to bed early so that he could rise in good time and begin the next day. He needn’t have bothered, because when he got up the work was already finished. Soon buyers came in and paid him generously, and he bought leather for four more pairs. Again he cut it out at night and found it finished in the morning, and so it went on for some time. Whatever he had cut out in the evening was always done by daybreak, and before long the good man was prospering and comfortable again.

One evening near Christmas, when he and his wife were sitting by the fire talking, he said to her, “I’d like to stay up tonight and watch, so we can see who comes and does my work for me.” His wife liked the idea. They left a light burning, hid in a corner of the room behind a curtain that hung there, and waited to see what would happen.

At the stroke of midnight two little naked dwarfs came in. They sat down at the shoemaker’s bench, picked up all the leather that had been cut out, and set to work with their small fingers, stitching and rapping and tapping so fast that the shoemaker was amazed and could not take his eyes off them. They kept at it until the job was completely finished and the shoes were standing ready on the table. This was long before daybreak, and then they hurried off, quick as lightning.

The next day the wife said to the shoemaker, “These little creatures have made us rich, and we should be grateful to them and do them a kindness if we can. It troubles me to see them running about like that, and it isn’t decent either, since they have nothing on their backs to keep out the cold. I’ll tell you what: I will make each of them a shirt, a coat and a waistcoat, and a pair of trousers as well, and you make each of them a little pair of shoes.”

The shoemaker liked the idea very much. One evening, when everything was ready, they laid the clothes out on the table in place of the cut leather, then hid themselves to see what the little elves would do.

Around midnight they came in, dancing and skipping, and hopped around the room. Then they went to sit down to their work as usual, but when they saw the clothes lying there for them, they laughed and chuckled and seemed tremendously pleased.
In the blink of an eye they were dressed, and they danced and capered and leaped about, as merry as could be, until at last they danced out of the door and away across the green.
The good couple never saw them again, but from then on everything went well for them for the rest of their lives.

chapters.title: The Juniper-Tree
paragraphs: A long, long time ago, some two thousand years or so, there lived a rich man who had a good and beautiful wife. They loved each other dearly, but it grieved them deeply that they had no children. They wanted one so badly that the wife prayed for a child day and night, and still they stayed childless.

In front of the house was a yard with a juniper tree growing in it. One winter day the wife was standing under the tree peeling apples, and as she peeled them she cut her finger, and the blood dropped onto the snow. “Ah,” the woman sighed heavily, “if only I had a child as red as blood and as white as snow!” As she said it, her heart grew light, and it felt to her as if her wish had been granted. She went back into the house glad and comforted. A month passed and the snow melted away, then another month went by and all the earth turned green. So the months followed one after another: first the trees budded in the woods, and soon the green branches grew thick and tangled, and then the blossoms began to fall. Once more the wife stood under the juniper tree, and it smelled so sweet that her heart leaped for joy, and she was so overcome with happiness that she fell to her knees. After a while the berries grew round and firm, and she was glad and at peace. But when they were fully ripe she picked them and ate them greedily, and then she became sad and sick. A little later she called her husband and said to him, in tears, “If I die, bury me under the juniper tree.” Then she felt comforted and happy again, and before another month was out she had a baby, and when she saw that it was as white as snow and as red as blood, she was so overjoyed that she died.

Her husband buried her under the juniper tree and wept bitterly for her. Little by little his sorrow eased, and although he still grieved now and then, he could carry on with his life as before. Later on he married again.

With his new wife he had a little daughter. The child of his first wife was a boy, and he was as red as blood and as white as snow. The mother loved her daughter dearly, and whenever she looked at her and then at the boy, it cut her to the heart to think that he would always stand in her own child’s way. She was forever scheming how to get the whole inheritance for her daughter. This wicked thought took hold of her more and more, and she began to treat the boy very cruelly. She chased him from one place to another with slaps and blows, so that the poor child went about in fear and had no peace from the moment he left school until the moment he went back.

One day the little girl ran to her mother in the storeroom. “Mother, give me an apple,” she said. “Of course, my child,” said the woman, and took a lovely apple from the chest, which had a very heavy lid and a big iron lock.
“Mother,” said the little daughter again, “can’t brother have one too?” The mother was angry at this, but she answered, “Yes, when he comes home from school.”

Just then she glanced out of the window and saw him coming, and it was as though an evil spirit got into her. She snatched the apple out of her little daughter’s hand and said, “You won’t have one before your brother.” She threw the apple into the chest and shut the lid. Then the little boy came in, and the evil spirit in the woman made her say sweetly to him, “My son, would you like an apple?” But she gave him a wicked look. “Mother,” said the boy, “you look dreadful! Yes, give me an apple.” The thought came to her that she would kill him. “Come with me,” she said, and she lifted the lid of the chest. “Take one out for yourself.” And as he bent over to do it, the evil spirit drove her on, and bang! The lid came down, and the little boy’s head flew off. Then she was overcome with terror at what she had done. “If only I can keep anyone from finding out that I did it,” she thought. So she went upstairs to her room and took a white handkerchief out of her top drawer. She set the boy’s head back on his shoulders and tied the handkerchief around it so that nothing could be seen, and she sat him on a chair by the door with an apple in his hand.

Soon afterward little Marleen came to her mother, who was standing at the fire stirring a pot of boiling water, and said, “Mother, brother is sitting by the door with an apple in his hand, and he looks so pale. I asked him to give me the apple, and he didn’t answer, and that frightened me.”

“Go to him again,” said her mother, “and if he doesn’t answer, box his ear.” So little Marleen went and said, “Brother, give me that apple,” but he didn’t say a word. Then she boxed his ear, and his head rolled off. She was so horrified that she ran to her mother, crying and screaming. “Oh!” she said, “I’ve knocked off brother’s head!” And she wept and wept, and nothing could make her stop.

“What have you done!” said her mother. “But nobody must know about this, so you must keep quiet. What’s done can’t be undone. We’ll make him into puddings.” And she took the little boy, cut him up, made him into puddings, and put him in the pot. Marleen stood by watching, and wept and wept, and her tears fell into the pot, so that it needed no salt.
Soon the father came home and sat down to his dinner. He asked, “Where is my son?” The mother said nothing, but gave him a big dish of black pudding, and Marleen went on weeping without a pause.
The father asked again, “Where is my son?”
“Oh,” answered the wife, “he has gone off to the country to visit his mother’s great-uncle. He’s going to stay there a while.”
“Why has he gone there? And he never even said goodbye to me!”
“Well, he likes it there. He told me he would be away a good six weeks, and he’s well looked after.”
“It makes me very uneasy,” said the husband, “in case something is wrong, and he should have said goodbye to me.”

He carried on with his meal. “Little Marleen, why are you crying?” he said. “Brother will be home before long.” Then he asked his wife for another helping of pudding, and while he ate he tossed the bones under the table.

Little Marleen went upstairs and took her best silk handkerchief out of her bottom drawer. She wrapped all the bones from under the table in it and carried them outside, weeping the whole time. Then she laid them in the green grass under the juniper tree, and no sooner had she done so than all her sadness seemed to leave her, and she stopped crying. And now the juniper tree began to stir. Its branches swayed back and forth, first apart from one another and then together again, as if someone were clapping their hands for joy. After that a mist gathered around the tree, and in the middle of it something burned like fire, and out of the fire flew a beautiful bird. It rose high into the air, singing gloriously, and when it could no longer be seen, the juniper tree stood there as before, and the silk handkerchief and the bones were gone.
Little Marleen now felt as light-hearted and happy as if her brother were still alive. She went back into the house, sat down cheerfully at the table, and ate.
The bird flew off and landed on a goldsmith’s house, and began to sing:

Inside his workshop the goldsmith was busy making a gold chain when he heard the bird’s song from his roof. It sounded so lovely to him that he sprang up and rushed out, and lost a slipper as he crossed the doorstep. He ran on regardless to the middle of the street, wearing one slipper and one sock. His apron was still tied on, and in his hands he still held the gold chain and the pincers. There he stood, staring up at the bird, as the sun beamed down on the street.
“Bird,” he said, “how beautifully you sing! Sing that song for me again.”
“No,” said the bird, “I don’t sing twice for nothing. Give me that gold chain, and I will sing it for you again.”
“Here is the chain, take it,” said the goldsmith. “Only sing that song for me again.”
The bird flew down and took the gold chain in its right claw. Then it landed again in front of the goldsmith and sang:
From there it flew off to perch on a shoemaker’s roof, and it sang:
The shoemaker heard it, jumped up, and ran out in his shirtsleeves. He stood looking up at the bird on the roof, with his hand over his eyes so the sun would not blind him.

“Bird,” he said, “what a beautiful voice you have!” Then he shouted through the door to his wife, “Wife, come out! There’s a bird out here. Come and see it, and listen to how sweetly it sings.” Next he called for his daughter and the children, and then the apprentices, girls and boys, and they all hurried up the street to see the bird. They saw how magnificent it was, with red and green feathers, a neck like burnished gold, and two bright stars for eyes.
“Bird,” said the shoemaker, “sing that song for me again.”
“No,” answered the bird, “I don’t sing twice for nothing. You must give me something.”
“Wife,” said the man, “go up to the attic. On the top shelf you’ll see a pair of red shoes. Bring them to me.” The wife went in and fetched the shoes.
“There, bird,” said the shoemaker, “now sing that song for me again.”
The bird swooped down and caught the red shoes in his left claw. Then he flew back up to the roof and sang:

Then he flew off. With the chain hanging from his right claw and the shoes from his left, he headed straight for a mill, and the mill was going ‘Click clack, click clack, click clack.’ Inside the mill, twenty of the miller’s men were chopping at a stone, and as they went ‘Hick hack, hick hack, hick hack,’ the mill went ‘Click clack, click clack, click clack.’
The bird landed in a lime-tree outside the mill and sang:
“My mother killed her little boy;
and one of the men stopped working,
My father mourned when I was gone;
and two more stopped and listened,
My sister loved me most of all;
and then four more put down their tools,

She spread her kerchief over me,
And gathered up my bones to lie
and now only eight were still working,
Beneath
and now just five,
the juniper-tree.
and now just one,
Kywitt, Kywitt, what a fine bird am I!’
and when he glanced up, the last man had stopped working too.
“Bird,” he said, “that is a lovely song you sing! Let me hear it as well. Sing it again.”
“No,” the bird answered, “I never sing twice for nothing. Give me that millstone and I will sing it again.”
“If it were mine alone,” said the man, “you could have it.”
“Yes, yes,” said the others, “if he sings it again, he can have it.”

The bird flew down, and all twenty millers got to work and heaved the stone up on a beam. The bird pushed his head through the hole, wore the stone around his neck like a collar, flew back to the tree with it, and sang—
When the song was over, he spread his wings and flew straight to his father’s house, with the chain in his right claw, the shoes in his left, and the millstone around his neck.
The father, the mother and little Marleen were sitting at dinner.
“I feel so light-hearted,” said the father, “so happy and cheerful.”
“Not me,” said the mother. “I feel so uneasy, as though a terrible thunderstorm were on its way.”
Little Marleen, meanwhile, just sat there weeping and weeping.
At that moment the bird came flying toward the house and perched on the roof.
“I feel so happy,” said the father, “and the sun is shining so beautifully. It’s as if I were about to meet an old friend again.”

“Oh!” said his wife. “I am so full of fear and unease that my teeth are chattering, and it feels as though there were fire in my veins.” And she tore open her dress. All the while little Marleen sat in the corner crying, and the plate on her lap was wet with her tears.
The bird now flew to the juniper-tree and began to sing:
“My mother killed her little boy;
The mother shut her eyes and covered her ears so that she would see and hear nothing, but a roar filled her ears like a raging storm, and her eyes burned and flashed like lightning:
My father mourned when I was gone;
“Look, wife,” said the man, “at that beautiful bird singing so gloriously! And how warm and bright the sun is, and what a lovely smell of spices in the air!”
My sister loved me most of all;
Then little Marleen dropped her head onto her knees and sobbed.
“I have to go outside and see that bird up close,” said the man.
“Oh, don’t go!” cried the wife. “I feel as if the whole house were on fire!”
But the man went out and looked at the bird.

She spread her kerchief over me,
And gathered up my bones to lie
Beneath the juniper-tree
Kywitt, Kywitt, what a fine bird am I!’
At that, the bird dropped the gold chain, and it landed right around the man’s neck, fitting him perfectly.
He went back inside and said, ‘Look what a splendid bird that is! He has given me this lovely gold chain, and he is so handsome himself.’
But the wife was so frightened and distressed that she collapsed on the floor, and her cap fell off her head.
Then the bird started singing again:
“My mother killed her little boy;
“Oh, dear!” cried the wife. “If only I were a thousand feet under the earth, so that I could not hear that song.”
My father mourned when I was gone;
and the woman fell down again as if she were dead.
My sister loved me most of all;
“Well,” said little Marleen, “I’ll go outside too and see if the bird will give me something.”
So she went out.

She spread her kerchief over me,
And gathered up my bones to lie
and he threw the shoes down to her,

Beneath the juniper-tree
Kywitt, Kywitt, what a fine bird am I!’

Suddenly she felt completely happy and light-hearted. She put on the shoes and danced and skipped about in them. ‘I was so miserable when I came out,’ she said, ‘but it has all gone away. What a splendid bird, and he has given me a pair of red shoes!’
The wife leapt up, her hair standing on end like tongues of flame. ‘Then I will go out too,’ she said, ‘and see if it eases my misery, for I feel as though the world were ending.’
But as she stepped over the threshold—crash!—the bird dropped the millstone on her head, and she was crushed to death.

The father and little Marleen heard the crash and ran outside. But all they saw was mist and flame and fire rising from the spot, and when it cleared, their little brother was standing there. He took the father and little Marleen by the hand, and the three of them rejoiced, went back inside together, sat down to dinner and ate.

chapters.title: The Turnip
paragraphs: Two brothers were both soldiers, one rich and one poor. The poor one decided to try to improve his lot, so he took off his red coat, became a gardener, dug his plot thoroughly, and planted turnips.

When the seeds sprouted, one plant grew bigger than all the others. It kept on growing and growing and seemed as though it would never stop, so that it could have been called the prince of turnips, since there had never been one like it before and never would be again. In the end it was so big that it filled a whole cart, and two oxen could barely pull it. The gardener had no idea what to do with it, or whether it would turn out to be a blessing or a curse for him. One day he said to himself, ‘What am I going to do with it? If I sell it, it will fetch no more than any other turnip, and for eating, the small ones are better. Perhaps the best thing is to take it to the king as a token of respect.’

So he yoked his oxen, hauled the turnip to the court, and presented it to the king. ‘What an amazing thing!’ said the king. ‘I have seen many strange things, but never a monster like this. Where did you get the seed? Or is it just your good luck? If so, you are a true child of fortune.’ ‘Oh, no,’ answered the gardener, ‘I am no child of fortune. I am a poor soldier who could never get enough to live on, so I put away my red coat and went to work on the land. I have a brother who is rich. Your majesty knows him well, and so does everyone else. But because I am poor, everybody forgets me.’

The king felt sorry for him and said, ‘You shall be poor no longer. I will give you so much that you will be even richer than your brother.’ Then he gave him gold, land and livestock, and made him so wealthy that his brother’s fortune could not begin to compare with his.

When the brother heard about all this, and how a turnip had made the gardener rich, he was bitterly jealous and began to think how he could win the same good fortune for himself. He decided, though, to go about it more cleverly than his brother. He collected a rich present of gold and fine horses for the king, and expected to receive a much bigger gift in return. After all, if his brother had been given so much for just a turnip, what would his own present be worth?

The king accepted the gift graciously and said he had nothing more valuable and wonderful to give in return than the great turnip. So the soldier had to load it onto a cart and drag it home. When he got there, he did not know whom to take his rage and spite out on, until finally wicked thoughts came into his head, and he decided to kill his brother.

He hired some villains to murder him, showed them where to hide in ambush, and then went to his brother and said, ‘Dear brother, I have found a hidden treasure. Let’s go and dig it up and split it between us.’ The other suspected no treachery, so they set off together. As they were walking along, the murderers leapt out at him, tied him up, and were about to hang him from a tree.

But while they were making everything ready, they heard a horse trampling in the distance, which scared them so much that they shoved their prisoner into a sack, head and shoulders together, hoisted him up to the tree with a cord, left him dangling there, and ran off. Meanwhile he worked and worked away at the sack until he had made a hole big enough to stick his head out.

The rider turned out to be a student, a cheerful fellow, traveling along on his horse and singing as he went. As soon as the man in the sack saw him passing under the tree, he called out, ‘Good morning! Good morning to you, my friend!’ The student looked all around, and seeing no one, and not knowing where the voice was coming from, called back, ‘Who is calling me?’

Then the man in the tree answered, ‘Raise your eyes, for here I sit in the sack of wisdom. In a short time I have learned great and wonderful things here. Compared with this seat, all the learning of the schools is empty air. A little longer, and I shall know everything a man can know, and I shall come out wiser than the wisest of mankind. Here I can read the signs and movements of the heavens and the stars, the laws that rule the winds, the number of the grains of sand on the seashore, the healing of the sick, and the powers of all herbs, birds and precious stones. If you were here for just a moment, my friend, you would feel and admit the power of knowledge.’

The student listened to all this in amazement. At last he said, ‘Blessed be the day and hour when I found you! Can’t you find a way to let me into the sack for a little while?’ The other answered, as though very reluctant, ‘I might let you sit here for a short time, if you reward me well and treat me kindly. But you must wait an hour down there, until I have learned a few small things that I still don’t know.’

So the student sat down and waited a while, but the time dragged, and he begged earnestly to go up at once, for his thirst for knowledge was great. Then the other pretended to give in and said, ‘You must let the sack of wisdom down by untying that cord over there, and then you may get in.’ So the student let him down, opened the sack, and set him free. ‘Now then,’ he cried, ‘let me up quickly!’ As he began to climb into the sack feet first, ‘Wait a moment,’ said the gardener, ‘that is not the way.’ Then he pushed him in head first, tied up the sack, and soon had the seeker after wisdom swinging in the air. ‘How are you, friend?’ he said. ‘Don’t you feel wisdom coming to you? Rest there in peace until you are wiser than you were.’
With that, he rode off on the student’s horse and left the poor fellow to gather wisdom until somebody came along and let him down.

chapters.title: Clever Hans
paragraphs: Hans’s mother said, ‘Where are you off to, Hans?’ Hans answered, ‘To Gretel’s.’ ‘Behave yourself, Hans.’ ‘Oh, I’ll behave. Goodbye, Mother.’ ‘Goodbye, Hans.’ Hans arrives at Gretel’s. ‘Good day, Gretel.’ ‘Good day, Hans. What have you brought that’s good?’ ‘I’ve brought nothing. I want to be given something.’ Gretel gives Hans a needle. Hans says, ‘Goodbye, Gretel.’ ‘Goodbye, Hans.’

Hans picks up the needle, pokes it into a hay-cart, and trails the cart home. ‘Good evening, Mother.’ ‘Good evening, Hans. Where have you been?’ ‘At Gretel’s.’ ‘What did you take her?’ ‘Took nothing; was given something.’ ‘What did Gretel give you?’ ‘Gave me a needle.’ ‘Where is the needle, Hans?’ ‘Stuck it in the hay-cart.’ ‘That was badly done, Hans. You should have stuck the needle in your sleeve.’ ‘Never mind, I’ll do better next time.’

“Where are you off to, Hans?” “To Gretel’s, Mother.” “Behave yourself, Hans.” “Oh, I’ll behave. Goodbye, Mother.” “Goodbye, Hans.” Hans arrives at Gretel’s. “Good day, Gretel.” “Good day, Hans. What have you brought that’s good?” “I’ve brought nothing. I want to be given something.” Gretel gives Hans a knife. “Goodbye, Gretel.” “Goodbye, Hans.” Hans takes the knife, sticks it in his sleeve, and goes home. “Good evening, Mother.” “Good evening, Hans. Where have you been?” “At Gretel’s.” “What did you take her?” “Took her nothing; she gave me something.” “What did Gretel give you?” “Gave me a knife.” “Where is the knife, Hans?” “Stuck in my sleeve.” “That was badly done, Hans. You should have put the knife in your pocket.” “Never mind, I’ll do better next time.”

“Where are you off to, Hans?” “To Gretel’s, Mother.” “Behave yourself, Hans.” “Oh, I’ll behave. Goodbye, Mother.” “Goodbye, Hans.” Hans arrives at Gretel’s. “Good day, Gretel.” “Good day, Hans. What have you brought that’s good?” “I’ve brought nothing. I want to be given something.” Gretel gives Hans a young goat. “Goodbye, Gretel.” “Goodbye, Hans.” Hans takes the goat, ties its legs, and stuffs it in his pocket. By the time he gets home, it has suffocated. “Good evening, Mother.” “Good evening, Hans. Where have you been?” “At Gretel’s.” “What did you take her?” “Took nothing; she gave me something.” “What did Gretel give you?” “She gave me a goat.” “Where is the goat, Hans?” “Put it in my pocket.” “That was badly done, Hans. You should have put a rope around the goat’s neck.” “Never mind, I’ll do better next time.”

“Where are you off to, Hans?” “To Gretel’s, Mother.” “Behave yourself, Hans.” “Oh, I’ll behave. Goodbye, Mother.” “Goodbye, Hans.” Hans arrives at Gretel’s. “Good day, Gretel.” “Good day, Hans. What have you brought that’s good?” “I’ve brought nothing. I want to be given something.” Gretel gives Hans a piece of bacon. “Goodbye, Gretel.” “Goodbye, Hans.”

Hans ties the bacon to a rope and drags it away behind him. The dogs come along and gobble it up. By the time he gets home, he is holding the rope, and nothing is attached to it anymore. “Good evening, Mother.” “Good evening, Hans. Where have you been?” “To Gretel’s.” “What did you bring her?” “I brought her nothing. She gave me something.” “What did Gretel give you?” “Gave me a bit of bacon.” “Where is the bacon, Hans?” “Tied it to a rope, brought it home, dogs took it.” “That was badly done, Hans. You should have carried the bacon on your head.” “Never mind, I’ll do better next time.”

“Where are you off to, Hans?” “To Gretel’s, Mother.” “Behave yourself, Hans.” “I’ll behave. Goodbye, Mother.” “Goodbye, Hans.” Hans arrives at Gretel’s. “Good day, Gretel.” “Good day, Hans. What good thing have you brought?” “I’ve brought nothing, but I’d like something given to me.” Gretel gives Hans a calf. “Goodbye, Gretel.” “Goodbye, Hans.”

Hans takes the calf, sets it on his head, and the calf kicks him in the face. “Good evening, Mother.” “Good evening, Hans. Where have you been?” “To Gretel’s.” “What did you bring her?” “I brought nothing, but she gave me something.” “What did Gretel give you?” “A calf.” “Where is the calf, Hans?” “I put it on my head and it kicked me in the face.” “That was badly done, Hans. You should have led the calf and put it in the stall.” “Never mind, I’ll do better next time.”
