“Where are you off to, Hans?” “To Gretel’s, Mother.” “Behave yourself, Hans.” “I’ll behave. Goodbye, Mother.” “Goodbye, Hans.”
Hans arrives at Gretel’s. “Good day, Gretel.” “Good day, Hans. What good thing have you brought?” “I’ve brought nothing, but I’d like something given to me.” Gretel says to Hans, “I’ll go with you.”

Hans takes Gretel, ties her to a rope, leads her to the hay rack, and fastens her there. Then Hans goes to his mother. “Good evening, Mother.” “Good evening, Hans. Where have you been?” “To Gretel’s.” “What did you bring her?” “I brought her nothing.” “What did Gretel give you?” “She gave me nothing. She came along with me.” “Where have you left Gretel?” “Led her by the rope, tied her to the rack, and scattered some grass for her.” “That was badly done, Hans. You should have given her friendly looks.” “Never mind, I’ll do better.”
Hans went into the stable, cut out the eyes of all the calves and sheep, and threw them in Gretel’s face. Gretel got angry, tore herself loose, and ran away, and she was Hans’s bride no longer.

chapters.title: The Three Languages
paragraphs: An old count once lived in Switzerland. He had an only son, but the boy was stupid and could learn nothing. One day the father said, “Listen, son. Whatever I try, I can’t get anything into your head. You have to leave here. I’m going to hand you over to a famous master, and he can see what he can make of you.” The young man was sent to an unfamiliar town and stayed with the master for a whole year. When the year was up, he came home, and his father asked, “Well, son, what have you learned?” “Father, I’ve learned what dogs are saying when they bark.” “Lord have mercy!” cried the father. “Is that all you’ve learned? I’ll send you to another town, to another master.” The young man was taken there and stayed a year with this master as well. When he returned, his father asked again, “Son, what have you learned?” He answered, “Father, I’ve learned what the birds say.” Then the father flew into a rage. “You hopeless creature! You’ve wasted your precious time and learned nothing. Aren’t you ashamed to show your face to me? I’ll send you to a third master, but if you learn nothing this time either, I’ll no longer be your father.” The young man spent a whole year with the third master too, and when he came home and his father asked, “Son, what have you learned?” he answered, “Dear father, this year I’ve learned what the frogs croak.” At that the father was seized by a furious anger. He jumped up, called his men together, and said, “This fellow is no longer my son. I cast him out, and I order you to take him into the forest and kill him.” They took him away, but when the moment came to kill him, they couldn’t bring themselves to do it out of pity, and they let him go. They cut the eyes and tongue out of a deer so they could bring them to the old man as proof.

The young man wandered on, and after a while he came to a fortress and asked for a bed for the night. “Yes,” said the lord of the castle, “if you’re willing to spend the night down there in the old tower, go ahead. But I warn you, your life will be at risk. It’s full of wild dogs that bark and howl without ever stopping, and at certain hours we have to hand them a man, whom they devour on the spot.” The whole region was in grief and terror because of these dogs, and yet nobody could do anything to end it. The young man, however, felt no fear. He said, “Just let me go down to the barking dogs, and give me something to throw to them. They won’t do me any harm.” Since he insisted on it, they gave him some food for the wild beasts and took him down to the tower. When he went inside, the dogs didn’t bark at him. They wagged their tails around him quite in a friendly way, ate what he put in front of them, and didn’t harm a single hair on his head. The next morning, to everyone’s amazement, he came out again safe and unhurt, and he told the lord of the castle, “The dogs have told me, in their own language, why they live there and bring misfortune on the land. They’re under a spell, and they have to guard a great treasure that lies deep in the tower. They can’t rest until it’s taken away, and from their talk I’ve also learned how that can be done.” Everyone who heard this was overjoyed, and the lord of the castle said he would adopt him as his son if he succeeded. He went down again, and since he knew what he had to do, he did it thoroughly and carried out a chest full of gold. After that, the howling of the wild dogs was never heard again. They had vanished, and the land was rid of its trouble.

Some time later he got it into his head to travel to Rome. On the way he passed a marsh where a number of frogs sat croaking. He listened to them, and when he understood what they were saying, he became very thoughtful and sad. At last he reached Rome. The Pope had just died, and the cardinals were deeply divided over whom to appoint in his place. In the end they agreed that the man chosen as pope should be marked by some divine and miraculous sign. Just as they decided this, the young count walked into the church, and suddenly two snow-white doves flew onto his shoulders and stayed there. The churchmen saw in this the sign from above and asked him right then and there whether he would be pope. He was unsure and didn’t know whether he deserved it, but the doves urged him on, and finally he said yes. Then he was anointed and consecrated, and so what he had heard from the frogs on his way, which had troubled him so much, came true: he was to be His Holiness the Pope. Then he had to sing a mass and didn’t know a single word of it, but the two doves kept sitting on his shoulders and told him all of it in his ear.

chapters.title: The Fox and the Cat
paragraphs: It so happened that the cat met the fox in a forest. She thought to herself, “He is clever and experienced, and highly regarded in the world,” so she spoke to him in a friendly way. “Good day, dear Mr Fox. How are you? How is everything with you? How are you getting along in these hard times?” The fox, puffed up with every kind of arrogance, looked the cat over from head to foot, and for a long while couldn’t decide whether to answer at all. At last he said, “Oh, you miserable whisker-washer, you spotted fool, you starving mouse-hunter, what are you thinking? How dare you ask how I’m getting along? What have you learned? How many arts do you know?” “I know only one,” replied the cat humbly. “What art is that?” asked the fox. “When the hounds are chasing me, I can spring up a tree and save myself.” “Is that all?” said the fox. “I’m master of a hundred arts, and on top of that I have a sackful of tricks. I feel sorry for you. Come with me, and I’ll teach you how to get away from the hounds.” Just then a hunter came along with four dogs. The cat leaped nimbly up a tree and sat at the very top, where the branches and leaves hid her completely. “Open your sack, Mr Fox, open your sack!” the cat called down to him, but the dogs had already caught him and were holding him fast. “Ah, Mr Fox,” cried the cat, “with all your hundred arts, you’ve been left in the lurch! If you could have climbed like me, you wouldn’t have lost your life.”

chapters.title: The Four Clever Brothers
paragraphs: “Dear children,” a poor man said to his four sons, “I have nothing to give you. You must go out into the wide world and try your luck. Start by learning some trade, and see how you get on.” So the four brothers took their walking sticks in their hands and their small bundles on their shoulders, said goodbye to their father, and all went out through the gate together. After they had gone some distance, they came to a place where four roads crossed, each leading to a different country. Then the eldest said, “Here we must part. But four years from today we’ll come back to this spot, and in the meantime each of us must see what he can do for himself.”

So each brother went his own way. As the eldest was hurrying along, a man met him and asked where he was going and what he wanted. “I’m going out to try my luck in the world, and I’d like to begin by learning some art or trade,” he answered. “Then come with me,” said the man, “and I’ll teach you to become the craftiest thief there ever was.” “No,” said the young man, “that isn’t an honest calling, and what can anyone expect to get out of it in the end except the gallows?” “Oh,” said the man, “you needn’t fear the gallows. I’ll only teach you to steal what is fair game, things nobody else can get or cares about, and in such a way that no one can find you out.” So the young man agreed to follow his trade, and he soon proved so clever that nothing escaped him once he had set his mind on it.

The second brother also met a man, who found out what he was setting out to do and asked what trade he meant to follow. “I don’t know yet,” he said. “Then come with me and become a stargazer. It’s a noble art, because once you understand the stars, nothing can be hidden from you.” The idea pleased him very much, and he soon became such a skilled stargazer that when he had served his time and wanted to leave his master, the master gave him a spyglass and said, “With this you can see everything that happens in the sky and on earth, and nothing can be hidden from you.”

The third brother met a huntsman, who took him along and taught him everything about hunting so well that he became highly skilled in the craft of the woods. When he left his master, the huntsman gave him a bow and said, “Whatever you shoot at with this bow, you’re sure to hit.”

The youngest brother also met a man, who asked him what he wanted to do. “Wouldn’t you like to be a tailor?” the man said. “Oh, no!” said the young man. “Sitting cross-legged from morning to night, pushing a needle and iron back and forth, will never suit me.” “Oh,” answered the man, “that’s not my kind of tailoring. Come with me, and you’ll learn a very different sort of craft.” Not knowing what better to do, he went along with the plan and learned tailoring from the very beginning. When he left his master, the man gave him a needle and said, “You can sew anything with this, whether it’s as soft as an egg or as hard as steel, and the join will be so fine that no seam will show.”

After four years, at the agreed time, the four brothers met at the crossroads. They greeted one another and set off toward their father’s home, where they told him everything that had happened to them and how each had learned a trade.

Then one day they were sitting in front of the house under a very tall tree, and the father said, “I’d like to see what each of you can do with your skills.” He looked up and said to the second son, “At the top of this tree there’s a chaffinch’s nest. Tell me how many eggs are in it.” The star-gazer took his glass, looked up, and said, “Five.” “Now,” said the father to the eldest son, “take the eggs away without letting the bird that’s sitting on them and hatching them notice anything of what you’re doing.” So the clever thief climbed the tree and brought his father the five eggs from under the bird. It never saw or felt what he was doing, but went on sitting there at its ease. Then the father took the eggs, put one on each corner of the table and the fifth in the middle, and said to the huntsman, “Cut all the eggs in two with one shot.” The huntsman took up his bow and with a single shot split all five eggs, just as his father wished.

“Now it’s your turn,” he said to the young tailor. “Sew the eggs and the young birds inside them back together, so neatly that the shot has done them no harm.” The tailor took his needle and sewed the eggs as he’d been told. When he had finished, the thief was sent to carry them back to the nest and put them under the bird without her knowing. She went on sitting and hatched them, and a few days later they crawled out, with only a thin red line around their necks where the tailor had sewn them together.

“Well done, sons!” said the old man. “You’ve made good use of your time and learned something worth knowing. But I honestly can’t say which of you should get the prize. Oh, if only a time would come soon when you could put your skills to use!”

Not long afterward the whole country was in an uproar. A mighty dragon had carried off the king’s daughter, and the king grieved over her day and night. He announced that whoever brought her back would have her as his wife. The four brothers said to one another, “This is our chance. Let’s see what we can do.” They agreed to try to free the princess. “I’ll find out where she is easily enough,” said the star-gazer, and he looked through his glass. Soon he cried, “I can see her far away, sitting on a rock in the sea, and the dragon is right beside her, keeping watch.” So he went to the king and asked for a ship for himself and his brothers, and together they sailed across the sea until they reached the spot. There they found the princess sitting on the rock, just as the star-gazer had said, and the dragon lay asleep with his head in her lap. “I don’t dare shoot him,” said the huntsman, “because I’d kill the beautiful young lady too.” “Then I’ll try my skill,” said the thief. He went and stole her out from under the dragon, so quietly and gently that the beast never noticed and just kept on snoring.

Full of joy, they hurried off with her in their little boat toward the ship. But before long the dragon came roaring through the air after them, for he had woken up and found the princess gone. As he swooped over the boat, ready to pounce and snatch her away, the huntsman picked up his bow and shot him straight through the heart, and he fell down dead. Even so, they were not safe yet, for the beast was so huge that when he fell he capsized the boat, and they had to float in the open sea on a few planks. Then the tailor took his needle and, with a few big stitches, joined some of the planks together. He sat on them and sailed around collecting all the pieces of the boat, and he sewed them together so fast that the boat was soon ready again. Then they reached the ship and got home safely.

When they brought the princess home to her father, there was great rejoicing. He said to the four brothers, “One of you shall marry her, but you must decide among yourselves which one.” A quarrel broke out. The star-gazer said, “If I hadn’t found the princess, all your skills would have been useless. So she should be mine.” “Your seeing her would have been useless,” said the thief, “if I hadn’t carried her off from the dragon. So she should be mine.” “No, she’s mine,” said the huntsman, “because if I hadn’t killed the dragon, he would have torn you and the princess to pieces.” “And if I hadn’t sewn the boat back together,” said the tailor, “you would all have drowned. So she’s mine.” Then the king spoke up. “Each of you is right,” he said, “and since all of you can’t have the young lady, the best thing is for none of you to have her. The truth is, there is someone she likes a great deal better. But to make up for your loss, I will give each of you half a kingdom as a reward for his skill.” The brothers agreed that this was far better than quarreling, or than marrying a lady who had no wish to have them. So the king gave each of them half a kingdom, just as he had promised, and they lived very happily for the rest of their days and took good care of their father. And somebody took better care of the young lady than to let either the dragon or any of the craftsmen have her again.

chapters.title: Lily and the Lion
paragraphs: A merchant who had three daughters was about to leave on a journey. Before he went, he asked each daughter what gift he should bring her. The eldest wanted pearls, the second wanted jewels, but the third, whose name was Lily, said, “Dear father, bring me a rose.” Finding a rose was no easy task, since it was the middle of winter. But she was his prettiest daughter and very fond of flowers, so her father said he would see what he could do. He kissed all three and said goodbye.

When it was time to head home, he had bought pearls and jewels for the two eldest, but he had searched everywhere for the rose without success. Whenever he walked into a garden and asked for one, people laughed at him and asked if he thought roses grew in the snow. This upset him deeply, because Lily was his dearest child. On the way home, as he was wondering what to bring her, he came upon a fine castle. Around it was a garden, where one half seemed to be in summer and the other half in winter. On one side the loveliest flowers were in full bloom; on the other, everything looked bleak and buried in snow. “What luck!” he said. He called his servant and told him to go to a beautiful bed of roses there and bring back one of the finest flowers.

That done, they were riding off well pleased when a fierce lion leaped out and roared, “Whoever has stolen my roses will be eaten alive!” The man said, “I didn’t know the garden was yours. Is there nothing that can save my life?” “No,” said the lion, “nothing, unless you promise to give me the first thing that meets you when you get home. If you agree to that, I will spare your life, and I will give you the rose for your daughter too.” But the man didn’t want to agree. He said, “It might be my youngest daughter, who loves me most and always runs to meet me when I come home.” The servant, badly frightened, said, “It might only be a cat or a dog.” In the end the man gave in with a heavy heart. He took the rose and said he would give the lion whatever met him first on his return.

As he came near home, the one who met him was Lily, his youngest and dearest daughter. She came running, kissed him and welcomed him home, and when she saw that he had brought her the rose, she was happier still. But her father grew very sad and began to weep. “Alas, my dearest child,” he said, “I bought this flower at a high price. I promised to give you to a wild lion, and when he has you, he will tear you to pieces and eat you.” Then he told her everything that had happened and said she must not go, no matter what came of it.
But she comforted him. “Dear father,” she said, “you must keep the word you gave. I will go to the lion and calm him down. Perhaps he will let me come home safely again.”

The next morning she asked which way she should go, said goodbye to her father, and walked into the woods with a brave heart. But the lion was an enchanted prince. By day he and his whole court were lions, but in the evening they turned back into their true shapes. When Lily arrived at the castle, he welcomed her so graciously that she agreed to marry him. They held the wedding feast and lived happily together for a long time. The prince could be seen only once evening came, and then he held court. But every morning he left his bride and went off alone, she did not know where, until night came again.

After some time he said to her, “Tomorrow there will be a great feast at your father’s house, because your eldest sister is getting married. If you’d like to go and see her, my lions will take you there.” She was delighted at the thought of seeing her father again, and she set out with the lions. Everyone was overjoyed to see her, since they had long thought she was dead. She told them how happy she was and stayed until the feast was over, and then she went back to the woods.

Soon afterward her second sister got married, and when Lily was invited to the wedding, she said to the prince, “This time I won’t go alone. You must come with me.” But he refused. He said it would be very dangerous, because if even the faintest ray of torchlight fell on him, his enchantment would become even worse: he would be turned into a dove and forced to wander the world for seven long years. But she gave him no peace and promised to make sure no light fell on him. At last they set out together, taking their little child with them. She picked a large hall with thick walls for him to sit in while the wedding torches were lit, but unluckily no one noticed that there was a crack in the door. The wedding was held with great pomp, but as the procession came back from the church and passed the hall with its torches, one very small ray of light fell on the prince. In an instant he vanished. When his wife came in and looked for him, she found only a white dove. It said to her, “For seven years I must fly back and forth over the face of the earth, but every so often I will drop a white feather to show you which way I’m going. Follow it, and in the end you may catch up with me and set me free.”

With that he flew out the door, and poor Lily followed. Every now and then a white feather fell and showed her which way to go. So she roamed through the wide world for seven years, looking neither right nor left and never resting. Then she began to feel glad, thinking that the time when all her troubles would end was fast approaching. But rest was still far off, for one day as she was traveling she lost sight of the white feather, and when she looked up, the dove was nowhere to be seen. “Now,” she thought, “no help from any human can do me any good.” So she went to the sun and said, “You shine everywhere, on the mountaintop and in the deepest valley. Have you seen my white dove anywhere?” “No,” said the sun, “I haven’t seen it. But I will give you a casket. Open it when your hour of need comes.”

She thanked the sun and went on until evening, and when the moon rose, she called out to it, “You shine through the night, over field and grove. Have you not seen my white dove anywhere?” “No,” said the moon, “I can’t help you, but I will give you an egg. Break it when you are in need.”

She thanked the moon and went on until the night wind began to blow. She raised her voice to it and said, “You blow through every tree and under every leaf. Have you not seen my white dove?” “No,” said the night wind, “but I will ask three other winds. Perhaps they have seen it.” Then the east wind and the west wind came and said they hadn’t seen it either, but the south wind said, “I have seen the white dove. He has fled to the Red Sea, where he has turned into a lion again, because the seven years are over. He is there fighting a dragon, and the dragon is an enchanted princess who wants to separate him from you.” Then the night wind said, “Let me give you some advice. Go to the Red Sea. On the right shore stand many rods. Count them, and when you reach the eleventh, break it off and strike the dragon with it. Then the lion will win, and both of them will appear to you in their own forms. After that, look around and you will see a griffin with wings like a bird, sitting by the Red Sea. Jump onto his back with your beloved as quickly as you can, and he will carry you home across the water. I will also give you this nut,” the night wind went on. “When you are halfway across, throw it down, and a tall nut tree will spring up at once out of the water, where the griffin can rest. Otherwise he wouldn’t have the strength to carry you the whole way. So if you forget to throw down the nut, he will let you both fall into the sea.”

So the poor wanderer set out and found everything just as the night wind had said. She pulled off the eleventh rod and struck the dragon, and at once the lion became a prince and the dragon became a princess again. But as soon as the princess was freed from the spell, she grabbed the prince by the arm, sprang onto the griffin’s back, and flew off with him.

So the unhappy traveler was abandoned and forlorn once more. But she took heart and said, “As far as the wind blows and as long as the cock crows, I will keep going until I find him again.” She went on for a long, long way, until at last she came to the castle where the princess had taken the prince. A feast was being prepared there, and she heard that the wedding was about to take place. “Heaven help me now!” she said. She took the casket the sun had given her and found inside a dress as dazzling as the sun itself. She put it on and went into the palace, and everyone stared at her. The bride liked the dress so much that she asked whether it was for sale. “Not for gold and silver,” said Lily, “but for flesh and blood.” The princess asked what she meant, and Lily said, “Let me talk with the bridegroom in his chamber tonight, and I will give you the dress.” At last the princess agreed, but she told her chamberlain to give the prince a sleeping draft so that he would neither hear nor see her. When evening came and the prince had fallen asleep, Lily was led into his chamber. She sat down at his feet and said, “I have followed you for seven years. I have been to the sun, the moon, and the night wind to look for you, and in the end I helped you defeat the dragon. Will you really forget me completely?” But the prince slept so soundly the whole time that her voice just passed over him, like the wind whistling through fir trees.

Then poor Lily was led away and forced to give up the golden dress. Seeing there was no help for it, she went out to a meadow, sat down, and wept. But as she sat there, she remembered the egg the moon had given her. When she broke it, out came a hen with twelve chicks, all of pure gold, which played around for a bit and then nestled under the mother hen’s wings, making the loveliest sight in the world. She got up and drove them ahead of her until the bride saw them from her window. The bride was so delighted that she came out and asked whether Lily would sell the brood. “Not for gold or silver, but for flesh and blood. Let me speak with the bridegroom in his chamber again this evening, and I will give you the whole brood.”

The princess figured she could fool Lily again as before and agreed to everything Lily asked. But when the prince went to his room, he asked the chamberlain why the wind had whistled so in the night. The chamberlain told him everything: he had given him a sleeping draft, a poor girl had come and spoken to him in his room, and she was due to return that night. So the prince made sure to throw away the sleeping draft. When Lily came and began once more to tell him of the hardships she had suffered and how loyal and true she had been to him, he recognized the voice of his dear wife and jumped up. “You have woken me as if from a dream,” he said. “The strange princess cast a spell over me, and I had completely forgotten you. But Heaven has sent you to me at just the right moment.”

Then they slipped out of the palace in the night without anyone noticing and climbed onto the griffin, who flew them back across the Red Sea. When they were halfway over, Lily dropped the nut into the water, and at once a great nut tree rose up out of the sea. The griffin rested on it for a while and then carried them safely home. There they found their child, who had grown up handsome and fair, and after all their troubles they lived happily together until the end of their days.

chapters.title: The Fox and the Horse
paragraphs: A farmer had a horse that had served him loyally and well for years. Now the horse was too old to work, so the farmer stopped feeding him. “I don’t need you anymore,” he said. “Get out of my stable. I won’t take you back until you’re stronger than a lion.” Then he opened the door and drove him out.

The poor horse was miserable. He wandered through the woods, looking for a bit of shelter from the cold wind and rain. Before long a fox met him. “What’s wrong, my friend?” he asked. “Why are you hanging your head and looking so lonely and sorry for yourself?” “Ah,” said the horse, “justice and greed never live under one roof. My master has forgotten everything I did for him all these years, and now that I can’t work anymore, he has thrown me out. He says he won’t take me back unless I become stronger than a lion. How could I ever manage that? He knows I can’t, or he wouldn’t say such a thing.”

The fox told him to cheer up. “I’ll help you,” he said. “Lie down over there, stretch out stiff, and play dead.” The horse did as he was told. The fox went straight to the lion, who lived in a cave nearby, and said, “There’s a dead horse lying not far from here. Come along with me, and you can make a fine meal of him.” The lion was delighted and set off at once. When they reached the horse, the fox said, “You won’t be able to eat him in comfort here. Here’s what we’ll do: I’ll tie you tight to his tail, and then you can drag him to your den and eat him whenever you like.”

The lion liked this idea and lay down quietly so the fox could fasten him to the horse. But the fox tied the lion’s legs together as well, and he knotted everything so tightly that the lion, for all his strength, could not get loose. When the job was done, the fox slapped the horse on the shoulder and cried, “Giddy-up, Dobbin! Giddy-up!” The horse jumped to his feet and trotted off with the lion dragging behind him. The lion began to roar and bellow until every bird in the forest flew off in fright. But the horse let him bellow and walked calmly across the fields to his master’s house.

“Here he is, master,” he said. “I’ve beaten him.” When the farmer saw his old servant, his heart softened. “You shall stay in your stable,” he said, “and be well looked after.” And so the poor old horse had plenty to eat and lived on until he died.

chapters.title: The Blue Light
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a soldier who had served the king faithfully for many years. But when the war ended, his many wounds meant he could serve no longer. The king said to him, “You may go home. I have no more need of you, and you will get no more money, because I pay wages only to those who do work for me.” The soldier had no idea how to earn a living. He left in great distress and walked all day, until toward evening he came to a forest. As darkness fell, he saw a light and made his way to it, and found a house where a witch lived. “Please give me a night’s lodging and a little food and drink,” he said to her, “or I’ll starve.” “Ha!” she answered. “Who gives anything to a runaway soldier? Still, I’ll be kind and take you in, if you’ll do what I want.” “What do you want?” asked the soldier. “That you dig up my whole garden for me tomorrow.” The soldier agreed, and the next day he worked with all his strength, but by evening he had not finished. “I can see you can do no more today,” said the witch, “but I’ll keep you another night. In return, tomorrow you must chop me a load of wood, and chop it small.” The soldier spent the whole day at it, and in the evening the witch suggested he stay one more night. “Tomorrow you’ll have only a very small job. Behind my house there’s an old dry well, and my light has fallen into it. It burns blue and never goes out, and you’re to bring it back up.” The next day the old woman led him to the well and lowered him down in a basket. He found the blue light and signaled for her to pull him up. She did pull him up, but when he was near the edge, she reached down her hand and tried to snatch the blue light from him. “No,” said he, seeing her wicked purpose. “I won’t hand over the light until I’m standing with both feet on the ground.” The witch flew into a rage, dropped him back into the well, and walked away.

The poor soldier landed on the damp ground without being hurt, and the blue light kept burning, but what good was that to him? He could see clearly that there was no escape from death. He sat for a while in deep sorrow. Then he suddenly reached into his pocket and found his tobacco pipe, still half full. “This will be my last pleasure,” he thought. He took it out, lit it at the blue light, and began to smoke. When the smoke had curled around the cavern, a little black dwarf suddenly stood before him and said, “Master, what are your orders?” “My orders?” said the soldier, completely astonished. “I must do everything you tell me,” said the little man. “Good,” said the soldier. “Then first of all, help me out of this well.” The little man took him by the hand and led him along an underground passage, and he did not forget to bring the blue light along. On the way the dwarf showed him the treasures the witch had gathered and hidden there, and the soldier took as much gold as he could carry. Once he was above ground, he said to the little man, “Now go and tie up the old witch and bring her before the judge.” Before long she came rushing past like the wind, riding a wild tomcat and screaming horribly. It was not long before the little man appeared again. “It is done,” he said. “The witch is already hanging on the gallows. What other orders does my master have?” asked the dwarf. “None at the moment,” answered the soldier. “You can go home, but be ready to come at once if I call you.” “All you need to do is light your pipe at the blue light, and I will appear before you right away.” With that he vanished from sight.

The soldier went back to the town he had come from. He took a room at the best inn, ordered himself fine clothes, and told the innkeeper to give him the finest room possible. When it was ready and the soldier had moved in, he called the little black manikin and said, “I served the king faithfully, but he dismissed me and left me to starve, and now I want revenge.” “What shall I do?” asked the little man. “Late tonight, when the king’s daughter is in bed, bring her here while she sleeps. She is going to work as my servant.” The manikin said, “That is easy for me to do, but very dangerous for you. If it’s found out, you’ll be in trouble.” When the clock struck twelve, the door flew open, and the manikin carried in the princess. “Aha! So you’re here!” cried the soldier. “Get to work right now! Fetch the broom and sweep the room.” When she had done that, he ordered her over to his chair, stretched out his feet, and said, “Pull off my boots.” Then he threw them in her face and made her pick them up again, clean them, and polish them. She did everything he told her without protest, in silence, with her eyes half shut. At the first crow of the rooster, the manikin carried her back to the royal palace and laid her in her bed.

The next morning, when the princess got up, she went to her father and told him she had had a very strange dream. “I was carried through the streets as fast as lightning,” she said, “and taken to a soldier’s room, where I had to wait on him like a maid. I swept his room, cleaned his boots, and did all sorts of lowly chores. It was only a dream, and yet I’m as tired as if I had really done it all.” “The dream may have been true,” said the king. “Here is my advice. Fill your pocket with peas and make a little hole in it. Then if you’re carried off again, the peas will fall out and leave a trail in the streets.” But the king didn’t see that the manikin was standing right beside him as he spoke, and heard every word. That night, when the sleeping princess was carried through the streets again, some peas did fall from her pocket, but they marked no trail, because the clever manikin had scattered peas in every street in town beforehand. And once more the princess was forced to do servant’s work until the rooster crowed.

The next morning the king sent his men out to look for the trail, but it was no use, because in every street poor children were sitting and picking up peas, saying, “It must have rained peas last night.” “We’ll have to think of something else,” said the king. “Keep your shoes on when you go to bed, and before you leave the place where you’re taken, hide one of them there. I’ll soon find a way to track it down.” The black manikin overheard this plan. That night, when the soldier again ordered him to bring the princess, he told the soldier about it. He said he knew no way to get around this trick, and that if the shoe were found in the soldier’s house, things would go badly for him. “Just do as I tell you,” answered the soldier. And so on this third night the princess again had to work like a servant, but before she left, she hid her shoe under the bed.

The next morning the king had the whole town searched for his daughter’s shoe. It was found at the soldier’s lodging. The soldier himself, who had gone outside the town gate at the dwarf’s urging, was soon brought back and thrown into prison. In his flight he had forgotten the two most valuable things he owned, the blue light and the gold, and had only a single ducat in his pocket. Now, weighed down with chains, he was standing at his dungeon window when he happened to see one of his old comrades go by. The soldier tapped on the windowpane, and when the man came over, he said to him, “Be so good as to fetch me the little bundle I left at the inn, and I’ll give you a ducat for it.” His comrade ran off and brought back what he wanted. As soon as the soldier was alone again, he lit his pipe and called the black manikin. “Don’t be afraid,” the manikin told his master. “Go wherever they take you and let them do what they like. Just take the blue light with you.” The next day the soldier was put on trial, and although he had done nothing evil, the judge sentenced him to death. As he was led out to die, he begged the king for one last favor. “What is it?” asked the king. “To smoke one more pipe on the way.” “You may smoke three,” the king answered, “but don’t imagine I will spare your life.” Then the soldier took out his pipe and lit it at the blue light, and as soon as a few curls of smoke had risen, the manikin was there with a small club in his hand. “What does my master command?” he asked. “Strike down that crooked judge and his constable, and don’t spare the king who has treated me so badly.” Then the manikin fell upon them like lightning, darting this way and that, and anyone his club so much as touched dropped to the ground and did not dare to move again. The king was terrified. He threw himself on the soldier’s mercy, and just to be allowed to live, he gave him his kingdom and his daughter as wife.

chapters.title: The Raven
paragraphs: There was once a queen who had a little daughter, still too small to walk by herself. One day the child was very fussy, and no matter what the mother did, she could not quiet her. She lost her patience, and when she saw the ravens flying around the castle, she opened the window and said, “I wish you were a raven and would fly away, so I could have a little peace.” The words had barely left her mouth when the child in her arms turned into a raven and flew out of the open window. The bird flew to a dark forest and stayed there a long time, and in all that while the parents heard nothing of their child.

Long afterward, a man was making his way through the forest when he heard a raven calling, and he followed the sound of its voice. As he came closer, the raven said, “I am a king’s daughter by birth, but I am under some enchantment now. You can set me free, though.” “What must I do?” he asked. She answered, “Go deeper into the forest until you come to a house where an old woman lives. She will offer you food and drink, but you must take neither. If you do, you will fall into a deep sleep and won’t be able to help me. In the garden behind the house there is a big heap of tanbark, and you must stand on it and watch for me. I will drive up in my carriage at two o’clock in the afternoon for three days in a row. The first day it will be pulled by four white horses, the second day by four chestnut horses, and the last by four black ones. But if you fail to stay awake and I find you asleep, I will not be set free.”

The man promised to do everything she asked, but the raven said, “Alas, I already know that you will accept something from the woman, and then you won’t be able to save me.” Again he assured her that under no circumstances would he touch any food or drink.
When he arrived at the house and stepped inside, the old woman came to meet him. “You poor man, you look so tired!” she said. “Come in and rest, and let me give you something to eat and drink.”
“No,” the man answered, “I won’t eat or drink anything.”
But she wouldn’t leave him be. She kept pressing him: “If you won’t eat, you could at least have a glass of wine. One drink is nothing.” In the end he let himself be talked into it, and he drank.

As the appointed hour drew near, he went out into the garden and climbed onto the tan-heap to wait for the raven. Suddenly a heaviness came over him that he couldn’t fight off. He lay down for just a little while, fully determined to stay awake, but within a minute his eyes had closed by themselves, and he sank into a sleep so deep that nothing in the world could have woken him. At two o’clock the raven came driving up, pulled by her four white horses. Before she even arrived, she sighed and said to herself, “I know he has fallen asleep.” When she reached the garden, she found him just as she had feared, lying on the tan-heap, sound asleep. She climbed down from her carriage and went to him. She called his name and shook him, but it was no use. He kept on sleeping.

At noon the next day the old woman came to him again with food and drink, and again he turned them down at first. But she begged so persistently that he finally gave in, picked up the glass, and drank once more.

Around two o’clock he went out to the garden and onto the tan-heap to watch for the raven. He hadn’t been there long when he grew so tired that his legs could hardly hold him and he couldn’t stand up any longer. So he lay down again and fell fast asleep. The raven came driving up with her four chestnut horses, and she said sadly to herself, “I know he has fallen asleep.” She went to look for him as before, but he slept on, and there was no waking him.
The day after, the old woman said to him, “What’s the matter with you? You aren’t eating or drinking anything. Do you want to kill yourself?”
He answered, “I mustn’t, and I won’t, eat or drink.”
But she set the dish of food and the glass of wine down in front of him, and when he caught the smell of the wine, he couldn’t hold out against the temptation. He took a long drink.

When the hour came around again, he went out as usual to the tan-heap in the garden to wait for the king’s daughter. But he felt even more weighed down by weariness than on the two days before, and he threw himself down and slept like a log. At two o’clock the raven came into sight, and this time her coachman and everything about her, horses included, were black.

She was sadder than ever as she drove up, and she said mournfully, “I know he has fallen asleep, and he won’t be able to set me free.” She found him sleeping heavily, and nothing she did could wake him. So she laid beside him a loaf of bread, some meat, and a flask of wine, the kind that never runs out, however much he takes from it. Then she pulled a gold ring off her finger, with her name engraved on it, and slid it onto one of his. Last of all, she left a letter beside him. In it she told him exactly what food and drink she had left for him, and she ended with these words: “I see that as long as you stay here, you will never be able to set me free. But if you still want to, come to the golden castle of Stromberg. It is well within your power to do that.” Then she went back to her carriage and drove off to the golden castle of Stromberg.

When the man woke up and realized he had been asleep, his heart sank. “She must have come and driven away again,” he said, “and now it’s too late for me to save her.” Then he noticed the things lying beside him. He read the letter and understood everything that had happened. He got up at once, eager to set out for the castle of Stromberg, but he had no idea which way to go. He wandered for a long time looking for it, and at last he came to a dark forest. He kept walking through it for fourteen days and still couldn’t find his way out. Night fell once more, and, worn out, he lay down under a bush and went to sleep. The next day he went on through the forest again, and that evening, hoping to rest, he lay down as before, but there was such howling and wailing that he couldn’t sleep. He waited until it was darker and people had started lighting the lamps in their houses. Then he saw a faint glimmer ahead of him and walked toward it.

The light came from a house, which looked smaller than it was because an enormous giant stood in front of it, towering over it. The man thought, “If the giant sees me go in, my life won’t be worth much.” Still, after a while he gathered his courage and went forward. When the giant saw him, he called out, “It’s lucky you’ve come. I haven’t had a bite to eat in ages. Now I can have you for supper.” “I’d rather you didn’t,” said the man, “because I’m not willing to be eaten. But if you’re hungry, I have enough to fill you up.” “In that case,” the giant replied, “I’ll leave you alone. I only thought of eating you because I had nothing else.”

So they went inside together and sat down, and the man took out the bread, the meat, and the wine, which, although he had eaten and drunk from them, were still undiminished. The giant was delighted with the fine meal and ate and drank until he was satisfied. When he had finished, the man asked whether he could tell him the way to the castle of Stromberg. “I’ll check my map,” the giant said. “All the towns, villages, and houses are marked on it.” He fetched the map and searched for the castle, but couldn’t find it. “Never mind,” he said. “I have bigger maps upstairs in the cupboard. We’ll look at those.” But they searched in vain, because the castle wasn’t marked on those either. The man now wanted to continue on his way, but the giant asked him to stay a day or two longer, until his brother came back from looking for food. When the brother got home, they asked him about the castle of Stromberg, and he said he would check his own maps as soon as he had eaten and taken the edge off his hunger. So when he had finished his supper, they all went up to his room together and went through his maps, but the castle wasn’t there. Then he brought out other, older maps, and they kept looking until at last they found it. It was many thousands of miles away. “How will I ever get there?” asked the man. “I have two hours to spare,” said the giant, “and I’ll carry you to somewhere near the castle. After that I have to go back and look after the child who is in our care.”

So the giant carried the man to within about a hundred leagues of the castle and set him down there. “You can walk the rest of the way yourself,” he said. The man traveled on, day and night, until he reached the golden castle of Stromberg. He found it standing on a glass mountain, and looking up from the bottom, he saw the enchanted maiden drive around her castle and then go inside. He was overjoyed to see her and longed to reach the top of the mountain, but its sides were so slippery that every time he tried to climb, he slid back down. When he saw that he could not get to her, he was deeply grieved. “I’ll stay here and wait for her,” he told himself. So he built a little hut and sat there watching for a whole year. Every day he saw the king’s daughter drive around her castle, and every day he was still unable to get any closer to her.

One day, looking out from his hut, he saw three robbers fighting, and he called out to them, “God be with you.” They stopped when they heard him, but they looked around and saw nobody, and went back to fighting even more fiercely than before. “God be with you,” he cried again. Again they paused and looked about, and seeing no one, returned to their fight. A third time he called out, “God be with you.” Then, wanting to know what the quarrel among the three men was about, he went out and asked why they were fighting each other so angrily. One of them said he had found a stick, and all he had to do was strike it against any door he wanted to go through, and the door would fly open. Another said he had found a cloak that made whoever wore it invisible. The third had caught a horse that would carry its rider over any obstacle, even up the glass mountain. They hadn’t been able to agree whether to stay together and share the things, or to part ways. When he heard this, the man said, “I’ll give you something in exchange for those three things. Not money, because I have none, but something worth far more. First, though, I have to test whether everything you’ve told me about them is true.” So the robbers made him get on the horse and handed him the stick and the cloak, and when he threw the cloak around himself, he couldn’t be seen anymore. Then he fell on them with the stick and beat them one after another, shouting, “There, you lazy good-for-nothings, you got what you deserve! Are you satisfied now?”

After that he rode up the glass mountain. When he reached the castle gate, he found it shut, but he struck it with his stick, and it flew wide open at once, and he went through. He climbed the steps and entered the room where the maiden sat with a golden goblet of wine in front of her. She couldn’t see him, because he was still wearing his cloak. He took the ring she had given him off his finger and threw it into the goblet, so that it rang as it hit the bottom. “That is my own ring!” she cried. “And if so, the man who is coming to set me free must be here too.”

She searched the castle for him but couldn’t find him anywhere. Meanwhile he had gone outside again, mounted his horse, and thrown off the cloak. So when she came to the castle gate, she saw him and cried out with joy. He dismounted and took her in his arms, and she kissed him and said, “Now you have truly set me free, and tomorrow we will celebrate our wedding.”

chapters.title: The Golden Goose
paragraphs: There was once a man who had three sons. The youngest was called Dummling,[1] and everyone despised him, mocked him, and sneered at him at every turn.
One day the eldest wanted to go into the forest to chop wood. Before he left, his mother gave him a lovely sweet cake and a bottle of wine, so that he wouldn’t go hungry or thirsty.

When he got to the forest, he met a little old man with gray hair, who wished him good day and said, “Please give me a piece of the cake in your pocket, and let me have a drink of your wine. I’m so hungry and thirsty.” But the clever son answered, “If I give you my cake and wine, I’ll have none left for myself. Get lost!” And he left the little man standing there and walked on.
But when he started chopping down a tree, it wasn’t long before he swung badly, and the axe cut into his arm, so that he had to go home and have it bandaged. And that was the little gray man’s doing.

Next, the second son went into the forest, and his mother gave him a cake and a bottle of wine, just as she had given the eldest. The little old gray man met him too and asked him for a piece of cake and a drink of wine. But the second son also said, quite sensibly, “Whatever I give you gets taken away from me. Get lost!” And he left the little man standing there and walked on. His punishment came quickly. After only a few blows at the tree, he struck himself in the leg and had to be carried home.

Then Dummling said, “Father, please let me go and cut wood.” His father answered, “Your brothers hurt themselves doing it. Leave it alone. You don’t know the first thing about it.” But Dummling begged for so long that finally his father said, “Oh, go on, then. You’ll learn something by hurting yourself.” His mother gave him a cake made with water and baked in the ashes, and a bottle of sour beer to go with it.

When he got to the forest, the little old gray man met him too, greeted him, and said, “Give me a piece of your cake and a drink from your bottle. I’m so hungry and thirsty.” Dummling answered, “All I have is ash-cake and sour beer. If that suits you, let’s sit down and eat.” So they sat down, and when Dummling took out his ash-cake, it had turned into a fine sweet cake, and the sour beer had become good wine. They ate and drank, and afterward the little man said, “Because you have a good heart and are willing to share what you have, I’ll give you some good luck. Over there stands an old tree. Cut it down, and you’ll find something among its roots.” Then the little man said goodbye.

Dummling went and cut down the tree, and when it fell, there in the roots sat a goose with feathers of pure gold. He picked her up, took her along, and went to an inn, where he planned to spend the night. Now, the innkeeper had three daughters. They saw the goose and were curious what kind of marvelous bird it could be, and each of them wished she had one of its golden feathers.
The eldest thought, “I’ll soon find a chance to pull out a feather.” As soon as Dummling had gone out, she grabbed the goose by the wing, but her finger and hand stuck fast to it.
The second came along soon afterward, thinking only of how to get a feather for herself, but she had barely touched her sister when she was held fast too.

Finally the third girl came along with the same idea, and the other two shrieked at her, “Stay away! For heaven’s sake, stay away!” But she had no idea why she should. “They’re over there,” she thought, “so I might as well be there too.” She ran up to them, and the moment she touched her sister, she was stuck fast. So all three had to spend the night beside the goose.

In the morning Dummling tucked the goose under his arm and went on his way, paying no attention to the three girls dangling from it. They had no choice but to keep running after him, veering left and then right, wherever his legs happened to take him.

Out in the middle of the fields they ran into the parson. Seeing the parade, he said, “Shame on you, you worthless girls! Why are you chasing this young man across the fields? Is that decent?” And with that he grabbed the youngest girl by the hand to pull her away. But the instant he touched her, he stuck fast too and had to run along behind.

Before long the sexton came by, and he was amazed to see his master, the parson, trotting after three girls. “Hey, your reverence!” he called. “Where are you off to in such a hurry? Don’t forget we have a christening today!” He ran up and caught the parson by the sleeve, and found himself held fast as well.

As the five of them trotted along in a line, two laborers carrying hoes came up from the fields. The parson shouted to them and begged them to pull him and the sexton loose. But they had barely touched the sexton when they stuck fast too, and now seven people were running behind Dummling and his goose.

Soon afterward he reached a city whose king had a daughter so solemn that nobody could make her laugh. The king had therefore issued a decree: whoever could make her laugh would marry her. When Dummling heard this, he went before the princess with his goose and its whole train. The moment she saw the seven people running on and on, one behind another, she burst out laughing, loudly, as if she would never stop. So Dummling asked to have her as his wife. But the king didn’t like the idea of him as a son-in-law and came up with all kinds of excuses. He said Dummling must first bring him a man who could drink a whole cellarful of wine. Dummling thought of the little gray man, who would surely be able to help. He went into the forest, and at the spot where he had cut down the tree he found a man sitting with a very sad face. Dummling asked him what was weighing so heavily on him, and the man answered, “I’m so thirsty, and nothing quenches it. I can’t stand cold water. I’ve just emptied a barrel of wine, but to me that was like a drop on a hot stone!”
“I can help you with that,” said Dummling. “Just come along with me, and you’ll get your fill.”

He took the man to the king’s cellar, and the man bent over the enormous barrels and drank and drank until his hips ached. Before the day was over he had emptied every barrel. Then Dummling asked again for his bride, but the king was annoyed that an ugly fellow whom everyone called Dummling should carry off his daughter, and he set a new condition: first Dummling must find a man who could eat a whole mountain of bread. Dummling didn’t stop to think. He went straight into the forest, and in the same place sat a man who was cinching a strap around his belly, pulling a terrible face, and saying, “I’ve eaten a whole ovenful of rolls, but what good is that to someone as hungry as I am? My stomach stays empty, and I have to tie myself up tight, or I’ll die of hunger.”

Dummling was delighted. “Get up and come with me,” he said. “You’ll eat until you’re full.” He brought him to the king’s palace, where all the flour in the entire kingdom had been gathered, and had a huge mountain of bread baked from it. The man from the forest planted himself in front of it and began to eat, and by the end of a single day the whole mountain was gone. For the third time Dummling asked for his bride, but again the king looked for a way out. This time he demanded a ship that could sail on land as well as on water. “Come sailing back in it,” he said, “and you shall have my daughter for your wife.”

Dummling went straight to the forest, and there sat the little gray man to whom he had given his cake. When the man heard what Dummling needed, he said, “You gave me food and drink, so I will give you the ship. I’m doing all this because you were kind to me once.” Then he gave him the ship that could sail on land and water. When the king saw it, he could no longer keep Dummling from marrying his daughter. The wedding was held, and when the king died, Dummling inherited his kingdom and lived happily with his wife for many years.
[1] Simpleton

chapters.title: The Water of Life
paragraphs: Long before you or I were born, in a land far, far away, there lived a king who had three sons. Once this king fell sick—so sick that nobody thought he would survive. His sons were deeply grieved by their father’s illness, and as they walked together in the palace garden, sunk in gloom, a little old man came up to them and asked what was wrong. They told him their father was gravely ill and they feared nothing could save him. “I know what could,” said the little old man. “The Water of Life. One drink of it and he would be well again. But it is very hard to get.” The eldest son said, “I’ll soon find it,” and he went to the sick king and begged to be allowed to go in search of the Water of Life, since it was the only thing that could save him. “No,” said the king. “I would rather die than send you into the great danger you would face on such a journey.” But the son pleaded so hard that the king gave in, and the prince thought to himself, “If I bring my father this water, he will make me the sole heir to his kingdom.”

So he set out, and after he had traveled for some time he came to a deep valley hemmed in by rocks and woods. Looking around, he saw a little ugly dwarf standing on a rock above him, wearing a sugarloaf cap and a scarlet cloak. The dwarf called down to him, “Prince, where are you off to in such a hurry?” “What business is that of yours, you ugly imp?” the prince said haughtily, and rode on.

The dwarf was furious at this rudeness and cast a fairy spell of bad luck on him. As the prince rode on, the mountain pass grew narrower and narrower, until at last it was so tight that he couldn’t take another step forward. When he tried to turn his horse around and go back the way he had come, a loud laugh rang out all around him, and he found the path closed off behind him, so that he was shut in on every side. Next he tried to get off his horse and make his way on foot, but again the laugh rang in his ears, and he found he couldn’t move a single step. So he had no choice but to stay there, held by the spell.

Meanwhile the old king lingered on, hoping every day for his son’s return, until at last the second son said, “Father, I’ll go and look for the Water of Life.” For he thought, “My brother must be dead, and the kingdom will come to me if I find the water.” The king was very reluctant at first to let him go, but in the end he gave way. So the second son set out along the same road his brother had taken, and he met the same elf, who stopped him at the same place in the mountains and said, as before, “Prince, prince, where are you off to in such a hurry?” “Mind your own business, you busybody!” said the prince scornfully, and rode on.

But the dwarf put the same spell on him that he had put on his older brother, and he, too, ended up trapped in the heart of the mountains. That is how it goes with proud, foolish people who think they are above everyone else and are too proud to ask for advice or accept it.

After the second prince had been gone a long time, the youngest son said he would go and search for the Water of Life, and he was sure he would soon be able to make his father well again. So he set out, and the dwarf met him too, at the same spot in the valley among the mountains, and said, “Prince, where are you off to in such a hurry?” The prince answered, “I’m looking for the Water of Life, because my father is ill and close to death. Can you help me? Please be kind and help me if you can!” “Do you know where to find it?” asked the dwarf. “No,” said the prince, “I don’t. Please tell me, if you know.” “Then, since you have spoken to me kindly and have the sense to ask for advice, I will tell you how and where to go. The water you want flows from a well in an enchanted castle. So that you can reach it safely, I will give you an iron wand and two small loaves of bread. Strike the iron door of the castle three times with the wand, and it will open. Inside, two hungry lions will be lying with their jaws open, waiting for prey, but if you throw them the bread, they will let you pass. Then hurry to the well and take some of the Water of Life before the clock strikes twelve, because if you stay any longer, the door will shut on you forever.”

The prince thanked his little friend in the scarlet cloak for his help. He took the wand and the bread and traveled on and on, over sea and over land, until he reached the end of his journey and found everything just as the dwarf had said. The door flew open at the third stroke of the wand, and once the lions were calmed he went on through the castle and came at last to a beautiful hall. In it he saw several knights sitting in a trance, and he pulled off their rings and put them on his own fingers. In another room he saw a sword and a loaf of bread lying on a table, and he took those too. Farther on he came to a room where a beautiful young lady sat on a couch. She welcomed him joyfully and said that if he freed her from the spell that bound her, the kingdom would be his, provided he came back in a year and married her. Then she told him that the well holding the Water of Life was in the palace gardens, and she urged him to hurry and draw what he needed before the clock struck twelve.

He walked on, and as he passed through beautiful gardens he came to a lovely, shady spot with a couch in it. Feeling tired, he thought he would rest a while and gaze at the lovely scenery around him. So he lay down, and sleep overtook him without his noticing, and he didn’t wake until the clock was striking a quarter to twelve. He jumped up from the couch, horribly frightened, ran to the well, filled a cup that stood beside him with water, and rushed to get out in time. Just as he was passing through the iron door, the clock struck twelve, and the door slammed shut so fast that it snapped off a piece of his heel.

Once he was safe, he was overjoyed to have the Water of Life, and as he headed homeward he passed the little dwarf again. When the dwarf saw the sword and the loaf, he said, “You have won a fine prize. With the sword you can cut down whole armies in a single blow, and the bread will never run out.” Then the prince thought, “I can’t go home to my father without my brothers.” So he said, “My dear friend, can you tell me where my two brothers are? They set out to find the Water of Life before I did, and they never came back.” “I have trapped them by a charm between two mountains,” said the dwarf, “because they were proud and badly behaved, and they scorned to ask for advice.” The prince pleaded so hard for his brothers that the dwarf finally freed them, though unwillingly, saying, “Beware of them, for they have wicked hearts.” Their brother, however, was very glad to see them, and he told them everything that had happened to him: how he had found the Water of Life and taken a cupful of it, how he had freed a beautiful princess from the spell that bound her, and how she had promised to wait a whole year and then marry him and give him the kingdom.

Then the three of them rode on together, and on the way home they came to a country devastated by war and a terrible famine, so that everyone feared they would all die of want. The prince gave the king of that land the bread, and his whole kingdom ate from it. He also lent the king the wonderful sword, and the king used it to destroy the enemy’s army, and so the kingdom was at peace again and had plenty to eat. In the same way he helped two other countries they passed through on the road.

When they reached the sea, they boarded a ship. During the voyage the two older brothers said to each other, “Our brother has found the water that we couldn’t find. So our father will cast us off and give him the kingdom, which is rightfully ours.” They were consumed with envy and a hunger for revenge, and they agreed together on how to ruin him. They waited until he was fast asleep, then poured the Water of Life out of his cup and kept it for themselves, filling his cup with bitter seawater instead.

When they reached home, the youngest son brought his cup to the sick king so that he could drink and be healed. But he had barely tasted the bitter seawater when he grew even worse than before. Then the two older sons came in and accused the youngest of what they themselves had done. They claimed that he meant to poison their father, and that they were the ones who had found the Water of Life and brought it back. The moment the king began to drink what they gave him, he felt his sickness leave him, and he was as strong and well as in his youth. Then the two went to their brother and laughed at him. “So, brother, you found the Water of Life, did you?” they said. “You did the work, and we get the reward. With all your cleverness, why couldn’t you keep your eyes open? Next year one of us will take your beautiful princess away, if you don’t watch out. You’d better not say a word of this to our father, because he doesn’t believe anything you say. And if you tell tales, you’ll lose your life as well. Keep quiet, and we’ll let you off.”

The old king was still furious with his youngest son. He believed the boy had truly meant to take his life, so he summoned his court and asked what should be done, and everyone agreed that the prince must die. The prince knew nothing of this until one day, when the king’s chief huntsman took him hunting. Alone with him in the forest, the prince noticed how sad the huntsman looked and asked, “My friend, what is wrong?” “I can’t tell you, and I don’t dare,” said the huntsman. But the prince pleaded with him. “Just tell me what it is,” he said, “and don’t worry that I’ll be angry. I will forgive you.” “Alas,” said the huntsman, “the king has ordered me to shoot you.” The prince flinched at this, then said, “Spare my life, and I’ll trade clothes with you. You can take my royal coat back to my father as proof, and give me your shabby one.” “Gladly,” said the huntsman. “I’m happy to save you, since I could never have shot you anyway.” So he took the prince’s coat, handed over his own shabby one, and walked away through the forest.

Some time later, three grand embassies arrived at the old king’s court, bringing rich gifts of gold and precious stones for his youngest son. They had been sent by the three kings to whom the prince had lent his sword and his loaf of bread, to rid them of their enemy and feed their people. This touched the old king’s heart. He began to think his son might be innocent after all, and he said to his court, “If only my son were still alive! How it grieves me that I had him killed!” “He is alive,” said the huntsman. “I’m glad I took pity on him. I let him go in peace and brought home his royal coat.” The king was overwhelmed with joy, and he announced throughout his whole kingdom that if his son would come back to court, he would forgive him.

In the meantime the princess was eagerly waiting for her deliverer to return. She had a road built leading up to her palace, made entirely of shining gold, and she told her courtiers that whoever came riding straight up that road to the gate was her true love, and they were to let him in. But anyone who rode beside the road, they could be sure, was not the right man, and they were to send him away at once.

Before long the eldest brother decided to hurry to the princess and claim that he was the one who had freed her, and that he should therefore have her as his wife, and the kingdom along with her. When he reached the palace and saw the golden road, he stopped to admire it. “It would be a shame to ride on such a beautiful road,” he thought, and he turned aside and rode along its right-hand edge. But when he got to the gate, the guards, who had watched which way he came, told him he could not be who he claimed to be, and that he should go on his way.

Soon afterward the second prince set off on the same errand. When he reached the golden road and his horse had put one hoof on it, he stopped to look, found it very beautiful, and said to himself, “What a shame it would be for anything to trample this!” So he too turned aside and rode along the left edge. But when he reached the gate, the guards said he was not the true prince, and that he too must go away. And away he went.

When a full year had gone by, the third brother came out of the forest where he had been hiding from his father’s anger, and set out to find his promised bride. He traveled along thinking of her the whole way, and rode so fast that he never even noticed what the road was made of. He simply rode his horse straight over it, and as he reached the gate it swung open. The princess welcomed him joyfully and declared that he was her deliverer, and would now be her husband and lord of the kingdom. When their first happiness at meeting had passed, the princess told him she had heard that his father had forgiven him and wanted him home. So before the wedding he went to see his father, and took her with him. He told the king everything: how his brothers had cheated and robbed him, and how he had put up with all those wrongs out of love for his father. The old king was furious and wanted to punish his wicked sons, but they got away. They boarded a ship and sailed off across the wide sea, and where they went, nobody knew and nobody cared.

Then the old king called his court together and invited his whole kingdom to the wedding of his son and the princess. Young and old, nobles and squires, gentle folk and common, all came at once when the summons went out. Among them came the friendly dwarf, in his sugarloaf hat and a new scarlet cloak.

The wedding was held, and the merry bells rang.
And all the good people, they danced and they sang,
And feasted and frolicked, I can’t say how long.

chapters.title: The Twelve Huntsmen
paragraphs: A king’s son once had a bride whom he loved dearly. One day, as he sat beside her, perfectly happy, word came that his father was sick and dying and wanted to see him one more time before the end. So he said to his beloved, “I have to go now and leave you. Here is a ring to remember me by. When I am king, I will come back and fetch you.” He rode off, and when he reached his father, the old man was gravely ill and close to death. He said, “Dear son, I wanted to see you once more before I die. Promise me you will marry the woman I choose,” and he named a certain king’s daughter as the intended wife. The son was so distressed that he hardly knew what he was saying. “Yes, dear father,” he answered, “it will be as you wish.” And with that, the king closed his eyes and died.

So after the son had been proclaimed king and the period of mourning was over, he had to keep the promise he had made to his father. He sent to ask for the king’s daughter in marriage, and she was promised to him. His first bride heard about it and grieved so much over his faithlessness that she nearly died. Her father asked her, “Dearest child, why are you so sad? You shall have whatever you want.” She thought for a moment and said, “Dear father, I want eleven girls who look exactly like me, in face, figure, and size.” Her father said, “If it can be done, you shall have your wish.” He had a search made through his whole kingdom, until eleven young women were found who matched his daughter exactly in face, figure, and size.

When they came to the king’s daughter, she had twelve identical huntsmen’s outfits made. The eleven girls had to put on huntsmen’s clothes, and she put on the twelfth suit herself. Then she said goodbye to her father and rode off with them to the court of the man she had once been promised to, whom she still loved so much. She asked whether he needed any huntsmen, and whether he would take all of them into his service. The king looked at her and did not recognize her, but they were such handsome fellows that he said yes, he would gladly take them. And so they became the king’s twelve huntsmen.

Now the king owned a lion, a marvelous animal, for it knew everything hidden and secret. One evening the lion said to the king, “You think you have twelve huntsmen?” “Yes,” said the king, “twelve huntsmen.” The lion went on, “You’re wrong. They are twelve girls.” “That can’t be true,” said the king. “How can you prove it?” “Oh, just have some peas scattered in the antechamber,” answered the lion, “and you’ll soon see. Men have a firm tread, so when they walk over peas, not one of them moves. But girls patter and skip and drag their feet, and the peas roll around.” The king liked the advice and had the peas scattered.

But one of the king’s servants was fond of the huntsmen. When he heard they were about to be tested, he went to them and told them everything. “The lion wants to make the king believe you are girls,” he said. The king’s daughter thanked him and told her girls, “Be strong, and step firmly on the peas.” The next morning, when the king summoned the twelve huntsmen and they entered the antechamber where the peas lay, they stepped so firmly and walked so steadily that not a single pea rolled or moved. After they had gone, the king said to the lion, “You lied to me. They walk just like men.” The lion said, “They were warned about the test, and they made themselves strong. Just have twelve spinning wheels brought into the antechamber. They’ll go over to them and take delight in them, which no man would do.” The king liked this advice too, and had the spinning wheels set up in the antechamber.

But the servant, who was still on the huntsmen’s side, went to them and revealed the plan. When they were alone, the king’s daughter said to her eleven girls, “Hold yourselves back, and don’t look at the spinning wheels.” The next morning, when the king called for his twelve huntsmen, they walked through the antechamber and never once glanced at the spinning wheels. The king said to the lion again, “You have deceived me. They are men, because they didn’t look at the spinning wheels.” The lion answered, “They kept themselves in check.” But the king no longer believed the lion.

The twelve huntsmen always rode behind the king when he went hunting, and his fondness for them kept growing. Then one day, while they were out hunting, word came that the king’s bride was on her way. When the true bride heard this, it hurt her so badly that her heart nearly broke, and she fell to the ground in a faint. The king thought something had happened to his dear huntsman. He ran to him, wanted to help, and pulled off his glove. Then he saw the ring he had given to his first bride, and when he looked into her face, he knew her. His heart was so moved that he kissed her, and when she opened her eyes he said, “You are mine, and I am yours, and nobody in the world can change that.” He sent a messenger to the other bride and begged her to go back to her own kingdom, because he already had a wife, and a man who has just found his old key has no need of a new one. Then the wedding was celebrated, and the lion was taken back into favor, because he had told the truth after all.

chapters.title: The King of the Golden Mountain
paragraphs: There was once a merchant who had one child, a son, so young he could barely run on his own. The merchant had two heavily loaded ships out at sea, with all his wealth aboard them, and he hoped to make great profits. Then news came that both ships were lost. From a rich man he suddenly became so poor that he had nothing left but one small plot of land. He often went there in the evening to walk and ease his mind a little of its troubles.

One day he was wandering along, lost in gloomy thought, brooding with little comfort on what he had been, what he was now, and what he was likely to become. All at once a little, rough-looking black dwarf stood in front of him. “Tell me, friend, why so sad?” he said to the merchant. “What weighs on you so deeply?” “I’d gladly tell you if you could help me,” said the merchant. “Who knows, I might,” said the little man. “Tell me what ails you, and perhaps you’ll find I can be of some use.” So the merchant told him how all his wealth had gone to the bottom of the sea, and how he had nothing left but that little plot of land. “Oh, don’t trouble yourself about that,” said the dwarf. “Just promise to bring me here, twelve years from now, whatever meets you first when you go home, and I’ll give you as much as you like.” The merchant thought this was no great thing to ask. It would most likely be his dog or his cat or some such creature, but he forgot his little boy Heinel. So he agreed to the bargain, and signed and sealed a bond promising to do as he was asked.

But as he came near home, his little boy was so glad to see him that he crept up behind him, grabbed hold of his legs, and looked up in his face, laughing. The father started, trembling with fear and horror, for he saw what he had bound himself to do. Still, since no gold had arrived, he comforted himself with the thought that the dwarf was only playing a joke on him, and that, in any case, when the money did come, he would see who brought it and refuse to accept it.

About a month later he went upstairs to a lumber room to look for some old iron to sell, so that he could raise a little money. There, instead of iron, he found a huge pile of gold lying on the floor. He was overjoyed at the sight, and forgetting all about his son, he went back into trade and became an even richer merchant than before.

Meanwhile little Heinel grew up, and as the twelve years drew to a close, the merchant began to remember his bond and grew sad and thoughtful, so that worry and sorrow showed on his face. One day the boy asked what was the matter, but for a long time his father would not say. At last he told him that, without realizing it, he had sold him for gold to a small, ugly, black dwarf, and that the twelve years were nearly up, when he must keep his word. Then Heinel said, “Father, don’t trouble yourself much about that. I’ll be too much for the little man.”

On the appointed day, father and son went out together to the agreed spot. The son drew a circle on the ground and had himself and his father stand in the middle of it. Before long the little black dwarf arrived. He circled round and round, but he could find no way in, and he either couldn’t or didn’t dare to leap across.
