Finally the boy spoke up. “Do you have something to say to us, my friend, or what is it you want?” Heinel, you see, had a friend in a kind fairy who was fond of him and had told him what to do, since she knew what good fortune lay ahead of him. “Have you brought me what you promised?” the dwarf asked the merchant. The old man kept silent, but Heinel asked again, “What do you want here?” The dwarf answered, “I’ve come to speak with your father, not with you.” “You have tricked and cheated my father,” said the son. “Give him back his bond right now.” “Gently, gently,” said the little old man. “Right is right. I paid my money, and your father took it and spent it, so be good enough to hand over what I paid it for.” “First you’ll need my consent,” said Heinel, “so please step in here and we’ll talk it over.” The old man grinned and bared his teeth, as though he’d have been delighted to get into the circle if he could. In the end, after a long discussion, they reached an agreement. Heinel consented that his father must give him up, and so far the dwarf got his way. But the fairy had told Heinel what fortune awaited him if he followed his own course, and he had no wish to be handed over to his hump-backed friend, who seemed so eager for his company.

To settle the matter with something like a draw, they agreed that Heinel would be put into an open boat lying on the shore close by, that his father would push him off with his own hand, and that he would be set adrift, left to the good or bad luck of wind and weather. Heinel said goodbye to his father and got into the boat. Before it had gone far, though, a wave hit it and it tipped, sinking low on one side. The merchant believed poor Heinel was lost and went home in deep sorrow, while the dwarf went off, thinking he had at least had his revenge.

The boat did not sink after all, because the good fairy looked after her friend and soon lifted it upright again, and it sailed on safely. The young man sat unharmed inside until at last the boat ran aground on an unknown land. As he leaped ashore, he saw a beautiful castle ahead of him, but it was empty and gloomy inside, for it was enchanted. “Here,” he said to himself, “I must find the prize the good fairy told me about.” So he searched the whole palace through once more, until at last he found a white snake coiled up on a cushion in one of the rooms.

Now, the white snake was an enchanted princess, and she was overjoyed to see him. “Have you finally come to set me free?” she said. “For twelve long years I have waited here for the fairy to bring you, as she promised, because only you can save me. Tonight twelve men will come. Their faces will be black and they will wear chain mail. They will ask what you are doing here, but give no answer. Let them do what they like, whether they beat you, whip you, pinch you, prick you or torture you, and bear it all. Only don’t speak a word, and at twelve o’clock they will have to leave. The second night twelve more will come, and the third night twenty-four, who will even cut off your head. But at the twelfth hour of that night their power will end, and I will be free. Then I will come and bring you the Water of Life, wash you with it, and restore you to life and health.” Everything happened just as she had said. Heinel endured it all and did not say a word, and on the third night the princess came and threw her arms around his neck and kissed him. Joy and gladness broke out all through the castle, the wedding was celebrated, and he was crowned king of the Golden Mountain.

They lived together very happily, and the queen had a son. Eight years went by like this, and then the king began to think of his father and to long to see him again. The queen was against his going. “I know well that misfortune will fall on us if you go,” she said. But he gave her no peace until she gave in. As he left, she gave him a wishing-ring and said, “Take this ring and put it on your finger. It will bring you whatever you wish for. Only promise me that you will never use it to bring me from here to your father’s house.” He promised to do as she asked, put the ring on his finger, and wished himself near the town where his father lived.

In a moment Heinel was standing at the town gates, but the guards wouldn’t let him in because his clothes were so strange. So he climbed a nearby hill where a shepherd lived, borrowed the man’s old smock, and walked into town unrecognized that way. When he reached his father’s house, he said he was the merchant’s son, but the merchant refused to believe it. He said he had only ever had one son, his poor Heinel, who he knew had died long ago. Since the man was dressed like a poor shepherd, the merchant wouldn’t even give him anything to eat. The king kept insisting that he was his son. “Is there no mark by which you would know me, if I really am your son?” he asked. “Yes,” said his mother, “our Heinel had a mark like a raspberry on his right arm.” Then he showed them the mark, and they knew he had told the truth.

Next he told them that he was king of the Golden Mountain, that he was married to a princess, and that they had a son seven years old. But the merchant said, “That can never be true. He must be a fine king indeed, going about in a shepherd’s smock!” This made the son angry, and forgetting his promise, he turned the ring and wished for his queen and son. In an instant they were standing in front of him. But the queen wept and said that he had broken his word and bad luck would follow. He did everything he could to comfort her, and in the end she seemed to calm down. She was not calm at all, however, and was only thinking about how to punish him.

One day he took her for a walk outside the town and showed her the place where the boat had been set adrift on the wide waters. Then he sat down and said, “I’m very tired. Sit beside me. I’ll rest my head in your lap and sleep for a while.” But as soon as he was asleep, she slipped the ring off his finger and crept quietly away, and she wished herself and her son back home in their own kingdom. When he woke up he found himself alone, and he saw that the ring was gone from his finger. “I can never go back to my father’s house,” he said. “They would call me a sorcerer. I will travel out into the world until I come to my kingdom again.”

With these words he set off and walked until he came to a hill where three giants were dividing their father’s belongings. When they saw him go by, they called out, “Little men have sharp wits. He can divide the goods between us.” There was a sword that cut off an enemy’s head whenever its wearer spoke the words “Heads off!”, a cloak that made its owner invisible or gave him any shape he liked, and a pair of boots that carried the wearer wherever he wished. Heinel said they must first let him try out these wonderful things, so that he would know how to put a value on them. They gave him the cloak, and he wished himself a fly, and in a moment he was a fly. “The cloak is fine,” he said. “Now give me the sword.” “No,” they said, “not unless you promise not to say ‘Heads off!’, because if you do, we are all dead men.” So they gave it to him, telling him to try it on a tree. Next he asked for the boots too, and the moment he had all three in his hands, he wished himself at the Golden Mountain, and there he was at once. And so the giants were left with no goods to divide or quarrel over.

As Heinel drew near his castle, he heard cheerful music, and the people nearby told him that his queen was about to marry another husband. So he wrapped his cloak around himself, walked through the castle hall, and stood beside the queen where no one could see him. Whenever food was placed on her plate, he took it away and ate it himself, and whenever a glass of wine was handed to her, he took it and drank it. So although they kept serving her meat and drink, her plate and cup were always empty.

At this, fear and remorse came over her. She went to her room alone and sat there weeping, and he followed her. “Alas!” she said to herself. “Was I not set free once? Then why does this enchantment still seem to hold me?”

“False and fickle one!” he said. “Yes, someone did come who set you free, and he is near you again now. But how have you treated him? Did he deserve such treatment from you?” Then he went out, sent the guests away, and declared the wedding over, because he had come back to his kingdom. But the princes, nobles and great men laughed at him. He would not argue with them, though, and simply asked whether they would leave in peace or not. At that they turned on him and tried to seize him, but he drew his sword. “Heads off!” he cried, and at the word the traitors’ heads fell at his feet, and Heinel was king of the Golden Mountain once more.

chapters.title: Doctor Knowall
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a poor peasant named Crabb, who drove a load of wood into town with two oxen and sold it to a doctor for two talers. As the money was being counted out to him, the doctor happened to be sitting at table, and when the peasant saw how well he ate and drank, his heart longed for what he saw, and he wished he could be a doctor too. So he stood there for a while, and finally asked whether he too could become a doctor. “Oh, yes,” said the doctor, “that’s easily done.” “What do I have to do?” asked the peasant. “First, buy yourself an A B C book, the kind with a rooster on the first page. Second, turn your cart and your two oxen into money, and get yourself some clothes and whatever else belongs to medicine. Third, have a sign painted that says ‘I am Doctor Knowall,’ and have it nailed up over your front door.” The peasant did everything he had been told. After he had practiced as a doctor for a short while, a rich and powerful lord had some money stolen. He was told about Doctor Knowall, who lived in such-and-such a village and must know what had become of the money. So the lord had the horses hitched to his carriage, drove out to the village, and asked Crabb whether he was Doctor Knowall. Yes, he said, he was. Then he was to come with the lord and get back the stolen money. “Oh, yes, but Grete, my wife, has to come too.” The lord agreed, gave both of them seats in the carriage, and they all drove off together. When they arrived at the nobleman’s castle, the table was set, and Crabb was told to sit down and eat. “Yes, but my wife, Grete, too,” he said, and he sat down at the table with her. When the first servant came in with a dish of fine food, the peasant nudged his wife and said, “Grete, that was the first,” meaning the servant who brought the first dish. The servant, however, thought he meant “That is the first thief,” and since he really was one, he was terrified. He said to his fellow servant outside, “The doctor knows everything. We’re in trouble. He said I was the first.” The second servant did not want to go in at all, but he was forced to. When he went in with his dish, the peasant nudged his wife and said, “Grete, that is the second.” This servant was just as alarmed and got out as fast as he could. The third did no better, for the peasant again said, “Grete, that is the third.” The fourth had to carry in a covered dish, and the lord told the doctor to show his skill and guess what was under the cover. There were crabs in it, in fact. The doctor looked at the dish, had no idea what to say, and cried, “Ah, poor Crabb.” When the lord heard that, he cried, “There! He knows it! Then he must also know who has the money!”

At this the servants looked terribly uneasy, and they signaled to the doctor that they wanted him to step outside for a moment. When he went out, all four of them confessed that they had stolen the money. They said they would gladly give it back and pay him a large sum besides, if he would not expose them, because if he did they would be hanged. They led him to the place where the money was hidden. The doctor was satisfied with this, went back into the hall, sat down at the table, and said, “My lord, now I will search in my book to find where the gold is hidden.” The fifth servant, however, had crept into the stove to find out whether the doctor knew even more. The doctor sat still and opened his A B C book, flipped the pages back and forth, and looked for the rooster. Since he couldn’t find it right away, he said, “I know you’re in there, so you had better come out!” The fellow in the stove thought the doctor meant him, and in a panic he jumped out, crying, “That man knows everything!” Then Doctor Knowall showed the lord where the money was, but did not say who had stolen it. He received a great deal of money as a reward from both sides, and became a famous man.

chapters.title: The Seven Ravens
paragraphs: Once there was a man who had seven sons, and last of all a daughter. The little girl was very pretty, but she was so weak and tiny that they thought she would not live, and they said she should be baptized at once.

The father sent one of his sons running to the spring for water, and the other six ran along with him. Each of them wanted to be the first to fill his pitcher, and in their rush all seven dropped their pitchers into the well. There they stood, looking at one another like fools, with no idea what to do, because none of them dared go home. Meanwhile the father grew restless and couldn’t think what was keeping the boys so long. “Surely,” he said, “all seven of them have lost track of time over some game.” And when he had waited longer still and they hadn’t come, he flew into a rage and wished them all turned into ravens. He had barely finished speaking when he heard a croaking overhead. He looked up and saw seven coal-black ravens circling round and round. He was sorry to see his wish come true, but he didn’t know how to undo what was done, and so he consoled himself as best he could for the loss of his seven sons with his dear little daughter, who soon grew stronger and more beautiful every day.

For a long time she had no idea she ever had brothers, since her father and mother were careful never to mention them in front of her. But one day she happened to overhear some people talking about them. “Yes,” they said, “she is beautiful, all right, but it’s a shame her brothers were lost because of her.” This upset her terribly, and she went to her father and mother and asked whether she had any brothers and what had happened to them. They didn’t dare hide the truth from her any longer. They told her it had been the will of Heaven, and that her birth was only the innocent cause. But the little girl grieved over it every day and felt she had to do everything she could to bring her brothers back. She had no peace or rest until at last, one day, she slipped away and set out into the wide world to find her brothers, wherever they might be, and to set them free, whatever it cost her.

She took nothing with her except a little ring from her father and mother, a loaf of bread in case she got hungry, a little pitcher of water in case she got thirsty, and a little stool to sit on when she got tired. So she walked on and on until she reached the end of the world. She came to the sun, but the sun was far too hot and fiery, so she hurried off to the moon. The moon was cold and chilly, and it said, “I smell flesh and blood around here!” So she left in a hurry and came to the stars. The stars were friendly and kind to her, and each star sat on his own little stool. The morning star stood up and gave her a small piece of wood, saying, “Without this piece of wood you can’t unlock the castle on the glass mountain, and that is where your brothers live.” The little girl took the piece of wood, wrapped it up in a cloth, and went on until she reached the glass mountain and found the door locked. She felt for the piece of wood, but when she unwrapped the cloth it wasn’t there. She had lost the gift of the good stars. What was she to do? She wanted to save her brothers, and she had no key to the castle on the glass mountain. So this faithful little sister took a knife from her pocket and cut off her little finger, which was just the size of the piece of wood she had lost. She pushed it into the lock, and the door opened.

As she stepped inside, a little dwarf came up to her and asked, “What are you looking for?” “I’m looking for my brothers, the seven ravens,” she answered. The dwarf said, “My masters aren’t at home, but if you’d like to wait until they come back, please come in.” The little dwarf was just preparing their dinner. He brought their food on seven little plates and their drink in seven little glasses and set them on the table. Their sister ate a small bite from each little plate and drank a small sip from each little glass, but into the last glass she dropped the ring she had brought with her.

Suddenly there was a fluttering and croaking in the air, and the dwarf announced, “My masters are coming.” They came in hungry and thirsty and hunted for their little plates and glasses. One after another, they said,
“Who has eaten from my little plate? And who has been drinking from my little glass?”

“Caw! Caw! it seems to me
Human lips have been here, I see.”

When the seventh raven reached the bottom of his glass and found the ring there, he looked at it and recognized it as his father’s and mother’s. He said, “If only our little sister would come! Then we would be free.” The little girl had been standing behind the door the whole time, listening. When she heard this, she ran forward, and in an instant all the ravens took their true shape again. They hugged and kissed one another, and they all went happily home.

chapters.title: Wedding of Mrs Fox: First Story
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was an old fox with nine tails who suspected that his wife wasn’t faithful to him, and he decided to test her. He stretched out under the bench, didn’t move a muscle, and acted as if he were stone dead. Mrs Fox went up to her room and locked herself in, while her maid, Miss Cat, sat by the fire and did the cooking. Once word got around that the old fox was dead, suitors started to appear. The maid heard someone at the front door, knocking. She went and opened it, and there stood a young fox, who said,

“What are you up to, Miss Cat?
Are you asleep, or are you awake?”
She answered,

“I’m not asleep, I’m awake,
Want to know what I’m making?
I’m heating beer with butter in it,
Will you be my supper guest?”
“No, thank you, miss,” said the fox. “What is Mrs Fox doing?” The maid replied,

“She sits up in her room,
Crying in her gloom,
Weeping her little eyes red,
Because old Mr Fox is dead.”
“Please tell her, miss, that a young fox is here and would like to court her.” “Certainly, young sir.”

The cat goes up the stairs, trip, trap,
At the door she goes tap, tap, tap,
“Mistress Fox, are you in there?”
“Oh yes, my little cat,” she cried.
“A suitor is standing at the door.”
“And what does he look like, dear?”
“Does he have nine beautiful tails, like the late Mr Fox?” “Oh no,” answered the cat, “he has only one.” “Then I won’t have him.”

Miss Cat went downstairs and sent the suitor away. Soon there was another knock, and another fox stood at the door who wanted to court Mrs Fox. He had two tails, but he fared no better than the first. More came after that, each with one more tail than the one before, and all of them were turned away, until at last one came who had nine tails, just like old Mr Fox. When the widow heard this, she said happily to the cat,

“Now throw the gates and doors wide open,
And carry old Mr Fox right out.”
But just as the wedding was about to begin, old Mr Fox stirred under the bench, beat the whole rabble with a stick, and drove them and Mrs Fox out of the house.

chapters.title: Wedding of Mrs Fox: Second Story
paragraphs: After old Mr Fox died, a wolf came to court the widow. He knocked at the door, and the cat, who was Mrs Fox’s servant, opened it for him. The wolf greeted her and said,

“Good day, Mrs Cat of Kehrewit,
Why do you sit here all alone?
What good thing are you cooking?”
The cat replied,

“I’m crumbling sweet bread into milk,
Will you be my guest and eat?”
“No, thank you, Mrs Cat,” answered the wolf. “Isn’t Mrs Fox at home?”
The cat said,

“She sits upstairs in her room,
Mourning over her sorry doom,
Mourning her troubles, deep and sore,
For old Mr Fox is no more.”
The wolf answered,

“If she wants a husband now,
Would she kindly come down and see?”
The cat runs quickly up the stairs,
Her tail flying here and there,
Until she reaches the parlor door.
With her five gold rings she knocks at the door:
“Are you in there, good Mistress Fox?
If you want a husband now,
Would you kindly come down and see?”
Mrs Fox asked, “Is the gentleman wearing red stockings, and does he have a pointed mouth?” “No,” answered the cat. “Then he’s no good for me.”

After the wolf left, a dog came, then a stag, a hare, a bear, a lion, and all the beasts of the forest, one after another. But each of them lacked one of the good qualities old Mr Fox had had, and the cat had to keep sending the suitors away. At last a young fox came. Then Mrs Fox said, “Is the gentleman wearing red stockings, and does he have a little pointed mouth?” “Yes,” said the cat, “he does.” “Then let him come upstairs,” said Mrs Fox, and she told the servant to get the wedding feast ready.

“Sweep the room as clean as you can,
Open the window, throw out my old man!
He brought home many a fat mouse, it’s true,
But never a thought for his wife he knew,
He gobbled up every one he caught.”
Then the wedding was held with young Mr Fox, and there was great celebration and dancing. And if they haven’t stopped, they’re dancing still.

chapters.title: The Salad
paragraphs: A cheerful young huntsman was walking briskly through a wood when a little old woman came up to him and said, “Good day, good day. You look cheerful enough, but I am hungry and thirsty. Please give me something to eat.” The huntsman felt sorry for her, reached into his pocket, and gave her what he had. Then he wanted to be on his way, but she held on to him and said, “Listen, my friend, to what I’m about to tell you. I will repay you for your kindness. Go on your way, and after a while you will come to a tree where nine birds sit on a cloak. Shoot into the middle of them and one will fall down dead, and the cloak will fall with it. Take it. It is a wishing-cloak, and when you wear it you will find yourself at any place you wish to be. Cut open the dead bird, take out its heart, and keep it, and every morning when you get up you will find a piece of gold under your pillow. It is the bird’s heart that will bring you this good luck.”

The huntsman thanked her and thought to himself, “If all this really happens, it will be a fine thing for me.” After about a hundred steps he heard screeching and chirping in the branches above him. He looked up and saw a flock of birds pulling at a cloak with their beaks and claws, screaming, fighting, and tugging at one another as if each wanted it for himself. “Well,” said the huntsman, “this is amazing. It’s happening just as the old woman said.” Then he shot into the middle of them, so that feathers flew everywhere. The flock flew off, chattering, but one bird fell down dead, and the cloak with it. Then the huntsman did as the old woman had told him: he cut open the bird, took out the heart, and carried the cloak home with him.

The next morning when he woke up, he lifted his pillow, and there lay the piece of gold, glittering underneath. The same thing happened the next day, and in fact every day when he got up. He piled up a great deal of gold, and finally he thought to himself, “What good is this gold to me while I stay at home? I’ll go out into the world and have a look around.”

So he said goodbye to his friends, hung his bag and bow around his neck, and went on his way. One day it happened that his road led through a thick wood, and at the end of it stood a large castle in a green meadow. At one of the windows an old woman stood looking out, with a very beautiful young lady beside her. The old woman was a witch, and she said to the young lady, “There’s a young man coming out of the wood who is carrying a wonderful prize. We must get it away from him, my dear child, because it suits us better than it suits him. He has a bird’s heart that brings a piece of gold under his pillow every morning.” Meanwhile the huntsman came closer, looked at the lady, and said to himself, “I’ve been traveling so long that I’d like to go into this castle and rest, since I have money enough to pay for anything I need.” But the real reason was that he wanted to see more of the beautiful lady. So he went into the house and was kindly welcomed, and before long he was so much in love that he thought of nothing but gazing into the lady’s eyes and doing whatever she wished. Then the old woman said, “Now is the time to get the bird’s heart.” So the lady stole it from him, and he never found any more gold under his pillow, because it now lay under the young lady’s, and the old woman took it away every morning. But he was so much in love that he never missed his prize.

“Well,” said the old witch, “we have the bird’s heart, but not the wishing-cloak yet, and we have to get that too.” “Let’s leave him that,” said the young lady. “He has already lost his wealth.” The witch grew very angry and said, “A cloak like that is a rare and wonderful thing, and I must and will have it.” So she did as the old woman told her: she sat down at the window, looked out over the countryside, and seemed very sad. The huntsman asked, “Why are you so sad?” “Alas, dear sir,” she said, “over there lies the granite rock where all the precious diamonds grow. I want so badly to go there that whenever I think of it I can’t help being sad. But who can get there? Only the birds and the flies. Man cannot.” “If that’s all that troubles you,” said the huntsman, “I’ll gladly take you there.” So he drew her under his cloak, and the moment he wished to be on the granite mountain, they were both there. The diamonds glittered so on every side that they were delighted by the sight and picked up the finest ones. But the old witch cast a deep sleep over him, and he said to the young lady, “Let’s sit down and rest a little. I’m so tired I can’t stand any longer.” So they sat down, and he laid his head in her lap and fell asleep. While he slept, she took the cloak from his shoulders, hung it on her own, gathered up the diamonds, and wished herself home again.

He woke to find that his lady had tricked him and left him alone on the wild rock. “What roguery there is in this world!” he said, and he sat there in misery and fear, with no idea what to do. The rock was the home of fierce giants, and soon he saw three of them striding about. “My only hope is to pretend I’m asleep,” he thought, and he lay down as though he were sleeping soundly. The giants came up, and the first pushed him with his foot. “What’s this worm curled up here?” he said. “Stamp on him and kill him,” said the second. “Not worth the bother,” said the third. “Let him live. He’ll crawl higher up the mountain, and some cloud will roll in and carry him off.” And they moved on. But the huntsman had heard every word. As soon as they were gone, he climbed to the summit, and after he had sat there a little while, a cloud came rolling around him, swept him up in a whirlwind, and carried him along for some time, until it set down in a garden. He dropped softly to the ground among the greens and cabbages.

He looked around and said, “If I don’t find something to eat, I’ll be worse off than ever. I don’t see any apples or pears or fruit of any kind here, only vegetables.” Finally he told himself, “I could eat some salad. It would refresh me and give me strength.” So he picked a fine head and ate some of it. But he had barely swallowed two bites when he felt himself changing, and to his horror he saw that he had become a donkey. Still, he was very hungry, and the salad tasted good, so he kept eating until he reached a different kind of salad. He had hardly tasted it when another change came over him, and he saw, to his great luck, that he had his old shape back.

Then he lay down and slept off some of his weariness. The next morning when he woke, he picked a head each of the good salad and the bad, and he thought, “This will put me back on the road to fortune, and let me pay some people back for their treachery.” He set off to look for the castle of his friends, and after wandering for a few days he happened to find it. He stained his face brown all over, so that even his own mother would not have known him, then went into the castle and asked for a bed for the night. “I’m so tired I can’t go any farther,” he said. “Countryman,” said the witch, “who are you, and what brings you here?” “I’m a messenger,” he said. “The king sent me to find the finest salad that grows under the sun. I’ve been lucky enough to find it, and I have it with me. But the sun is so hot that it’s starting to wilt, and I don’t know whether I can carry it any farther.”

When the witch and the young lady heard about this wonderful salad, they were eager to taste it. “Dear countryman,” they said, “just let us have a taste.” “Of course,” he answered. “I have two heads of it with me, and I’ll give you one.” He opened his bag and handed them the bad one. The witch took it into the kitchen herself to be prepared. When it was ready, she couldn’t wait for it to be brought upstairs. She took a few leaves right away and put them in her mouth, and no sooner had she swallowed them than she lost her own shape and ran out into the courtyard, braying, as a donkey. Then the maid came into the kitchen, and when she saw the salad ready, she started to carry it up. On the way, though, she felt the same urge as the old woman to taste it, and she ate a few leaves. She too turned into a donkey and ran after the other, and the dish with the salad fell to the ground. All this time the messenger was sitting with the beautiful young lady. Since nobody came with the salad, and she was longing to taste it, she said, “I wonder where the salad is.” He guessed that something had happened and said, “I’ll go to the kitchen and see.” On his way he saw two donkeys running around in the courtyard, and the salad lying on the ground. “Good!” he said. “Those two have had their share.” He gathered up the rest of the leaves, put them on the dish, and brought them to the young lady. “I’ve brought the dish myself so you won’t have to wait any longer,” he said. She ate some, and like the others she ran off into the courtyard, braying.

Then the huntsman washed his face and went out into the courtyard so that they would recognize him. “Now you’ll pay for your roguery,” he said. He tied all three to a rope and led them along until he came to a mill, where he knocked at the window. “What is it?” said the miller. “I have three troublesome animals here,” said the huntsman. “If you’ll take them, give them food and a place to stay, and treat them the way I tell you, I’ll pay whatever you ask.” “Gladly,” said the miller, “but how am I to treat them?” The huntsman said, “Beat the old one three times a day and feed her hay once. Beat the next one, the maid, once a day and feed her hay three times. And the youngest, the beautiful lady, gets hay three times a day and no beatings.” He couldn’t bring himself to have her beaten. After that he went back to the castle, where he found everything he could want.

A few days later the miller came to him and said that the old donkey was dead. “The other two are alive and eating,” he said, “but they’re so miserable that they can’t last long.” The huntsman took pity on them. He told the miller to bring them back, and when they arrived, he gave them some of the good salad to eat. The beautiful young lady threw herself on her knees before him. “Dearest huntsman,” she said, “forgive me for all the harm I did you! My mother made me do it. It was against my will, for I always loved you dearly. Your wishing-cloak is hanging in the closet, and I’ll give you the bird’s heart as well.” But he said, “Keep it. It will come to the same thing, because I mean to make you my wife.” So they were married, and they lived happily together until they died.

chapters.title: The Story of the Youth Who Went Forth to Learn What Fear Was
paragraphs: A certain father had two sons. The elder was clever and sensible and could do anything, but the younger was stupid and couldn’t learn or understand a thing. When people saw him, they said, “That one will be a burden to his father!” Whenever there was work to be done, the elder son had to do it all. But if the father sent him for something late in the day, or in the middle of the night, and the way led through the churchyard or some other gloomy place, the younger would answer, “Oh no, father, I won’t go there. It makes me shudder!” He was afraid. And when stories were told by the fire at night that made people’s flesh creep, the listeners would often say, “Oh, it makes us shudder!” The younger son sat in his corner listening along with the rest and couldn’t imagine what they meant. “They keep saying, ‘It makes me shudder, it makes me shudder!’ It doesn’t make me shudder,” he thought. “That must be another skill I know nothing about!”

One day his father said to him, “Listen, you there in the corner. You’re getting big and strong, and you have to learn something to earn your living. Look how hard your brother works, while you don’t even earn your salt.” “Well, father,” he replied, “I’m quite willing to learn something. In fact, if it could be arranged, I’d like to learn how to shudder. I don’t understand that at all yet.” The elder brother smiled when he heard this and thought, “Good heavens, what a blockhead my brother is! He’ll never amount to anything as long as he lives! If you want to be a sickle, you have to start bending young.”
The father sighed and answered, “You’ll soon find out what it is to shudder, but you won’t earn a living by it.”

Soon afterward the sexton came to the house for a visit, and the father poured out his troubles, telling him how backward his younger son was in every way, knowing nothing and learning nothing. “Imagine,” he said, “when I asked him how he planned to earn his bread, he actually said he wanted to learn to shudder.” “If that’s all,” said the sexton, “he can learn it with me. Send him to me, and I’ll soon knock the rough edges off him.” The father was glad to agree, thinking, “It will do the boy some good.” So the sexton took him into his house, and the boy’s job was to ring the church bell. A day or two later, the sexton woke him at midnight and told him to get up, climb the church tower, and ring the bell. “You’ll soon learn what shuddering is,” the sexton thought. He slipped off secretly ahead of the boy. When the boy reached the top of the tower, turned around, and was about to take hold of the bell rope, he saw a white figure standing on the stairs across from the sounding hole. “Who’s there?” he called, but the figure gave no answer and didn’t move or stir. “Answer,” the boy called, “or get out of here. You have no business being here at night.”

The sexton, though, stood perfectly still so that the boy would take him for a ghost. The boy called out a second time, “What do you want here? Speak if you’re an honest man, or I’ll throw you down the steps!” The sexton thought, “He can’t mean it as badly as he says,” and he made no sound, standing as if he were made of stone. The boy called to him a third time, and when that did no good either, he charged at him and shoved the ghost down the stairs. It tumbled down ten steps and lay in a corner. Then the boy rang the bell, went home, and without a word got into bed and fell asleep. The sexton’s wife waited a long time for her husband, but he didn’t come back. At last she grew worried and woke the boy. “Do you know where my husband is?” she asked. “He went up the tower ahead of you.” “No, I don’t,” said the boy. “But someone was standing by the sounding hole across from the steps, and since he wouldn’t answer and wouldn’t go away, I took him for a scoundrel and threw him downstairs. Go and look, and you’ll see whether it was him. I’d be sorry if it was.” The woman ran off and found her husband lying in the corner, groaning. His leg was broken.

She carried him down, and then, screaming loudly, she hurried to the boy’s father. “Your boy,” she cried, “has caused a terrible disaster! He threw my husband down the steps and broke his leg. Get that good-for-nothing out of our house!” The father was horrified. He ran over and scolded the boy. “What wicked tricks are these?” he said. “The devil must have put them in your head.” “Father,” the boy replied, “please listen to me. I’m completely innocent. He was standing there in the night like someone planning something evil. I didn’t know who it was, and I begged him three times to either speak or leave.” “Ah,” said the father, “you bring me nothing but misery. Get out of my sight. I never want to see you again.”

“Yes, father, gladly. Just wait until daylight. Then I’ll go out and learn how to shudder, and at least I’ll have one skill to support me.” “Learn whatever you like,” said the father. “It’s all the same to me. Here are fifty talers. Take them and go out into the wide world, and don’t tell anyone where you come from or who your father is, because I have good reason to be ashamed of you.” “Yes, father, I’ll do as you say. If that’s all you ask, I can easily remember it.”

So when day broke, the boy put his fifty talers in his pocket and set out along the high road, saying to himself over and over, “If only I could shudder! If only I could shudder!” A man approached and overheard the youth talking to himself. When they had walked a bit farther, to a place where the gallows came into view, the man said to him, “Look, there’s the tree where seven men married the ropemaker’s daughter and are now learning to fly. Sit down under it and wait for night, and you’ll soon learn how to shudder.” “If that’s all it takes,” the youth answered, “it’s easily done. But if I learn to shudder that fast, you can have my fifty talers. Come back to me early in the morning.” The youth went to the gallows, sat down beneath it, and waited for evening. He was cold, so he built himself a fire. But at midnight the wind blew so hard that even with the fire he couldn’t get warm. The wind knocked the hanged men against one another, swinging them back and forth, and he thought, “If you’re shivering down here by the fire, how those up there must freeze and suffer!” Feeling sorry for them, he set up the ladder, climbed up, untied them one after another, and brought all seven down. Then he stirred up the fire, blew on it, and sat them all around it to warm themselves. But they sat there without moving, and the fire caught their clothes. So he said, “Be careful, or I’ll hang you up again.” The dead men didn’t hear him. They stayed silent and let their rags go on burning. That made him angry. “If you won’t be careful, I can’t help you,” he said. “I’m not going to burn along with you.” And he hung them up again, one by one. Then he sat down by his fire and fell asleep. The next morning the man came and wanted his fifty talers. “Well, do you know how to shudder now?” he asked. “No,” the youth answered. “How would I? Those fellows up there never opened their mouths, and they were so stupid they let the few old rags on their backs burn up.” The man saw that he wouldn’t get the fifty talers that day, and he went away saying, “I’ve never met a youth like this before.”

The young man moved on too, and again muttered to himself: “If only I could shudder! If only I could shudder!” A wagon driver walking close behind heard him and asked, “Who are you?” “I don’t know,” said the young man. “Where are you from?” “I don’t know that either.” “Who is your father?” “I’m not allowed to tell you.” “And what is it you keep mumbling under your breath?” “Oh,” the young man answered, “I want so badly to shudder, but nobody can teach me how.” “Enough of that silly talk,” said the driver. “Come along with me, and I’ll see about a place for you.” The young man went with him, and that evening they reached an inn where they meant to spend the night. In the doorway of the taproom the young man said again, quite loudly, “If only I could shudder! If only I could shudder!” The innkeeper heard it and laughed. “If that’s what you want,” he said, “you’ll find a fine chance for it here.” “Oh, hush,” said the innkeeper’s wife. “Plenty of nosy people have lost their lives already. It would be a pity and a shame if a pair of eyes as lovely as these never saw daylight again.”

But the young man said, “However hard it is, I’m going to learn it. That’s the very reason I set out from home.” He gave the innkeeper no peace until the man told him that not far away stood a haunted castle, where anyone could easily find out what shuddering was, if only he would keep watch there for three nights. The king had promised his daughter in marriage to anyone who dared to try, and she was the loveliest girl the sun ever shone on. The castle also held great treasures, guarded by evil spirits. Those treasures would be freed, and would make a poor man rich enough. Many men had already gone into the castle, but so far none had come out again. So the next morning the young man went to the king and said, “With your permission, I will gladly keep watch for three nights in the haunted castle.”

The king looked him over, and since he liked the young man, he said, “You may ask for three things to take into the castle with you, but they must be things that have no life.” He answered, “Then I ask for a fire, a lathe, and a carving bench with its knife.”

During the day the king had these things carried into the castle. As night came on, the young man went up and built himself a bright fire in one of the rooms. He set the carving bench and knife beside it and sat down at the lathe. “Oh, if only I could shudder!” he said. “But I won’t learn it here either.” Toward midnight he was about to stir up his fire, and as he was blowing on it, something suddenly cried out from a corner: “Meow, meow! We’re so cold!” “You fools!” he called. “What are you howling about? If you’re cold, come over, sit by the fire and warm yourselves.” No sooner had he said it than two huge black cats came bounding over in one great leap. They sat down on either side of him and glared at him wildly with their fiery eyes. After a little while, when they had warmed up, they said, “Friend, shall we play a game of cards?” “Why not?” he answered. “But first let me see your paws.” They stretched out their claws. “My,” he said, “what long nails you have! Hold on, I have to trim them for you first.” With that he grabbed them by the neck, laid them on the carving bench and clamped their paws tight. “I’ve taken a good look at your fingers,” he said, “and I’ve lost all taste for cards.” Then he beat them to death and threw them out into the water. But when he had finished off those two and was about to sit down by his fire again, black cats and black dogs with red-hot chains came swarming out of every hole and corner. More and more of them came, until he could not move. They howled dreadfully, jumped onto his fire, scattered it and tried to put it out. For a while he watched them calmly, but at last, when they were going too far, he grabbed his carving knife and shouted, “Get away, you vermin!” and started cutting them down. Some ran off, and the rest he killed and threw into the fish pond. When he came back, he blew the embers of his fire back to life and warmed himself. As he sat there, his eyes refused to stay open any longer, and he felt like sleeping. He looked around and saw a big bed in a corner. “Just what I need,” he said, and climbed in. But just as he was about to close his eyes, the bed began to move by itself and rolled through the whole castle. “Good,” he said. “Now go faster.” The bed raced along as though six horses were pulling it, up and down, over doorsills and stairs. Then suddenly, hop, hop, it flipped upside down and lay on top of him like a mountain. He heaved the quilts and pillows into the air, crawled out and said, “Now whoever wants to can do the driving.” He lay down by his fire and slept until daylight. In the morning the king arrived, and seeing him stretched out on the floor, he thought the evil spirits had killed him and that he was dead. “What a shame,” he said, “for such a handsome man.” The young man heard this, got up and said, “It hasn’t come to that yet.” The king was amazed, but very glad, and asked how he had fared. “Very well indeed,” he answered. “One night is over, and the other two will pass the same way.” Then he went to the innkeeper, who stared at him wide-eyed. “I never expected to see you alive again,” the man said. “Have you learned to shudder yet?” “No,” said the young man, “it’s all for nothing. If only somebody would tell me how!”

On the second night he went up into the old castle again, sat down by the fire and started in on his old refrain: “If only I could shudder!” At midnight a racket began, a noise of things tumbling around. It was soft at first, then grew louder and louder. After a quiet spell, half a man came down the chimney with a loud scream and dropped in front of him. “Hey!” he cried. “There’s another half that goes with that. This isn’t enough!” Then the racket started up again, with roaring and howling, and the other half fell down as well. “Wait,” he said, “I’ll build up the fire a bit for you.” When he had done so and looked around again, the two pieces had joined together, and a hideous man was sitting in his seat. “That wasn’t part of our deal,” said the young man. “The bench is mine.” The man tried to shove him off, but the young man would not stand for it. He pushed the man away with all his strength and sat back down in his own place. Then more men dropped down one after another. They had brought nine dead men’s legs and two skulls, and they set them up and played ninepins with them. The young man wanted to play too and said, “Say, can I join you?” “Yes, if you have money.” “Money enough,” he replied, “but your balls aren’t quite round.” He took the skulls, put them in the lathe and turned them until they were round. “There, now they’ll roll better!” he said. “Hooray! Now we’ll have some fun!” He played along and lost some of his money, but when the clock struck twelve, everything vanished from his sight. He lay down and went quietly to sleep. The next morning the king came to ask about him. “How did it go this time?” he asked. “I was playing ninepins,” the young man answered, “and I lost a couple of farthings.” “Didn’t you shudder, then?” “What?” he said. “I had a wonderful time! If only I knew what it was to shudder!”

On the third night he sat down on his bench again and said, quite gloomily, “If only I could shudder.” When it was late, six tall men came in carrying a coffin. “Ha, ha,” he said, “that must be my little cousin, who died just a few days ago.” He crooked his finger and called, “Come, little cousin, come here.” They set the coffin on the floor. He went over, took off the lid, and a dead man lay inside. He touched the face, and it was cold as ice. “Wait,” he said, “I’ll warm you up a little.” He went to the fire, warmed his hand and laid it on the dead man’s face, but the man stayed cold. So he lifted him out, sat down by the fire, set him on his chest and rubbed his arms to get the blood moving again. When that did no good either, he thought, “When two people lie in bed together, they warm each other.” He carried the dead man to the bed, covered him up and lay down beside him. After a while the dead man grew warm too and began to stir. “You see, little cousin,” said the young man, “didn’t I warm you up?” But the dead man got up and cried, “Now I’m going to strangle you.”

“What!” said the young man. “Is that how you thank me? Back into your coffin you go!” He picked him up, threw him in and shut the lid. Then the six men came and carried him away again. “I just can’t manage to shudder,” he said. “I’ll never learn it here, not as long as I live.”

Then a man came in who was taller than all the others and looked terrifying. He was old, though, and had a long white beard. “You wretch,” he cried, “you’re about to learn what it is to shudder, because you’re going to die.” “Not so fast,” the young man replied. “If I’m to die, I’ll have a say in it.” “I’ll have you in my grip in no time,” said the fiend. “Easy now, easy, don’t talk so big. I’m as strong as you are, maybe stronger.” “We’ll see about that,” said the old man. “If you’re stronger, I’ll let you go. Come, let’s test it.” He led him through dark passages to a blacksmith’s forge, took an axe and drove an anvil into the ground with a single blow. “I can do better than that,” said the young man, and he went to the other anvil. The old man stood close by to watch, and his white beard hung down. The young man grabbed the axe, split the anvil with one blow and caught the old man’s beard in the crack. “Now I’ve got you,” he said. “Now it’s your turn to die.” He seized an iron bar and beat the old man until he groaned and begged him to stop, promising him great riches if he did. The young man pulled out the axe and let him go. The old man led him back into the castle and showed him three chests full of gold in a cellar. “One share of this,” he said, “is for the poor, the second for the king, the third for you.” Just then the clock struck twelve, and the spirit vanished, leaving the young man standing in darkness. “I’ll still be able to find my way out,” he said. He felt around, found the way back to the room, and slept there by his fire. The next morning the king came and said, “Surely you’ve learned what shuddering is by now?” “No,” he answered. “What can it be? My dead cousin was here, and a bearded man came and showed me a pile of money down below, but nobody told me what it is to shudder.” “Then,” said the king, “you have saved the castle, and you shall marry my daughter.” “That’s all very well,” he said, “but I still don’t know what it is to shudder!”

Then the gold was brought up and the wedding was held. But no matter how much the young king loved his wife, and no matter how happy he was, he kept saying, “If only I could shudder, if only I could shudder.” In the end this made her angry. Her chambermaid said, “I’ll find a cure for him. He’ll soon learn what it is to shudder.” She went out to the stream that ran through the garden and had a whole bucketful of gudgeons brought to her. That night, while the young king slept, his wife was to pull the covers off him and pour the bucket of cold water and gudgeons over him, so that the little fish flopped all around him. He woke up and cried, “Oh, what is making me shudder so? What is making me shudder so, dear wife? Ah, now I know what it is to shudder!”

chapters.title: King Grisly-Beard
paragraphs: Far off in the East, a great king had a daughter of striking beauty. But she was so proud, so arrogant and so full of herself that not one of the princes who came courting was good enough for her, and she simply mocked them all.

One day the king gave a great feast and invited all her suitors. They sat in a row, arranged by rank: kings, princes, dukes, earls, counts, barons and knights. Then the princess came in, and as she passed along the row she had a spiteful remark for every one of them. The first was too fat. “He’s as round as a tub,” she said. The next was too tall. “What a maypole!” she said. The next was too short. “What a dumpling!” she said. The fourth was too pale, and she called him “Wallface.” The fifth was too red, so she called him “Coxcomb.” The sixth was not quite straight, so she said he was like a green stick that had been left to dry above a baker’s oven. And so she had a joke to crack about every one of them. But she laughed more than anyone at a good king who was there. “Look at him,” she said. “His beard is like an old mop. I’ll call him Grisly-beard.” And so the king got the nickname Grisly-beard.

But the old king was very angry when he saw how his daughter behaved and how she mistreated all his guests. He vowed that, whether she liked it or not, she would marry the first man to come to the door, be he prince or beggar.

Two days later a traveling fiddler came by and began to play under the window and beg for coins. When the king heard him, he said, “Let him come in.” They brought in a dirty-looking fellow, and when he had sung before the king and the princess, he asked for a reward. The king said, “You have sung so well that I will give you my daughter as your wife.” The princess begged and pleaded, but the king said, “I swore to give you to the first man who came, and I will keep my word.” Words and tears were no use. The parson was sent for, and she was married to the fiddler. When that was done, the king said, “Now get ready to leave. You can’t stay here. You must travel on with your husband.”

Then the fiddler set off and took her with him, and soon they came to a great forest. “Tell me,” she said, “whose forest is this?” “It belongs to King Grisly-beard,” he answered. “If you had taken him, it would all have been yours.” “Oh, what an unlucky wretch I am!” she sighed. “If only I had married King Grisly-beard!” Next they came to some fine meadows. “Whose are these beautiful green meadows?” she asked. “They belong to King Grisly-beard. If you had taken him, they would all have been yours.” “Oh, what an unlucky wretch I am!” she said. “If only I had married King Grisly-beard!”

Next they reached a great city. “Whose splendid city is this?” she asked. “It belongs to King Grisly-beard,” he said. “If you had taken him, it would all be yours now.” “Oh, what a wretch I am!” she sighed. “Why didn’t I marry King Grisly-beard?” “That’s no concern of mine,” said the fiddler. “Why should you want another husband? Am I not good enough for you?”

Finally they came to a tiny cottage. “What a miserable place!” she said. “Who owns this filthy little hole?” The fiddler answered, “It’s yours and mine. This is where we’ll live.” “Where are your servants?” she cried. “What would we do with servants?” he said. “You’ll do whatever needs doing yourself. Now light the fire, put the water on, and cook my supper. I’m very tired.” But the princess knew nothing about lighting fires or cooking, and the fiddler had to help her. After a very meager meal they went to bed, and early the next morning he woke her to clean the house. They lived like this for two days. When everything in the cottage had been eaten, the man said, “Wife, we can’t carry on like this, spending money and earning none. You must learn to weave baskets.” He went out, cut some willow branches, and brought them home. She began to weave, but it hurt her fingers badly. “I can see this work is no good,” he said. “Try spinning instead. Maybe you’ll be better at that.” So she sat down and tried to spin, but the thread cut her soft fingers until they bled. “Look at that,” said the fiddler. “You’re good for nothing. You can’t do any work at all. What a bargain I’ve made! Well, I’ll try setting up a business in pots and pans, and you can stand in the market and sell them.” “Oh no,” she sighed. “If anyone from my father’s court walks past and sees me standing in the market, how they’ll laugh at me!”

Her husband didn’t care about that. He said she had to work unless she wanted to starve. At first the business went well, because many people saw such a beautiful woman and bought her wares, paying without even thinking of taking the goods away. They lived off this as long as it lasted. Then her husband bought a new stock of pottery, and she settled down with it in a corner of the market. But soon a drunken soldier came along on his horse, rode straight into her stall, and smashed everything into a thousand pieces. She began to cry and had no idea what to do. “Oh, what will become of me?” she said. “What will my husband say?” She ran home and told him everything. “Who would ever have thought you could be so foolish,” he said, “as to set up a pottery stall in the corner of the market, where everybody walks by? But enough crying. I can see you’re not fit for this kind of work, so I went to the king’s palace and asked whether they needed a kitchen maid. They say they’ll take you, and there you’ll get plenty to eat.”
So the princess became a kitchen maid and helped the cook with all the dirtiest jobs. She was allowed to take home some of the leftover meat, and that was what they lived on.

She hadn’t been there long when she heard that the king’s eldest son was riding past on his way to be married. She went to one of the windows and looked out. Everything was ready, and all the splendor and glitter of the court was on display. She grieved bitterly then over the pride and foolishness that had brought her so low. The servants gave her some of the rich food, and she put it in her basket to take home.

Suddenly, just as she was leaving, the king’s son walked in, dressed in gold. When he saw a beautiful woman at the door, he took her by the hand and said she must dance with him. She shook with fear, because she saw that it was King Grisly-beard, who was making fun of her. But he held on tight and led her inside, and the lid of the basket came off, so that the food spilled all over the floor. Everyone laughed and jeered at her, and she was so ashamed that she wished she were a thousand feet underground. She dashed for the door to run away, but King Grisly-beard caught her on the steps and brought her back. “Don’t be afraid of me,” he said. “I am the fiddler who lived with you in the hut. I took you there because I truly loved you. I am also the soldier who overturned your stall. I did all of this only to cure you of your silly pride, and to show you how foolishly you had treated me. Now it’s all over. You have learned wisdom, and it’s time to hold our wedding feast.”

Then the chamberlains came and brought her the most beautiful dresses. Her father and his whole court had already arrived and welcomed her home to her wedding. There was joy on every face and in every heart. The feast was magnificent. They danced and sang, everyone was merry, and I only wish that you and I had been there too.

chapters.title: Iron Hans
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a king who owned a great forest near his palace, full of every kind of wild animal. One day he sent out a huntsman to shoot a roe deer for him, but the man never came back. “Perhaps something has happened to him,” said the king. The next day he sent out two more huntsmen to look for him, but they stayed away too. On the third day he summoned all his huntsmen and said, “Search the whole forest, and don’t give up until you have found all three.” But none of these came home either, and none was ever seen again. From then on nobody would dare to enter the forest. It lay there in deep stillness and solitude, and nothing could be seen of it except an eagle or a hawk now and then flying over. This went on for many years, until a huntsman nobody knew presented himself to the king, looking for a position, and offered to go into the dangerous forest. The king would not agree. “It isn’t safe in there,” he said. “I’m afraid you would do no better than the others, and you would never come out again.” The huntsman answered, “Sire, I’ll take the risk on myself. I don’t know what fear is.”

So the huntsman went off to the forest with his dog. Before long the dog picked up the scent of some game and wanted to chase it. But it had barely run two steps when it came to a deep pool and could go no farther. A naked arm reached up out of the water, seized the dog, and pulled it under. When the huntsman saw this, he went back and fetched three men with buckets to bail out the water. When they could see the bottom, there lay a wild man whose body was brown like rusty iron, and whose hair hung over his face and down to his knees. They tied him up with ropes and led him away to the castle. Everyone was astonished at the wild man. The king had him put in an iron cage in his courtyard and forbade anyone, on pain of death, to open the door, and the queen herself was to keep the key. From then on, everyone could safely go into the forest again.

The king had a son, eight years old, who was playing in the courtyard one day when his golden ball rolled into the cage. The boy ran over and said, “Give me my ball.” “Not until you open the door for me,” answered the man. “No,” said the boy. “I won’t do that. The king has forbidden it.” And he ran away. The next day he went again and asked for his ball. The wild man said, “Open my door,” but the boy refused. On the third day the king had ridden out to hunt, and the boy went once more and said, “I couldn’t open the door even if I wanted to, because I don’t have the key.” Then the wild man said, “It’s under your mother’s pillow. You can get it from there.” The boy, who wanted his ball back, threw every worry to the wind and brought the key. The door opened stiffly, and the boy pinched his fingers. Once it was open, the wild man stepped out, handed him the golden ball, and hurried off. The boy had grown frightened. He called and cried after him, “Oh, wild man, don’t go away, or I’ll be beaten!” The wild man turned back, picked him up, set him on his shoulder, and strode quickly into the forest. When the king came home, he noticed the empty cage and asked the queen how it had happened. She knew nothing about it and looked for the key, but it was gone. She called the boy, but nobody answered. The king sent people to search for him in the fields, but they didn’t find him. Then it was easy for him to guess what had happened, and great grief settled over the royal court.

When the wild man had reached the dark forest again, he lifted the boy down from his shoulder and said to him, “You will never see your father and mother again, but I’ll keep you with me, because you set me free and I feel pity for you. If you do everything I tell you, you’ll be well off. I have more treasure and gold than anyone in the world.” He made a bed of moss for the boy to sleep on. The next morning the man took him to a well and said, “Look, the golden well is as bright and clear as crystal. You are to sit beside it and make sure that nothing falls in, or it will be spoiled. I’ll come every evening to see whether you have obeyed my order.” The boy sat down at the edge of the well. Often he saw a golden fish or a golden snake appear in it, and he took care that nothing fell in. While he was sitting there, his finger began to hurt so badly that without meaning to he put it in the water. He pulled it out again quickly, but saw that it was completely gilded, and however hard he tried to wash the gold off, it was no use. In the evening Iron Hans came back, looked at the boy, and said, “What has happened to the well?” “Nothing, nothing,” he answered, and held his finger behind his back so the man wouldn’t see it. But Iron Hans said, “You dipped your finger in the water. This time I’ll let it pass, but make sure you never let anything fall in again.” At daybreak the boy was already sitting by the well, keeping watch. His finger hurt again, and he ran it over his head, and sadly, a hair fell into the well. He snatched it out quickly, but it was already completely gilded. Iron Hans came and knew right away what had happened. “You let a hair fall into the well,” he said. “I’ll allow you to watch over it one more time, but if it happens a third time, the well is spoiled and you can’t stay with me any longer.”

On the third day the boy sat by the well and didn’t move his finger, however much it hurt. But time dragged for him, and he looked at the reflection of his face on the surface of the water. As he leaned down further and further, trying to look straight into his own eyes, his long hair slid from his shoulders into the water. He straightened up quickly, but all the hair on his head had already turned to gold and shone like the sun. You can imagine how terrified the poor boy was! He took out his handkerchief and tied it around his head so the man wouldn’t see. When Iron Hans came, he already knew everything and said, “Take off the handkerchief.” Then the golden hair streamed out, and no matter how the boy tried to make excuses, it was useless. “You have failed the test and cannot stay here any longer. Go out into the world, and there you’ll learn what poverty is. But since you don’t have a bad heart, and since I mean well by you, there is one thing I’ll grant you. If you ever get into trouble, come to the forest and cry out ‘Iron Hans,’ and I will come and help you. My power is great, greater than you think, and I have gold and silver in plenty.”

Then the king’s son left the forest and walked on and on, over beaten paths and unbeaten ones, until at last he came to a great city. He looked for work there but found none, and he had learned nothing that could help him get by. In the end he went to the palace and asked whether they would take him in. The people at court had no idea what use they could make of him, but they liked him and told him to stay. Eventually the cook hired him and said he could carry wood and water and rake the cinders together. Once, when nobody else happened to be around, the cook ordered him to carry the food to the royal table. But because he didn’t want his golden hair to be seen, he kept his little cap on. Nothing like that had ever happened before in the king’s presence, and the king said, “When you come to the royal table, you must take your hat off.” He answered, “Ah, Sire, I can’t. I have a bad sore on my head.” Then the king had the cook summoned, scolded him, and asked how he could have taken on such a boy, and told him to send the boy away at once. The cook, however, felt sorry for him and swapped him for the gardener’s boy.

From then on the boy had to plant and water the garden, hoe and dig, and put up with the wind and every kind of weather. One summer day, when he was working alone out there, it was so hot that he took off his little cap to let the air cool his head. The sun struck his hair and made it glitter and flash, and the light reached into the king’s daughter’s bedroom. She jumped up to see what it was. She spotted the boy and called down to him, “Boy, bring me a wreath of flowers!” He pulled his cap back on as fast as he could, picked some wild flowers from the fields, and tied them together. As he was climbing the stairs with them, the gardener stopped him and said, “How can you bring the king’s daughter a garland of such ordinary flowers? Go back at once and get others. Look for the prettiest and the rarest.” “Oh, no,” the boy answered, “the wild ones smell sweeter, and she will like them better.” When he came into the room, the king’s daughter said, “Take off your cap. It isn’t proper to keep it on in front of me.” Again he said, “I can’t. My head is sore.” But she grabbed his cap and pulled it off, and his golden hair tumbled down over his shoulders, a wonderful sight. He tried to run out, but she held him by the arm and pressed a handful of ducats on him. He left with them, but he cared nothing for the gold. He took the coins to the gardener and said, “These are for your children. They can play with them.” The next day the king’s daughter called to him again and told him to bring her a wreath of field flowers. When he went in with it, she snatched at his cap at once and tried to take it from him, but he held on to it with both hands. Again she gave him a handful of ducats, and again he wouldn’t keep them, but gave them to the gardener as toys for his children. On the third day it all went the same way. She couldn’t get the cap off his head, and he wouldn’t take her money.

Not long after that, war broke out and the country was invaded. The king called his people together. He didn’t know whether he could stand against the enemy, who were stronger and had a mighty army. Then the gardener’s boy said, “I’m grown now, and I want to go to war too. Just give me a horse.” The others laughed and said, “Find one for yourself once we’re gone. We’ll leave one behind for you in the stable.” After they had marched off, he went to the stable and led the horse out. It was lame in one leg and went hobblety jib, hobblety jib, but he climbed on anyway and rode off toward the dark forest. At the edge of the trees he called “Iron Hans!” three times, so loudly that it rang through the woods. The wild man appeared at once and said, “What do you want?” “I need a strong horse, because I’m going to the war.” “You shall have it, and more than you ask.” Then the wild man went back into the forest. Before long a stable-boy came out leading a horse that snorted through its nostrils and could barely be held back. Behind them came a great troop of warriors, dressed from head to foot in iron, their swords flashing in the sun. The young man handed his three-legged horse over to the stable-boy, mounted the other, and rode at the head of the soldiers. By the time he neared the battlefield, a great many of the king’s men had already fallen, and the rest were close to giving way. The young man galloped in with his iron soldiers, swept over the enemy like a hurricane, and cut down everyone who stood against him. The enemy began to run, but he chased them and never stopped until not a single man was left. Instead of going back to the king, though, he led his troop along side paths to the forest and called out for Iron Hans. “What do you want?” asked the wild man. “Take back your horse and your soldiers, and give me my three-legged horse again.” Everything he asked for was done, and soon he was riding along on his three-legged horse. When the king came home to his palace, his daughter went out to meet him and congratulated him on his victory. “I’m not the one who won it,” he said. “A strange knight came to my aid with his soldiers.” The daughter wanted to know who the strange knight was, but the king couldn’t tell her. “He went after the enemy,” he said, “and I never saw him again.” She asked the gardener where his boy was. He smiled and said, “He’s just got home on his three-legged horse, and the others have been jeering at him and shouting, ‘Here comes our hobblety jib back again!’ They asked him, too, ‘What hedge were you sleeping under all this time?’ And he said, ‘I did the best of anyone, and things would have gone badly without me.’ That only made them laugh at him more.”

The king said to his daughter, “I’ll announce a great feast that will last three days, and you will throw a golden apple. Maybe the unknown man will show himself.” When the feast was proclaimed, the young man went out to the forest and called for Iron Hans. “What do you want?” asked the wild man. “I want to catch the king’s daughter’s golden apple.” “Consider it yours already,” said Iron Hans. “You’ll also have a suit of red armor for the day, and a spirited chestnut horse to ride.” When the day came, the young man galloped to the field and took his place among the knights, and no one recognized him. The king’s daughter stepped forward and threw a golden apple to the knights. None of them caught it except him, and the moment he had it he galloped away.

On the second day Iron Hans dressed him as a white knight and gave him a white horse. Once more he was the only one to catch the apple, and he didn’t stay a moment, but galloped off with it. The king became angry. “This is not allowed,” he said. “He must come before me and tell me his name.” He ordered that if the knight who caught the apple rode away again, they were to go after him, and if he refused to come back willingly, they were to cut him down and stab him.

On the third day Iron Hans gave him a suit of black armor and a black horse, and once more he caught the apple. But as he rode away with it, the king’s attendants chased him, and one of them came so close that the point of his sword wounded the young man in the leg. Still, he got away from them. But his horse bucked so wildly that the helmet fell off his head, and they saw that he had golden hair. They rode back and told the king.

The next day the king’s daughter asked the gardener about his boy. “He’s out working in the garden. That odd fellow went to the festival too, and only came home last evening. He’s even shown my children three golden apples that he won.”

The king had him called in, and he came with his little cap on his head again. But the king’s daughter went up to him and took it off, and his golden hair fell down over his shoulders. He was so handsome that everyone was amazed. “Are you the knight who came to the festival every day, always in different colors, and caught the three golden apples?” asked the king. “Yes,” he answered, “and here are the apples.” He took them out of his pocket and gave them back to the king. “If you want more proof, you can see the wound your men gave me when they chased me. And I am also the knight who helped you win the victory over your enemies.” “If you can do deeds like that, you are no gardener’s boy. Tell me, who is your father?” “My father is a mighty king, and I have as much gold as I could ever need.” “I can see that I owe you my thanks,” said the king. “Is there anything I can do to please you?” “Yes,” he answered, “there is. Give me your daughter for my wife.” The young woman laughed and said, “He doesn’t stand on ceremony, does he? But I had already seen from his golden hair that he was no gardener’s boy.” Then she went and kissed him. His father and mother came to the wedding and were overjoyed, for they had given up all hope of ever seeing their dear son again. And as they sat at the wedding feast, the music suddenly stopped, the doors opened, and a stately king walked in with a great retinue. He went up to the young man, embraced him, and said, “I am Iron Hans. I was turned into a wild man by enchantment, but you have set me free. All the treasures I own shall be yours.”

chapters.title: Cat-Skin
paragraphs: Once there was a king whose queen had hair of the purest gold. She was so beautiful that no one like her could be found anywhere on earth. But the beautiful queen fell ill, and when she felt that she was close to death, she called the king to her and said, “Promise me that you will never marry again, unless you find a wife who is as beautiful as I am and has golden hair like mine.” The king, in his grief, promised everything she asked. Then she closed her eyes and died. The king could not be comforted, and for a long time he never thought of taking another wife. At last, though, his wise men said, “This cannot go on. The king must marry again, so that we can have a queen.” So messengers were sent far and wide to look for a bride as beautiful as the dead queen. But there was no princess in the world so beautiful, and even if there had been, there wasn’t one to be found with golden hair. So the messengers came home, and all their trouble had been for nothing.

Now the king had a daughter who was every bit as beautiful as her mother and had the same golden hair. When she had grown up, the king looked at her and saw that she was just like the dead queen. Then he said to his courtiers, “May I not marry my daughter? She is the very image of my dead wife. If I can’t have her, I won’t find a bride anywhere on earth, and you tell me there must be a queen.” When the courtiers heard this, they were horrified. “Heaven forbid that a father should marry his daughter!” they said. “No good can come out of so great a sin.” His daughter was horrified too, but she hoped the king would soon give up such thoughts. So she said to him, “Before I marry anyone, I must have three dresses: one of gold, like the sun, another of shining silver, like the moon, and a third as dazzling as the stars. And I want a cloak made of a thousand different kinds of fur sewn together, to which every animal in the kingdom must give a piece of its skin.” She thought this would make him forget the matter. But the king had the most skilled workmen in his kingdom weave the three dresses, one golden like the sun, one silvery like the moon, and one sparkling like the stars. His hunters were ordered to track down every animal in the kingdom and take the finest fur from its skin, and so a cloak of a thousand furs was made.

When everything was ready, the king sent it all to her. But in the night, while everyone was asleep, she got up and took three of her trinkets, a gold ring, a gold necklace, and a gold brooch. She packed the three dresses, of the sun, the moon, and the stars, into a nutshell, wrapped herself in the cloak of all kinds of fur, and smeared her face and hands with soot. Then she commended herself to Heaven in her need and went away. She walked all night until at last she reached a large forest. She was very tired, so she sat down in the hollow of a tree and soon fell asleep, and she slept on until midday.

Now the king who owned the forest was hunting in it, and his dogs came to the tree. They began to sniff around, run in circles, and bark. “Be quick,” said the king to his huntsmen, “and see what kind of game is lying there.” The huntsmen went up to the tree, and when they came back they said, “In the hollow of the tree there’s a most wonderful animal, unlike anything we’ve ever seen. Its skin seems to be made of a thousand kinds of fur, but it’s lying there fast asleep.” “See if you can catch it alive,” said the king, “and we’ll take it with us.” So the huntsmen lifted it up, and the girl woke up, terribly frightened, and said, “I’m a poor child with no father or mother left. Have pity on me and take me with you.” Then they said, “All right, Miss Cat-skin, you’ll do for the kitchen. You can sweep up the ashes and do that sort of thing.” They put her in the coach and took her to the king’s palace. There they showed her a little corner under the staircase, where no daylight ever came, and said, “Cat-skin, you can lie down and sleep there.” Then she was sent into the kitchen, where she was made to fetch wood and water, blow on the fire, pluck the poultry, pick over the herbs, sift the ashes, and do all the dirty work.

So Cat-skin lived for a long time in great sorrow. “Ah, pretty princess,” she thought, “what will become of you now?” But one day a feast was to be held in the king’s castle, and she said to the cook, “May I go up for a little while and see what’s happening? I’ll be careful and stay behind the door.” The cook said, “Yes, you may go, but be back in half an hour to rake out the ashes.” Then she took her little lamp and went into her cabin, took off the fur skin, and washed the soot from her face and hands, so that her beauty shone out like the sun from behind the clouds. Next she opened her nutshell and took out the dress that shone like the sun, and so she went to the feast. Everyone made way for her, because nobody knew her, and they thought she must be nothing less than a king’s daughter. The king came up to her, held out his hand, and danced with her, and he thought to himself, “I have never seen anyone half so beautiful.”

When the dance ended she curtsied, and when the king looked around for her, she had vanished, and no one knew where. The guards posted at the castle gate were summoned, but they had seen nobody. The truth was that she had run to her little cabin, pulled off her gown, blackened her face and hands, thrown on the fur cloak, and turned back into Cat-skin.
