She went into the kitchen to start her work and began raking out the ashes, but the cook said, “Leave that until morning and heat the king’s soup. I’d like to run upstairs and take a peek myself. But be careful not to let a single hair fall into it, or you’ll never eat again.”

As soon as the cook had gone, Cat-skin heated the king’s soup. She toasted a slice of bread first, as well as she possibly could, and when the soup was ready she went to the cabin, fetched her little golden ring, and dropped it into the bowl. When the dancing was over, the king called for his soup, and he liked it so much that he thought he had never tasted anything so good. At the bottom of the bowl he saw a gold ring. He could not work out how it had got there, so he ordered the cook to be brought in. The cook was terrified at the summons and told Cat-skin, “A hair must have fallen into the soup. If it did, you’re in for a good beating.” Then he went before the king, who asked him who had made the soup. “I did,” said the cook. But the king replied, “That’s not true. It was better than anything you could make.” So the cook confessed, “To tell the truth, I didn’t make it. Cat-skin did.” “Then send Cat-skin up,” said the king. When she came, he asked her, “Who are you?” “I’m a poor child,” she said, “who has lost both her father and her mother.” “How did you come to be in my palace?” he asked. “I’m good for nothing,” she said, “except to be a scullery girl and have boots and shoes thrown at my head.” “But how did you get the ring that was in the soup?” asked the king. She would not admit to knowing anything about the ring, so the king sent her back to her work.

Some time later there was another feast, and Cat-skin asked the cook to let her go up and watch, as before. “Yes,” he said, “but come back in half an hour and cook the king the soup he likes so much.” She ran to her little cabin, quickly washed herself, took out the dress that was silver like the moon, and put it on. When she walked in, looking like a king’s daughter, the king came straight over, delighted to see her again, and when the dancing began he danced with her. When the dance was over she slipped away so cleverly that the king never saw where she went. She dashed into her cabin, turned herself back into Cat-skin, and went to the kitchen to make the soup. While the cook was upstairs, she took the golden necklace and dropped it into the soup. It was carried to the king, who ate it and liked it as much as before, and he sent for the cook, who again had to tell him that Cat-skin had made it. Cat-skin was brought before the king once more, but she still said she was only fit to have boots and shoes thrown at her head.

When the king ordered a feast for the third time, everything happened just as before. “You must be a witch, Cat-skin,” said the cook. “You always put something in your soup that makes the king like it better than mine.” Still, he let her go up as before. She put on the dress that glittered like the stars and went into the ballroom in it, and the king danced with her again and thought she had never looked so lovely. While they danced, he slid a gold ring onto her finger without her noticing, and he gave orders that the dance should go on for a long time. When it finally ended, he tried to hold her fast by the hand, but she tore free and darted so quickly through the crowd that he lost sight of her. She ran as fast as she could to her little cabin under the stairs. But this time she had stayed too long, well past the half hour, so there was no time to take off her fine dress. She threw her fur cloak over it, and in her hurry she did not blacken herself all over with soot, but left one finger white.

Then she ran into the kitchen and made the king’s soup, and as soon as the cook was gone, she put the golden brooch into the bowl. When the king reached the bottom, he had Cat-skin called once more, and right away he saw the white finger and the ring he had put on it during the dance. He seized her hand and held on tight, and when she tried to wrench herself free and run, the fur cloak slipped a little to one side, and the starry dress glittered underneath.

Then he grabbed the fur and ripped it off. Her golden hair and lovely figure were revealed, and she could hide no longer. She washed the soot and ashes from her face and showed herself to be the most beautiful princess on earth. The king said, “You are my beloved bride, and we will never be parted again.” The wedding feast was held, and it was as merry a day as anyone ever heard of or saw in that country, or in any other.

chapters.title: Snow-White and Rose-Red
paragraphs: Once there was a poor widow who lived in a lonely cottage. In front of the cottage was a garden with two rose trees growing in it, one with white roses and the other with red. She had two children who were like the two rose trees. One was named Snow-white and the other Rose-red. They were as good and happy, as busy and cheerful, as any two children in the world, except that Snow-white was quieter and gentler than Rose-red. Rose-red preferred to run through the meadows and fields, looking for flowers and chasing butterflies, while Snow-white stayed home with her mother, helping with the housework or reading aloud when there was nothing to do.

The two children loved each other so much that they always held hands when they went out together. When Snow-white said, “We will never leave each other,” Rose-red answered, “Not as long as we live,” and their mother would add, “Whatever one has, she must share with the other.”

They often wandered through the forest by themselves, picking red berries, and none of the animals harmed them. Instead the animals came up to them without fear. The little hare ate cabbage leaves from their hands, the deer grazed beside them, the stag bounded cheerfully past, and the birds sat still on the branches and sang every song they knew.

Nothing bad ever happened to them. If they stayed in the forest too late and night fell, they lay down next to each other on the moss and slept until morning. Their mother knew this and never worried about them.

Once, after they had spent the night in the woods, the dawn woke them, and they saw a beautiful child in a shining white robe sitting near their bed. He stood up and gave them a very kind look, but said nothing and walked off into the forest. When they looked around, they found they had been sleeping right beside a cliff, and in the darkness they would certainly have fallen over it if they had gone just a few steps farther. Their mother told them it must have been the angel who watches over good children.

Snow-white and Rose-red kept their mother’s little cottage so tidy that it was a joy to look inside. In summer Rose-red looked after the house, and every morning, before her mother woke, she laid a wreath of flowers beside her bed, with one rose from each tree. In winter Snow-white lit the fire and hung the kettle on the hob. The kettle was brass, and it was polished so well that it shone like gold. In the evening, when snowflakes were falling, the mother would say, “Snow-white, go and bolt the door.” Then they sat around the hearth, and the mother put on her spectacles and read aloud from a big book, while the two girls listened and spun. Close beside them a lamb lay on the floor, and behind them a white dove perched with its head tucked under its wing.

One evening, as they sat cozily together like this, someone knocked at the door, as if wanting to be let in. The mother said, “Quick, Rose-red, open the door. It must be a traveler looking for shelter.” Rose-red went and slid back the bolt, thinking it was a poor man. But it was not. It was a bear, and he poked his broad black head in through the door.

Rose-red screamed and jumped back, the lamb bleated, the dove fluttered, and Snow-white hid behind her mother’s bed. But the bear began to speak. “Don’t be afraid,” he said. “I won’t hurt you! I’m half frozen, and I only want to warm up a little next to you.”

“Poor bear,” said the mother. “Lie down by the fire, but be careful not to singe your fur.” Then she called, “Snow-white, Rose-red, come out. The bear won’t hurt you. He means well.” So they both came out, and little by little the lamb and the dove came closer too and stopped being afraid of him. The bear said, “Children, come and beat the snow out of my coat a little.” They fetched the broom and swept the bear’s hide clean, and he stretched out by the fire and growled happily and contentedly. Before long they felt completely at home and played tricks on their clumsy guest. They tugged his fur with their hands, put their feet on his back and rolled him around, or took a hazel switch and whacked him, and when he growled, they laughed. The bear took it all in good humor, and only when they got too rough did he call out, “Spare my life, children,

Snow-white, Rose-red,
Would you knock your suitor dead?”

At bedtime, when the rest went off to bed, the mother told the bear, “Stay right there by the hearth. You’ll be safe from the cold and the foul weather.” At first light the two girls let him out, and he padded away over the snow and into the forest.

From then on the bear came every evening at the same hour, lay down by the hearth, and let the children play with him as much as they wanted. They grew so used to him that the door was never bolted until their black friend had arrived.

When spring came and everything outside was green, the bear said to Snow-white one morning, “Now I have to leave, and I can’t come back all summer.” “Where are you going, dear bear?” asked Snow-white. “I have to go into the forest to guard my treasures from the wicked dwarfs. In winter, when the ground is frozen hard, they have to stay underground and can’t dig their way out. But now that the sun has thawed and warmed the earth, they break through and come out to pry and steal. And whatever falls into their hands and goes into their caves doesn’t easily see daylight again.”

Snow-white was very sad to see him go. As she unbolted the door for him and the bear hurried out, he snagged on the bolt and a piece of his hairy coat was torn away. It seemed to Snow-white that she saw gold shining through it, but she wasn’t sure. The bear bounded off and was soon out of sight among the trees.

Not long afterward, the mother sent her children into the forest to gather firewood. There they found a large tree lying felled on the ground, and next to the trunk something was hopping back and forth in the grass, though they could not tell what it was. As they drew closer, they saw a dwarf with an old, shriveled face and a snow-white beard a yard long. The tip of the beard was stuck in a crack in the tree, and the little fellow was leaping about like a dog on a leash, with no idea what to do.

He glared at the girls with his fiery red eyes and shouted, “What are you standing there for? Can’t you come over and help me?” “What happened, little man?” asked Rose-red. “You stupid, nosy goose!” the dwarf answered. “I was going to split the tree to get a bit of wood for cooking. Heavy logs burn up the little food we have right away. We don’t gobble down as much as you coarse, greedy people. I had driven the wedge in safely, and everything was going as I wanted, but the cursed wedge was too smooth and suddenly popped out, and the tree snapped shut so fast that I couldn’t pull out my beautiful white beard. Now it’s stuck tight and I can’t get away, and you silly, sleek, milk-faced things laugh! Ugh, how hateful you are!”

The children tried hard, but they could not pull the beard out. It was stuck too fast. “I’ll run and get someone,” said Rose-red. “You senseless goose!” snarled the dwarf. “Why would you fetch someone? There are already two of you too many for me. Can’t you think of something better?” “Don’t be so impatient,” said Snow-white. “I’ll help you.” She took her scissors out of her pocket and snipped off the end of the beard.

As soon as the dwarf felt free, he grabbed a sack lying among the roots of the tree, which was full of gold, and hoisted it up, grumbling to himself, “Rude people, cutting off a piece of my fine beard. Bad luck to you!” Then he swung the sack onto his back and left without so much as a glance at the children.

Some time later, Snow-white and Rose-red went to catch a dish of fish. As they came near the brook, they saw something like a big grasshopper hopping toward the water, as if it meant to jump in. They ran over and found that it was the dwarf. “Where are you going?” said Rose-red. “Surely you don’t want to go into the water?” “I’m not such a fool!” cried the dwarf. “Can’t you see that this cursed fish is trying to pull me in?” The little man had been sitting there fishing, and unluckily the wind had tangled his beard in the fishing line. A moment later a big fish bit, and the feeble creature did not have the strength to haul it out. The fish had the upper hand and was dragging the dwarf toward it. He clung to every reed and rush, but it did little good, for he had to follow the fish’s movements, and he was in terrible danger of being pulled into the water.

The girls got there just in time. They grabbed hold of him and tried to work his beard loose from the fishing line, but it was no use: beard and line were hopelessly tangled together. The only thing left was to take out the scissors and snip the beard, and a small piece of it was lost that way. When the dwarf saw this, he shrieked: “Is that any way to behave, you toadstools, disfiguring a man’s face like that? Wasn’t it bad enough that you trimmed the tip of my beard? Now you’ve hacked off the best part! I can’t let my own people see me like this. I wish you had been made to run the soles off your shoes!” Then he picked up a sack of pearls that was lying in the rushes, and without another word he hauled it off and vanished behind a stone.

Not long afterward, the mother sent the two girls into town to buy needles and thread, along with laces and ribbons. Their road took them over a heath scattered with huge chunks of rock. There they spotted a big bird hanging in the air, circling slowly above them. It sank lower and lower, and finally came down beside a rock not far off. At that moment they heard a sharp, pitiful scream. They ran over and saw, to their horror, that an eagle had seized their old acquaintance the dwarf and was about to carry him away.

Full of pity, the children immediately grabbed the little man and held on tight, pulling against the eagle until it finally let go of its prey. As soon as the dwarf had gotten over his first scare, he squeaked in his shrill voice: “Couldn’t you have been more careful? You yanked at my brown coat until it’s all torn and full of holes, you clumsy things!” Then he picked up a sack full of precious stones and slipped back under the rock into his hole. The girls were used to his ingratitude by now, so they went on their way and took care of their errands in town.

On their way home they crossed the heath again, and there they came upon the dwarf. He had tipped out his bag of precious stones on a clean patch of ground, never imagining that anyone would come by so late. The evening sun shone on the gems, and they glittered and sparkled in every color so beautifully that the children stopped and stared. “What are you standing there gawking for?” shouted the dwarf, and his ash-gray face turned copper-red with fury. He was still cursing when they heard a loud growl, and a black bear came trotting out of the forest toward them. The dwarf jumped up in terror, but he could not make it to his cave, because the bear was already too near. Then, in the fear of his heart, he cried out: “Dear Mr Bear, spare me! I’ll give you all my treasures. Look at those beautiful jewels lying there! Let me live. What do you want with a skinny little fellow like me? You would hardly feel me between your teeth. Here, take these two wicked girls instead. They’re tender morsels, as plump as young quails. For mercy’s sake, eat them!” The bear paid no attention to his words. He gave the wicked creature a single blow with his paw, and the dwarf never moved again.

The girls had run off, but the bear called after them: “Snow-white and Rose-red, don’t be afraid. Wait, I’ll come with you.” They recognized his voice and stopped, and when he reached them, his bearskin suddenly dropped away, and there stood a handsome man, dressed all in gold. “I am a king’s son,” he said, “and that wicked dwarf, who had stolen my treasures, put a spell on me. I had to roam the forest as a wild bear until his death set me free. Now he has received the punishment he deserved.”

Snow-white married the prince, and Rose-red married his brother, and the two couples shared the great treasure that the dwarf had piled up in his cave. The old mother lived on peacefully and happily with her children for many years. She took the two rose trees with her, and they stood in front of her window, and every year they bore the most beautiful roses, white and red.
